Uniform Title: Nigamasāranirṇaya Author: Rāmāramaṇadeva Manuscript: NGMCP manuscript no. 3-333 Reel No.: B 129/5

Description: Description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski: The *Kālikula* is the most ancient of all the Trika systems, and it is considered the very foundation of the entire Trika tradition. It is said that the *Kālikula* was revealed by the goddess Kālī herself to the sage Durvāsas, who then transmitted it to the lineage of the Siddhas. This system is characterized by its emphasis on the worship of the Goddess as the primordial power (*mūlakalā*) and its focus on the practice of the *krama*, which involves the sequential unfolding of the cycles of consciousness. The *Kālikula* is divided into two main branches: the *Kālikula* proper and the *Krama*. The former is further subdivided into the *Vijñānabhairava*, the *Tantrasadbhāva*, and the *Triśirobhairava*. The *Krama* branch, on the other hand, is known for its elaborate ritual cycles and its complex system of visualization (*dhyāna*) and phonemic emanation (*varṇodaya*). The central teaching of the *Kālikula* is the doctrine of the three powers (*triprakriyā*), namely: *icchā* (will), *jñāna* (knowledge), and *kriyā* (action). These powers are understood to be the dynamic aspects of the Supreme Reality, which manifests as the universe through their interplay. The ultimate goal of this system is the realization of the identity between the individual soul (*ātman*) and the universal consciousness (*paramātman*), achieved through the integration of these three powers within one's own being. The *Kālikula* is also renowned for its esoteric practices, including the ritual of the *cakrasaṃkrama* (the transference of consciousness through the centers of energy) and the consumption of the five *makāras* (liquor, meat, fish, grain, and sexual union) as means of attaining liberation while remaining in the world. Through these methods, the practitioner seeks to transcend dualistic perception and attain the state of *anuttara* (the unsurpassed), wherein all distinctions dissolve into the undifferentiated light of consciousness.

The term *nigama*—used for Tantra in general as opposed to *āgama* for the Veda—emerges in the later period of the development of Śākta Tantra after the 13th century. It came to denote more specifically the Kaula Śākta Tantra. Accordingly, we find a considerable number of Kaula works that incorporate this term into their titles. Examples include the *Nigamalatātantra*, the *Nigamakalpadruma*, the *Nigamatattvasāra*, and this work, the *Nigamasāranirṇaya*, by Ramāramaṇadeva. This text primarily deals with the worship of Kaula goddesses. The rituals are drawn from a variety of sources, which Ramāramaṇa first quotes and then comments upon. He thus attempts to present the *nirṇaya* (definitive conclusion), which is the *sāra* (essence) of the *nigama*. He quotes the *Tantrakaumudī*, written by Govinda Thakkur, who served as the court paṇḍit to Malladeva Naranārāyaṇa, the 16th-century king of Kūcabihāra. Consequently, the *Nigamasāranirṇaya* could not have been composed prior to that time. Most of the Tantras he cites belong to the period between the 13th or 14th century and the 16th. An exception is the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*, which likely dates to the 11th century. These include: [The list of cited texts follows.]

The *Phetkāriṇītantra*, *Vāmkeśvaratantra*, *Vārāhītantra*, *Mṛḍālītantra*, *Agastyasaṃhitā*, *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitātantra*, *Kālītantra*, *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, *Tantrakaumudī*, *Gandharvatantra*, *Jñānārṇava*, *Bālātantra*, *Bhairavatantra*, *Kubjikātantra*, *Svatantratantra*, and *Kumārītantra*.

Although, as is customary, this work is primarily concerned with ritual, Rāmāramaṇa also occasionally discusses related matters. One interesting example is his discussion of the coherence and consistency (*ekavākyatā*) of the Tantras.
