Country of Publication: India Oṃ, salutations to Her and to Gaṇeśa!
Within the pores of whose body, millions of universes are like insects.
We take refuge in that ocean of compassion, unfathomable and boundless.
Having bowed to his Guru, his supreme Guru known as Parāpara, and the Guru who is even beyond that,
this venerable Ramarama extracts the essence from the ocean of all the scriptures and compiles these subjects;
for a person, having gone to various distant places, gathers diverse things from those most remote regions.
Through diligent efforts, when these [factors] converge in one place and are obtained before one by destiny, who among the wise would turn away?
In this regard, first, after having worshipped the deities, the deliberation on mantras proceeds; therefore, for the sake of that determination, the *Purohara-cakra* is here described.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the unsurpassed Hara-cakra;
by knowing which, one becomes possessed of knowledge in this world and the best among those who know mantras.
"Otherwise, one should avoid the mantra," the Blessed Lord Śiva has said eternally;
therefore, the wise person who would investigate [this] should do so with every effort.
One should construct the *kṣatra* of the gods, provided with star-cells;
in its center, one should divide four cells with colored threads.
One should cast Durgā, Vāṇī, Tārā, and Bhairavī into the directions; then, situated upon the ear-line, one should join them starting from Īśāna on both sides.
Tripurā, Bhuvaneśī, Pīṭheśī, and Tryambaka;
Vāsudeva, Śrī, Chinnamastā, and Caṇḍikā.
One should worship Vivasvat beginning with Īśāna in sequence, followed by Vatvaritā,
Indrākṣī, Vahneramba, and immediately thereafter Pitāmaha.
One should draw Mahāmāyā, Kālī, and whatever other deity there may be, as well as the fifty letters, starting from the northeast square and so forth, in due order.
1b) The name bestowed by the mother and father, refined by Vedic mantras,
should be applied to all rites, as well as to the examination of weapons and their corresponding mantras.
Starting from the letter *nā* up to the range of the letter *deva*,
one should perform the recitation when they are completely purified, but never when they are impure.
He is both relative and son, yet greed and death; he is both agitated liberation and bliss, as well as Dharma, the enemy, the friend, and the granter of desires.
One should contemplate the terrifying "Koṣṭhacakra" (the wheel of compartments).
Having drawn a wheel consisting of twelve compartments like a zodiacal circle (*rāśicakra*), one should inscribe the four [deities] beginning with Durgā in the cardinal directions.

Having written [the names] beginning with Tripurā and ending with Candra in the corners starting from the northeast (īśāna), one should then write the fifty letters beginning with 'A' in a clockwise sequence starting from the northeast corner. In whichever square the first letter of the month falls, one should proceed clockwise through the twelve squares beginning with Bandhu in that square.

One should contemplate this in sequence. Herein, whatever is the name of a square, that is the form of the deity residing in that square; its capacity to bestow results follows from specific designations—this is the summary.

Having thus introduced the determination of the deities, since even a single deity may possess multiple colors, the *Cakra* (Wheel/Diagram) is now described for the purpose of determining which deity presides over which mantra. In that regard, [the deities are assigned] to two, three, eleven, nine, two, twelve, ten, six, eight, sixteen, fourteen, five, and one [syllables], as well as to the netherworld (*pātāla*).
Then the wise one, O Śambhu, should inscribe fifteen [syllables] one by one in the compartments of fire (three) and the moon (one), in due order;
he should inscribe the letters within a square consisting of four compartments.
Starting from the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa', [one should place them] according to the first letter of one's own name.
2a) The mantra-practitioner should determine the categories beginning with *siddha*, and again, he should act by means of those beginning with *siddha*.
A *siddha* mantra bestows success through recitation; a *sādhya* [mantra] is [accomplished] by means of oblations and so forth.
By the mere attainment [of the mantra], Susiddhi becomes an enemy to the practitioner;
Siddha syllables are to be known as kinsmen, while Sādhya syllables are remembered as servants.
Those that are well-perfected (susiddha) are to be known as nourishers, while those that are enemies (śatru) are considered destroyers;
in the house of perfection (siddhakoṣṭha), according to what has been stated, the practitioner attains success through doubling [the effort].

The *Siddha-susiddha* [yoga] leads to partial victory; the *Siddhāri* destroys one's kinsmen. From the *Dviguṇa* [yoga], there is success in what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), whereas the *Sādhyasādhya* is fruitless.

A *sādhya* [mantra] becomes well-accomplished (*susiddha*) by half the recitation; a *sādhya-ari* (enemy of the sādhya) destroys one's kinsmen. A *susiddha-siddha* [mantra] becomes well-accomplished by half the recitation, and a *susiddhi-sādhya* by double that amount.
A well-accomplished [mantra] becomes well-accomplished at that very moment; it is said that an enemy [mantra] destroys one's caste.
A well-accomplished [mantra] destroys the wife, while an enemy [mantra] is likewise a foe that destroys oneself.
An *arisiddha* [enemy] would destroy the *sūtra*, whereas an *arisādhya* [enemy to be subdued] would destroy one's desire;
this is determined by the initial letter of one's own name according to the clockwise sequence.

Having drawn a square wheel consisting of sixteen compartments, one should inscribe the fifty letters there in order from Indra (the east) to Agni (the southeast). Then, starting from whichever compartment one's own first name-letter falls upon, four compartments are the *siddha* (accomplished) squares, and the four compartments to their right are the *sādhya* (to-be-accomplished) squares.

The four squares to its west are the *susiddha* (well-accomplished) squares; the four squares to its north are the *ari* (enemy) squares. Within those same four *siddha* squares, there is the square for the letters of the name, which is the *siddha-siddha* square. To its south is the *siddha-sādhya* square, and to its west is the [next] square.
Siddha-susiddha follows that; likewise, Siddhāri, Sādhya, and so forth—these four names [are applied] to each of the four squares of the Sādhya [section]. (2b)

Thus, in the *susiddha* square as well, there is a set of four names beginning with *susiddha* and *susiddha*; likewise, in the *ari* square, there is a set of four names beginning with *arisiddha*. This constitutes sixteen squares. Among them, *susiddhi* and *susiddha* are most excellent; *susiddha* and [the other] are more excellent; and *siddha* is excellent.

The *sādhyasusiddha* and *siddhasādhya* types are favorable for oneself, though their success comes only after a long time; however, the *ari* type and others are forbidden in all squares, as they must be entirely avoided by an enemy— this is the summary.
Now, the wheel of the unmade.

One should draw two lines from east to west; then, piercing through the center between them, one should pierce [the other lines] in sequence from Maheśa (north) to Rakṣodhipati (south), and likewise from Vāyu (northwest) to Hutāśana (southeast).

One should write the vowels beginning with *a* (the "impotent" vowels) such that *a*, *ka*, *ḍa*, and *ma* reside in the first square; even here, the *siddha* and other classes of mantras are present. Furthermore, by means of those four [groups] in their respective order, and again by those three, one's own name—starting from the first letter and ending with the final letter of the mantra—is to be written, encircled by them. By that, two lines are formed from east to west.
By the word "should perform," the zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*) consisting of six or twelve compartments is formed. Having written the letters beginning with *ka*, excluding *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*,

starting from the first letter of one's own name up to the first letter of the mantra, [one determines] the *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* [categories] within those respective compartments.

The meaning is that one should purify [the elements] in sequence. Thus, in the determination of mantras according to the sequence beginning with the Siddhas, one should join and apply the vowels and mantras; for that purpose, the zodiacal wheel (*rāśicakra*) is drawn: *a, ā, i, ī* shall be Aries;
*u, ū, ṛ* is known as Taurus; *ṝ, ḷ, ḹ* is declared to be Gemini; *e, ai* is Cancer.
Smṛta is [the letter] *o*; *au* is Siṃha; *ñaṃ* and *aḥ* are Śa, Ṣa, and Sa; *phala* is Kṣa; and *ca* is Kanyā.
3a) The *ka*-group is said to be Libra, and the *ca*-group is Scorpio;
the *ṭa*-group is the bow-bearer (Sagittarius), and the *ta*-group is remembered as Capricorn.
The letter-group *pa* is called Kumbha (Aquarius), and the letter-group *ya* is known as Mīna (Pisces).
Relatives are said to reside in the first, ninth, fifth, and tenth houses from one's own sign.
Two planets situated in the sixth and tenth houses are proclaimed as servants;
those situated in the third, seventh, and eleventh houses are proclaimed as nourishers.
It is determined that the twelfth, eighth, and fourth houses are destroyers;
they correspond respectively to the ascendant, wealth, brothers, enemies, children, kinsmen, and wife.

Death, dharma, action, and expenditure are the twelve signs [of the zodiac]. Thus, having drawn the wheel of signs (*rāśicakra*), one then considers the ascendant, wealth, and so forth, starting from one's own sign, or from the sign corresponding to the first letter of one's name. Here too, the result corresponds to the name. As it is said in another tantra:

Having written the letters starting with *va* (the six vowels) in the zodiac signs beginning with Aries— counting two, two, three, four, three, five, five, and four [syllables] for each sign— one should contemplate them as being inscribed upon a young woman. Furthermore, the fifth, ninth, or tenth house from one's own natal sign becomes a "kinsman" sign when joined by the second house.
The sixth [syllable] would be the servant; if it is measured by the number of Rudras (eleven), fires (three), and natural notes (six), it is considered the nourisher in the Tantra itself;
and the mantra measured by twelve, eight, and four is remembered as the killer.

Thus, because of the necessity of the Nakṣatra-cakra, and since the Gaṇa-śuddhi-cakra is included within it, it is also inscribed here. A Ā [Aśvinī] is the divine (deva) class; I Bha [Bharaṇī] is remembered as human (nara); Ī U Ū [Kṛttikā] is proclaimed to be demonic (rākṣasa); Ṛ Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ [Rohiṇī] is proclaimed to be human (manuṣya).
3b) Thus, O King, Mṛgaśirā is considered divine; Ārdrā is remembered as human; and likewise, by its very nature, Punarvasū consists of the two vowels *o* and *au*, which are divine.
Puṣya is known as divine, Āśleṣā as belonging to the birds (khaga), and Maghā is remembered as belonging to the Rākṣasas.
The syllables Gha and Ṅa likewise belong to the Rākṣasas, while Pūrvaphālgunī belongs to humans.
Chitra and Uttara-phalgunī are remembered as human;
Svāti, Hasta, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla are Rākṣasa.
Ḍa and sva are declared as Nirjara; ḍha and ṇa are Viśākhā, which is Rākṣasa; and ta, tha, da, and ca are Anurādhā, proclaimed as the Deva group.
Dha is said to be the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, a Rākṣasa; na-ya-pa is Mūlā, a Rākṣasa;
va is Pūrvāṣāḍhā, belonging to humans; and uttarāṣāḍhaka is a human.
The host of gods is in Aśvinī, while Rākṣasa is in Dhaniṣṭhā;
likewise, the Rakṣas is in Śatabhiṣā, and the Vasus are in the two Pūrvabhādrapadās.
The human class is proclaimed as ṣa, sa, ha, u, tt, rā, bh, ā, dro;
and the divine class is proclaimed as aṃ, aḥ, la, kṣā, and revatī.

Birth, prosperity, adversity, security, enmity, accomplishment, slaughter, friendship, and supreme friendship—these states, beginning with birth, recur again and again. Among gods, asuras, and humans, there is great enmity among asuras and great affection among humans. One should know that the celestial state is the highest by its own qualities, while the human state is middling.

If the deity of enmity (*vairadaitya*) is among the gods, death occurs; if it is among humans or *asuras*, [the result is likewise]. Where the Guru, the Mantra-syllables, and the deities reside within a single *nāḍī*, one should predict the results of hatred, disease, and death in that order. This is determined by starting from one's own natal asterism (*svanakṣatra*) and calculating the asterism of the mantra-syllables, following the sequence of birth, prosperity, and so forth.

One should purify it. As it is stated in another tantra: "The [elements] consisting of two fortnights, one, three, years, forms (0), earth (1), arms (2), moon (1), yugas (4), pairs (2), earth (1), and pairs (2)...

Two, one, two, one, two, three, one, three, seven, ten, one, one, two, one, and three fires (three)—these are declared here as the letters in order starting from Aśvinī; for the remaining asterisms, there are the bindu and visarga. From the sky (the letter *kha*), one should then calculate the birth and prosperity in their respective order.
In this manner, having determined one's own birth star (*nakṣatra*) even in the *Gaṇa-śuddhi-cakra*, one should contemplate it there alongside the number of mantra syllables;

in that purity, the mantra bestows the desired fruit—this is the summary. Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭpada-cakra* as well, because of the hearing of censure, that too must necessarily be examined; therefore, it is also written here. And the *Ṣaṭpada* is:
Having written the sequence [of letters] starting from the east and proceeding through the directions,
one should write the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣ*, one by one.
The investigation begins from whichever letter corresponds to the first syllable of one's own name.
When it has risen, its fruit is desirable; in the second [period], there is the destruction of calamities;
in the third, one should know there is steadfastness; and in the fourth, conflict with kinsmen.
In the fifth [day] one would become of a doubting nature; in the sixth, a destroyer of all.
This is its meaning.
Having fashioned a six-petaled wheel, one should write the fifty letters upon the petals starting from the east and so forth;

then, beginning from the first letter of one's own name up to the first letter of the mantra, one should investigate [the result]. The summary of the fruit is as follows: "The fruit is joy," and so on.

Thus, even in the *varga-śuddhi* wheel, because the fifth house of one's own *varga* is designated as an enemy, that too must certainly be considered. Garuḍa, lion, cat, snake, rat, elephant, and hare—these are declared to be the lords of the *vargas*; [an asterism] situated five places from its own *varga* is an enemy.
Kalāsvara is Vainateya; the ka-group is said to be Ruci. The ca-group is called Siṃha, and the ṭa-group is proclaimed to be Śvā.
The *va*-group is to be known as the serpent (*bhujaga*); the *ya*-group is also called the demon (*āsu*).
The *ya*-group is the intoxicated elephant (*mattamātaṅga*); such is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures.

The letter *śa*-group is declared to be the rabbit (*śaśaka*); the fifth from one's own group is the enemy. The meaning of this is as follows: [the animals corresponding to the groups starting from the first letter of one's name are] the bird, the cat, the mongoose, the dog, the snake, the elephant, and so forth.
The rabbit (the letter *śa*) is, in sequence, of the same class as the letters beginning with *a*, while the others are of different classes.

Thus, when the mantra has been determined by all the wheels (*cakras*), it is said that "the mantra bestows fruit when it is a debtor" (*ṛṇī*); therefore, the sequence of the debtor and the creditor is now written down.

One should calculate the fifteen squares [of the grid] by multiplying them by eighteen, eight, and seven; then, one should multiply the letters of the practitioner's name by ten, nine, seven, four, eight, seven, four, six, and three. Furthermore, two vowels each are placed within the five auspicious squares.

The remainder [of the calculation] is the tone (*svara*); divide the remaining [number] by six, and divide the remainder again by eight; the remainder that remains is the *ṛṇinī*. This is the meaning [of the verse].
Having written [the grid] by multiplying eleven squares by four,

having written the ten vowels in pairs in the first and eleventh squares, having written the remaining vowels one by one, and having written the consonants beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'pha' in the remaining squares, [one should contemplate] the meaning of the mantra above.

Having written the eleven examiners' marks beginning with *dig-bhū* (102), one should sum those numbers and divide by eight; whichever remainder is greater is the debtor (*ṛṇī*). By this, the mantra itself should be taken as the debtor, or alternatively, the debtor is determined by the subtracted mark; thus is the clearing of the debtor and creditor performed.

5a) Six, six, time (two), sky (zero), fire (three), ocean (four), Veda (four), and khā (zero)— these are indeed the burning syllables of the practitioner (sādhaka). [The next group is] pair (two), twice-five (ten), sky (zero), joined with ambara (zero), moon (one), and sky (zero).
The letters of the practitioner are indeed twenty-two. The subtraction of debt and wealth is performed by these limbs situated above and below. Now, another method:
starting from the first letter of the name up to the letters of the mantra and so forth.
Having divided it threefold, one should split it by means of vowels; the other is the reverse of that.
This is its meaning:

Having taken the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra, one should multiply the number of those syllables by seven and divide by three; this is for the practitioner's side. On the mantra's side, however, it is otherwise: having taken the first letter of the mantra up to the letter of the name, one should [proceed] with as many syllables as there are.
Having multiplied by three, one should divide by seven; the remainder greater than half indicates a debtor. "By the seven vowels" is the meaning.
Therefore it has been said:
"Starting from the first letter of the name until the appearance of the first letter of the mantra."
One should divide by seven; the remainder, if three or more, should be subtracted from ten to determine the debt, wealth, and so forth.
Starting from the first syllable of the mantra until the disappearance of the letters,
one should take that which remains three times protracted and sevenfold, provided it is not exceeded by others, and so forth.
Alternatively, the name of the person to be accomplished, doubled and joined with that of the practitioner, should be divided by eight; the remainder is one thing, while the other is its opposite.

One should take all the syllables of the mantra and as many as there are initial syllables of the practitioner’s name, double them, and divide by eight; this is for the side of the mantra. However, for the side of the practitioner, one should multiply the previously mentioned syllables by eight and divide by two; whichever remainder is greater is the debtor. One should proceed according to whichever of these four methods is appropriate.
The summary is this: having cleared one's debts and wealth, one should undertake the reception of the mantra.
5b) In this *Nigamasāranirṇaya* composed by Śrī Ramāramaṇadevaśarman,
the first chapter, which is the sole cause for accomplishing all perfections, has been successfully extracted.

Now, if at any time—due to delusion, negligence, or great ignorance—one should abandon a mantra that has been obtained, such abandonment must certainly be performed; otherwise, there will be self-destruction. In this regard, the authoritative proof is set forth:
Now, the procedure for the complete relinquishment of the enemy-mantra is correctly explained:
having become pure and composed, one should begin on an auspicious day.
For the destruction of all suffering without exception, the Teacher [prescribed] an excellent ritual;
therein, first, in a beautiful dwelling, one should perform the rite of initiation according to the sequence of the ritual for the water-pot (kumbha).
The wise one should place [the vessel] within the mandala and fill it with auspicious water;
having invoked the deity there by reciting the mantra in reverse order.

Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa and completed the worship, one should worship the ancillary deities (āvaraṇas); thus, having worshipped the deity of the mantra along with its enclosures, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) [should proceed].
Having offered even cow-ghee with the *viloma* mantra, O twice-born one,
he should then present the *bali* offering to the deities with perfumes and other substances according to the prescribed rule.
And likewise in the intermediate directions, according to the sequence to be described: "Oṃ, come, O Indra, lord of the *svadhā* offering, you of a hundred sacrifices, husband of Śacī!"
Salutations to you; accept this offering of flowers, incense, and so forth.
Oṃ! Come, O Lord of all splendors, bestower of the supreme sacrificial oblation.
Accept these flowers, incense, and so forth; accept this offering which has been worshipped.
Oṃ! O King of Pretas, come hither, O Wind-god of radiant splendor! Accept this offered oblation; being well-pleased, become a granter of boons.
Oṃ! Homage to you, O Lord of the Rākṣasas, Nirṛti; you have come here.
Accept this offering, worship, and so forth, presented by me with devotion.
Oṃ! Come, O Lord of the World and Guardian of the Western Direction; salutations to you!
Having accepted this worship offered with devotion, may you find delight.
Oṃ! O Prabhāñjana, Lord of Life, you together with your retinue, please accept with respect this offering presented by me according to the prescribed rite.
Oṃ! May Kubera and Tārakodhīśa, the two best of gods, depart;
may they, being pleased by flowers, incense, and other offerings, grant me boons.
Oṃ! O Blessed One, you alone are sovereignty; O Lord, refuge of all vidyās!
Being worshipped with flowers, incense, and other offerings, may you be pleased for the sake of prosperity. (The reading "pūjitaiḥ" [by those who have worshipped] is also found.)
Oṃ! Come, O Lord of all castes; accept this my worship of Brahmā.
Ward off all obstacles for me; salutations be unto you.
Oṃ! Come, O bestower of boons, O Manifest One, O Lord of the universe!
Worshipped with supreme devotion, may you be the giver of happiness to me.
Then one should worship the deity of the mantra along with his retinue,
using flowers, incense, and other offerings while reciting the mantra in reverse order.
Then the wise one, having observed his own desire, should pray to the worshiped deity of the mantra, [saying]: "By me, whose intellect is wavering..."
O Lord, that which has been received and honored by me is of the very nature of mantra;
by that, dispel every agitation of the mind.
May evil be warded off, and may there be eternal well-being;
may my devotion to you alone extend my auspiciousness for as long as this world endures.
Having thus made this prayer, one should write the mantra, ending with the mantra-termination (mantrānta), in reverse order upon the vessel,
and worship it with *mala*, camphor, and sandalwood.
Having again placed [the vessel] upon the pitcher with supreme devotion,
and having subsequently bound that vessel and the images upon one's own head,
one should bathe with the auspicious waters filled with mantras contained within the worshipped pitcher.
Furthermore, having filled another jar with water while remaining self-controlled,
one should place the mantra-leaf within it and then perform worship.
O Lord, one should then cast it into the waters of a river or even into a pure reservoir; and the Brahmins, O Lord, should offer it according to their capacity.
For one who has performed the ritual in this manner, the diseases arising from the mantras of enemies are destroyed without a doubt; gradually, clarity of mind ensues.
One is born endowed with intense power and gradually increases one's own lineage;
this is the doctrine proclaimed in the Mālinīvijaya.
Now, the manual (paddhati).

Having eaten a single meal without meat on the previous day, and having performed his daily obligatory rites (*nityakṛtya*) on the day of the fire-ritual (*agnimadina*), he should go to the pavilion of shade (*chāyāmaṇḍapa*), place the water-pot (*kumbha*) according to the sequence of the initiation ritual (*dīkṣāvidhi*), and fill it with pure water from the *sarvatobhadra* mandala while reciting the *viroma* mantra.

Having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), and having worshipped [the deity] with verses and so forth according to the instruction using the reverse mantra (*vilomamantra*), one should worship the enclosures (*āvaraṇas*). Then, having performed the installation of the fire (*vahnisthāpana*), one should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) one hundred and eight times with the *virūpākṣa* mantra. Then, as prescribed, one should worship the ten [directional deities] in sequence with scents and other offerings, beginning with "Oṃ, obeisance to Indra" (*oṃ indrāya namaḥ*).

Having worshipped the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and offered an oblation (bali) to each one, he should present the oblation to each individually with the mantra beginning with "āyāhi" and so forth. Then, having worshipped the deity of the mantra along with its retinue using the reverse mantra (viloma-mantra), he should pray to the deity of the mantra with the mantra beginning with "ātmalokye" and so forth. Thereafter, [he should place] the mantra in the vessel in reverse order.

Having written [the mantra] and placed it upon a water-pot smeared with stainless camphor, sandalwood, and other substances, having performed the *jīvanyāsa*, and having worshipped it with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings;

Having placed that vessel upon one's own head with supreme devotion and having worshipped it, one should bathe from the water-pot (*kumbha*). Then, having refilled that pot with water and cast the vessel into its midst, one should deposit the pot into a reservoir of water.
Thereafter, having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor and performed the rite of sealing the ritual without defect (*acchidrāvadhāraṇa*), [one should honor] the Brahmins.
Then, one should feed [the guests] according to the sequence prescribed for initiation; thereafter, one should receive the mantra adorned by all the cakras—this is the summary.

Now, that which is to be done when a mantra is occasionally obtained through dreams and the like is set forth here. Having examined the *Yoginītantra* regarding the procedure for a mantra obtained in a dream, [one should recite] the *praṇava*.

I shall explain for the benefit of practitioners, especially those who have obtained [the mantra] in a dream or been given by a woman; it is perfected through the ritual consecration alone. If that which was obtained in a dream is impure, one should cause it to dwell in the presence of the Guru.
Having written [the mantra] on a banyan leaf or in saffron, it is taken up;
from that, one attains success, otherwise it would be fruitless.
Thus, when the mantra is obtained through dreams or other means, having installed the water-pot according to the sequence prescribed for initiation, with a banyan leaf...
Having written [the mantra] with saffron and performed the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should receive the mantra from the Guru.
Alternatively, one may take another mantra that has been examined within all the wheels (*cakra*) of that deity;
for since the object of worship consists of a single mantra, the instruction regarding the object of worship occurs even in a dream under the guise of a mantra. Therefore, that mantra as well—
"What need is there to speak of a man who possesses the *vāhmantra*? He is Śiva himself. Such is the summary, based on hearing these words of praise and so forth.
Now follows the consecration by means of mantras.
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
Birth (the reading *jajanaṃ* also occurs), life, striking, and likewise awakening;
then consecration, purification, and thereafter nourishment.
7b) Satisfying (tarpaṇa), inflaming (dīpana), and concealing (gopana) are recorded as the tenth;
the extraction of mantras from the letters of the Mātṛkā is recorded as "birth" (jajana).
Having likewise interspersed each syllable of the mantra with the *praṇava*, one should recite it; by that, the "life" (*jīvana*) [of the mantra] is proclaimed.
One should indeed strike each syllable of the mantra upon the vessel with sandalwood water using the mantra; this [procedure] has been fully proclaimed.
One should sprinkle each of the mantra-syllables with sandalwood water;
the awakening [of the mantra] is performed with *karavīra* flowers equal in number to the syllables.
One should again install the water-pot according to the very sequence prescribed for initiation,
using *aśvattha* shoots as many times as there are syllables in the mantra.
Sprinkling [the disciple] while reciting the root mantra is known as the consecration;
one should contemplate the mantra mentally by means of the light-mantra alone.
The burning away of the three impurities is known as the purification;
one should sprinkle each of the syllables of the mantra with water from *kuśa* grass.
Reciting the mantra mentally is known as nourishment (āpyāyana);
reciting the mantra while in water is known as libation (tarpaṇa).
The "kindling" (dīpana) of the mantra is said to result from the conjunction of Tāra, Māyā, Rama, and so forth; its "concealment" (gopana), however, is its non-disclosure.
Indeed, these consecrations for mantras have been taught as those which grant swift accomplishment.
Thus, when a mantra is received in this sequence—whether obtained in a dream or by other means—the mantras become efficacious; this is the summary.
For example, a light-mantra (*jyotirmantra*): *hrauṃ*.
Now follows the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*) according to the *Vāmeśvaratantra*.
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā),
since without it the fruit of all mantras cannot be accomplished.
Therefore, it is proclaimed as *īkṣā* by the teachers who are knowers of ritual action;
it is declared to be fourfold: consisting of action (*kriyāvatī*), consisting of letters (*varṇamayī*), consisting of parts (*kalāvatī*), and consisting of piercing (*vedhamayī*).
That which has been proclaimed in all the tantras is now stated here.
The definition of initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the Vāmakeśvaratantra.
The entire world has initiation as its root; for initiation is indeed the supreme austerity.
Initiation shall always be one's station, and the seashore its refuge.
Whatever sin has been committed throughout ten million births, whether done knowingly or unknowingly, it flees at the mere taking of initiation; of this there is no doubt.
From that, there shall be the attainment of one's desires, bestowing an abundance of wealth and grain;
in the end, served by divine attendants, one goes to the abode of the gods.
In the Mahākāla Tantra.
Knowledge is bestowed within, and the accumulation of sins is destroyed;
therefore, it is called *dīkṣā*, which accomplishes all desired aims.
Therefore, one should bestow divine knowledge and likewise effect the destruction of sins;
by that, it is proclaimed as "initiation" (dīkṣā) in this world by those who have reached the further shore of the Tantras.
A person who takes refuge in initiation destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin, the sins of stealing gold,
and hundreds of thousands of minor offenses (upapātaka).
An initiated Brāhmaṇa goes to the stainless world of Brahmā;
likewise, a Kṣatriya goes to the world of Indra, and a Vaiśya to that of Prajāpati.
By nature, a Śūdra’s initiation leads him to a city of Gandharvas;
therefore, initiation is prescribed for the four varṇas alone.
In the worship of Rāma.
By the mere act of receiving initiation, the heap of sins flees;
that very person then becomes personally worthy of performing the rites for the gods and ancestors.
Or rather, whatever action is performed is like an oblation poured into ashes.
In the Mahogratārā-kalpa.
But that lowest of men who, having seen [the image] of Tārā during a kalpa, seizes it—
no atonement whatsoever exists for him even in thousands of manvantaras.
One should receive the Great Vidyā, the destroyer of sins, from the mouth of the Guru on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, under an auspicious ascendant and at a favorable moment.
When joined with the constellation Pūrvabhādrapadā and associated with the star Maitra (Anurādhā) and so forth,
or likewise with Anurādhā or Revatī, it is highly commended.
One should know the auspicious time for the reception of the mantra,
especially during the month of Īṣa and particularly in Kārttika.
An oblation of one hundred and eight offerings is performed with bilva leaves;
alternatively, one may perform eighteen or twenty-eight.
One should offer milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, sweetmeats, and candied sugar; one should present an offering of goat meat and the most excellent meat of the monitor lizard.
Then one should offer cow's milk, rice cooked with honey, and coconut water;
that indeed is the ritual offering.
One should satisfy one's own guru with cows, land, gold, garments, and so forth;
or, being compassionate, one should give one's entire wealth as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or even half of that.
Just as one who is contented and serene gives [to] the initiated... [and so forth].
As it is stated in the Vārāhītantra:
And for one who has not been initiated, death does not turn back from Raurava;
[therefore], relying upon the Tantra, the Tantrika [should act]... [of him].
In the Mṛḍālī Tantra:
"He who is deluded by Māyā and surrounded by Kinnaras shall never attain initiation; he is destined for hell."
Now, for one who has abandoned initiation, sin prevails upon the earth;
afflicted, he falls into the pit of the hell of the darkness of delusion.
One who is devoid of initiation and is impure is [unfit] for all ritual acts in the Mantrayāma; thus it is said in the [Mantra]yāmala.
I consider everything performed by one who is uninitiated to be useless;
a man who is pure yet devoid of initiation attains the womb of a beast.
In the Yoginītantra.
Upon seeing a man who is not a mantra-practitioner, one should not have him perform any rite;
for such a person is a veritable flesh-eating beast in human form.
Therefore, initiation (dīkṣā) must be performed for all purposes whatsoever. Now follows the initiation for that specific occasion (tātkālikī dīkṣā).
This initiation is common [to both]; however, hear the fruit regarding a solar eclipse:
a lunar eclipse is equal in merit to a solar eclipse.
This mantra bestows wealth, long life, the gain of sons, prosperity, honor, and fame;
it destroys sins even when Venus has entered Rāhu’s mouth.
Because it bestows supreme liberation through equanimity and grants accomplishment in the three times,
it is said to be a hundred thousand times more meritorious during an eclipse or on one's own natal day.

The immediate initiation has been described out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners; indeed, it is not restricted by prohibitions regarding days of the week, lunar months, or even the auspiciousness of the ascendant and other astrological factors.
Initiation bestows all desired objects and grants accomplishment at that very moment;

therefore, the meaning is that there is no need for deliberation regarding prohibitions such as the avoidance of specific astrological conjunctions (*lagna*) during the commencement of study and other rites, based on these statements.
Now, the determination of the Guru. From the *Ṣoḍhārṇava*:
He is peaceful, self-controlled, of noble birth, humble, possessed of pure attire,
of pure conduct, perfectly purified, clean, skillful, and highly intelligent.
One who belongs to a spiritual order (āśramin), is devoted to meditation, is proficient in the tantras and mantras,
and is capable of both restraint and grace is called a guru.
Pure by birth on both his mother’s and father’s side, pure in disposition, and having conquered his senses;
he was a knower of the essence of all scriptures and one who had taken the deity into his very heart.
The conduct of the observance.
When the Guru is pleased with Śiva’s feet,
there is no object on earth that, if given to him by one who is displeased with the Guru, would not cause one to become an enemy.
The arrival of the Goddess and the words of Śiva.
One must never step over the bed, seat, vehicle, sandals, or throne of the guru, nor his bath-water, nor his shadow.
Now, the accomplished master (siddhaguru).
One who is sonless, whose sons have died, who is dwarfed, wrathful, deceitful, diseased, talkative, or a chatterer— free from these defects, such a person is a preceptor for a disciple.
One should not receive a mantra from one's father, nor likewise from one's maternal grandfather; nor from one who is younger, nor from one who is distant, nor from one who has resorted to an enemy.
Or from negligence? Likewise, having [received] initiation through knowledge...
one should then perform an expiation and undergo initiation once again.
Therein, through initiation, the initiation of initiation is revealed;
and by means of the mantra of the father, as well as that of the mother, the Great One is purified.
A mantra that has been performed by chance, or one that has been interrupted, or one done through deception;
In the ocean.
Peaceful, disciplined, pure-souled, and endowed with faith, [she is] the one who pierces the armor of passion.
He was devoted to that goal;
pure in descent from both his mother’s and father’s side, he was pure in disposition and had his senses fully subdued.
10a) Possessing great enthusiasm for the work of mantra, a donor according to his means—
one endowed with such qualities becomes a disciple devoted to that [practice].
Now, regarding the prohibited disciple, it is said in the *Ṣoḍhārṇava*:
The mantra should not be given to one who is deceitful, cruel, foolish, a mere lip-service practitioner, devoid of devotion, or corrupted; it is like sowing a fine seed in a wasteland.

It should not be given to those who take pleasure in the wives of others, to those who seize upon pretexts, to those who are full of passion, nor to the disciples of others, nor to those devoted to the practices of others.
One should never bestow the mantra upon one who is excessively reckless, who reviles the family tradition, or who is intent on disparaging the family.
Now follows the determination of devotion to the Guru, according to the Kulāgama.
An offering made once into the fire yields a hundredfold merit; that given to a guru yields a hundred-thousandfold merit;
and that which is received by one who has realized the deathless yields ten-millionfold merit. One should grasp this supreme nectar.
He who accumulates wealth where there is no supreme trust will be carried off by kings,
or forcibly taken away by thieves and robbers.
The wings droop and the fire does not burn for a long time;
having abandoned its buried state, it dies, and thus it is truly not tormented by it.
Therefore, even for a person who has attained perfection and performs actions for the sake of liberation,
deities and others constantly create obstacles.
They cause the mind of that seeker of liberation to wander through various paths to release;
having abandoned deceit regarding wealth, one should have all tasks performed.
Avarice in wealth quickly destroys one's son, wife, fame, and strength; for whatever accumulation of wealth one performs by deceiving the guru and the gods [is fruitless].
Therefore, that [wealth] is neither milked nor stolen by thieves;
this entire [spiritual attainment] has the guru as its root, therefore one should always worship the guru.
Therefore, it is neither stolen nor carried away by thieves;
the Guru is the father, the Guru is the mother, and the Guru is indeed Śiva himself.
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one at all.
Therefore, one must perform what is beneficial for the Guru through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
O Goddess, by practicing what is harmful, one is born as a worm in excrement;
O Goddess, he who is of deluded intellect and violates the command of his guru [suffers likewise].
He will be born in a terrible hell or attain the state of a *piśāca*.
This is the summary of devotion to the Guru. Now follows the rule regarding the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), as stated in the *Kulārṇava* and the *Jñānārṇava*:
O fair-faced one, during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day and under a favorable weekday,
one should perform the practice of the Aghora mantra during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
O Goddess of the gods, there is no fault even in an inauspicious lunar day during an eclipse of the moon or sun; it is pure as before, as are the days of the solstices and other auspicious times.
In Caitra, one should know the result to be undesirable; in Vaiśākha, there is birth of a son; in Jyeṣṭha, death shall occur.
In Vaiśākha, there is also the gain of land. In Jyeṣṭha, death shall occur.
In Āṣāḍha there is the loss of kinsmen, and in Śrāvaṇa, a hundred weapons;
one is patient in the month of Bhādrapada, and in Āśvina, there is an accumulation of jewels.
In Kārttika there shall be prosperity; in Mārgaśīrṣa, great wealth;
in Pauṣa, all enjoyments; and in Māgha, the highest fortune.
In Phālguna, all rites [are auspicious]; such is the fruit of the months. Thus, one should perform initiation during a pure month, at an auspicious lunar mansion (lagna), and so forth.
In that regard, the sequence is as follows.
On the preceding day, having eaten only once a day without meat, one who desires the destruction of all sins should recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times.
On the following day, having gone to the shadow-pavilion (*chāyā-maṇḍapa*) and drawn the *sarvatobhadra* mandala,

and having performed the selection of the preceptor (*guru-varaṇa*) according to his means, [he should place] there a new cloth (*navavāsa*) that is doubled over, with five red inner linings and five sprouts at its opening.

11a) Having placed a jar covered with a cloth there and having worshipped the deity of the disciple according to one's means, one should bring the bathed disciple to one's left and cause him to perform the *saṃkalpa*: "Today," and so forth.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)— "Desiring to attain the highest object of desire preceded by the destruction of the accumulation of sins acquired in previous births, I shall perform the initiation"— one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth. Then, once the purification of the elements has been performed upon the disciple, the Guru, having placed *dūrvā* grass and unhusked rice (*akṣata*) on the disciple’s head and taught the placement of the *mātṛkā* (*mātṛkānyāsa*), [should do so] in the right ear.
Then one should perform the rites for the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, deity, and so forth; thereafter, having applied the *nivṛtti*-kalā and the others to the head of the disciple as follows:

"Salutation to Nivṛtti" from the soles of the feet up to the knees; "Salutation to Pratiṣṭhā" from the knees up to the navel; "Salutation to Vidyā" from the navel up to the throat; "Salutation to Śānti" from the throat up to the forehead; [and "Salutation to Śāntyatītā"] from the forehead upward.

Having placed the Śāntyatītā [kalā] up to the head, one should place it in reverse order. One should recite the mantra three times over the right ear. Then, the disciple, having likewise muttered the received mantra according to his capacity and having worshipped the self and the deity of the mantra according to his means, should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru according to his means.
In accordance with what has been stated, the offering of oblations (*validāna*), the fire sacrifice (*homa*), and so forth should be performed. We shall explain this further below;
this is the summary.

In the *Nigamasāranirṇaya* composed by Śrī Rasāramaṇa Devaśarman, it is stated that once the teacher and disciple have been purified through initiation on an auspicious day, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) while avoiding prohibited mantras.
In that regard, there is a restriction concerning the location for the *puraścaraṇa* of Caṇḍikā.
A field of merit, a riverbank, a cave, a mountain peak,
sacred sites, the confluence of rivers, a desert, and a forest.
Secluded gardens, the foot of a bilva tree, and the base of a mountain.
A grove of *tulasī* in a cow-pen, a bull-pen devoid of bulls, a stable for horses,
the root of a *malakī* tree, and a cow-shed in the middle of water;
The bank of a temple, pure substances, one's own home,
the presence of gurus, and likewise a place of singular concentration of wealth.
The Pretabhūmi and so forth have been revealed in their respective Kalpas;
relying on one or another of these places, one should perform the recitation.
Now follows the determination regarding the seat; and [the procedure] for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) in the case of Caṇḍikā.
A tiger skin leads to all accomplishments; a deer skin leads to the accomplishment of knowledge;
a cloth seat removes passion, while a lotus-seat increases prosperity.
Silk is said to bestow nourishment, while woolen cloth brings about suffering;
black-colored [cloth] is for malevolent rites (abhicāra), and red for the rite of subjugation (vaśya).
For pacifying rites, a white [skin] is prescribed; for all rites, a [white] chin (?);
for inciting enmity, a jackal's skin is prescribed; and for prosperity, the skin of a cow is used for pacifying rites.
Poverty results from a bamboo seat, misfortune from a wooden seat;
the arising of suffering occurs on the bare ground, and the birth of misery occurs on a stone seat.
On a seat of grass there is loss of fame; on a snake-seat, confusion of mind; on a brick-seat, mental distress; such are the results for common recitation (japa).

One who has not been initiated should dwell anywhere; however, an ascetic, a forest-dweller, a student, and one who has completed his Vedic studies should dwell in a house made of the skin of the black antelope.
On a seat of kuśa grass and an antelope skin, one should prepare a square area measuring either one cubit or two cubits, raised four finger-breadths high.
Then, one should dwell there without agitation, following the sequence beginning with the *svastika* posture;
namely, the fourfold set consisting of the *svastika*, *padmaka*, *vīra*, and *siddha*.
This which has been praised has thus been proclaimed by me incidentally, O God.
Now follows the determination of prohibited postures (*niṣiddhāsana*), according to the *Stripurāmahārṇava*.
A seat made of mango, neem, or reed grass brings about total destruction;
likewise, those who sit upon a *vakula*, a *kiṃśuka*, or a *panasa* tree have their fortune destroyed.

Now the tortoise diagram (kūrmacakra) is taught for the purpose of determining the location of a lamp site; O Goddess of Gods, I shall now declare the most excellent mantra within the tortoise diagram.
First, having made a circle, one should fashion nine squares;
the central square should consist of nine parts, and one should write in that same manner in the eastern [square].
O Lord of Lakṣmī, one should write the seven groups beginning with the *ka*-group [in the eight directions],
and in the middle, within the eight squares, one should write the vowels in pairs.
In the central square, there is the excellent wheel named Kṣatra, shaped like a tortoise;
in that square, the syllable named Kṣa is known as the face, being the first letter.
On both sides of the face, one should draw two pairs of arms; then the region of the belly, then the pair of feet, and finally, at the end, one should draw the tail.
If [the lines] are on the face, undertakings succeed; if on the shoulders, one encounters distress;
if on the belly, there is excessive suffering; and if on the feet, it is said that there will be loss.
In the tail there will be loss of wealth, while the face is known as the location of the lamp;
this tortoise diagram (kūrmacakra) is proclaimed for the sake of obtaining the location of the lamp.
Thus, having determined the location for the lamp, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) in the place and posture as previously described;
this is the summary.
Now, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). In the *Rāmārcana* and the *Caṇḍikā*:

"Without the purification of the elements, the practitioner's rites such as recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*), even if performed according to the prescribed method, immediately become fruitless. From the *Kulārṇava*.

Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should effect drying, burning, and floating with the mantras *vāk*, *agni*, *lalitā*, and *andārī*, respectively, by means of the *kalā*, *vidyā*, and *veda* [mantras].
O Goddess, by means of the arts and sciences known to the wise, one should, through the sequence beginning with *pūraka*,
dry up and burn the personification of sin situated within the belly.
In the Vārāhī Tantra.
Drying, burning, reducing to ashes, dissolving, extracting nectar,
and flooding— these should be performed through mere mental visualization for the sake of purification.
Thus ends the classification of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). Now, the breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The practitioner of mantra should draw in the external air through the iḍā for sixteen mātrās;
he should then retain the filled breath for sixty-four mātrās.
Having properly [inhaled] through the Suṣumnā situated in the center with thirty-two measures slowly, one should exhale through the Piṅgalā nāḍī according to the supreme teacher’s instruction.
By means of these, one should thoroughly expel it; then one should perform worship and retention.
After that, one should perform exhalation very slowly, again and again.
One should drink the breath when released, one should retain it when released;
one should drink the divine breath when released again and again—in this way, one shall attain perfection.
In the Agastyasaṃhitā, and also in the Pañcamītantra.
One should restrain the vital air (cidvāyu) according to one's capacity and hold it in the pot (kumbhaka) according to one's capacity;
one should drink the wind of one's own nature, and therein one shall attain perfection.
Those proficient in the treatises on yoga call this *prāṇāyāma*;
it is performed again and again, gradually, during each successive portion of exhalation.
From the root of the little finger to the root of the index finger,
the wise know that the measures (mātrās) are differentiated by sixteen syllables (varṇas).
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
The practitioner of mantra, well-composed, should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the rule;
O Goddess of gods, having filled the belly with the root mantra through the left nostril.
One should practice with the right [nostril] through the threefold movement of *kumbhaka*;
this is also stated in the *Kālītantra*.

One should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) with either the root mantra or the syllable Om (praṇava). The holding of the nostrils is performed by using the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.
Prāṇāyāma should be understood as being performed without the index finger and the middle finger.
Thus ends the method of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Now follows the determination of the yantras and so forth, according to the Śrīkramasaṃhitā.
In a block of heartwood, in a gem, in a yantra, in an image, and on cloth;
likewise in the sun, in fire, in water, and in lingas, icons, and jars.
One should always worship in the sky; twelve [types of supports] are recorded as recommended:
in gold, silver, copper, on birch bark, and likewise upon the ground.
Without the application of the yantra, the deity is not pleased.
Tripurā is in the great ocean.
They say that the yantra consists of mantra, and the deity has the form of mantra;
just as there is a distinction between the body and the self, so too is there a distinction between the mantra and the deity.
Because it is the means of cognition here, it is called "mantra" by the wise.
In the Kulāmṛta [Tantra].
This body composed of the yantra pacifies all evil and protects the practitioner from great fear through worship and meditation.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, what is the meaning of the yantra? What is said to be the meaning of the mantra? And what is that which is called mudrā? Tell me this, O Śiva, O Lord.
The Lord said:
Those who know the mantras say that the body is the *yantra* and that the knowledge of the mantra is indivisible;
they declare the body to be twofold: the material (*bhautika*) and the mental (*mānasa*).
The supreme, eternal mass of water is continuous and consists of pure knowledge;
they say that the mudrā is material, while the yantra is supernatural and free from disease.
Know that the yantra consists of knowledge; thus the body becomes threefold.
Mudrā is also mental for a person; there is no certainty regarding the physical.
Therefore, it is traditionally taught that these two exist as one without a disciple.
Pārvatī said:
13b) O Lord of my life, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, I have heard that my body is a machine;
tell me, O Master, if you are pleased with me, what is my body’s mudrā?
Īśvara said:
The Great Seal (mahāmudrā) in the form of the source (yoni) is proclaimed as the body;
it consists of agitation, melting, attraction, subjugation, intoxication, and the great goad.
And Khecarī is proclaimed as being in the form of the seed-syllable (*bīja*);
these [mantras] are proclaimed to be the Great Union (*mahāmela*) within one month.
In the Kulāmṛta:

It protects from great delusion (*māyā*) and from the darkness of ignorance; it is the Śrīcakra, which [bestows] [bliss] incessantly. Thus, in the manner described, even during the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
Mantras are accomplished [only] when they are not obstructed by the first [syllable], nor bound by the middle,
nor severed by the last; otherwise, that vidyā does not succeed.
Likewise, in the Tantracūḍāmaṇi, [the Lord] said:
O Mother, witness of all phenomenal expansions,
there is no fear for one such as I to speak out of dread of your anger.
O Lord, when you are pleased with me, grant me your grace;
O ocean of compassion, tell me why there is emptiness in my heart.
The Goddess said:
By that very [means],
the Sadāśivas are always present;
they have come for the worship of the Great Goddess, ever free from duality and withered of passion.
O Lord, she is that very one whom you alone protect among all worlds;
neither Brahmā, nor Hari, nor even I, O bull among men, possess such a vision.
Requested by his devotees and desiring to show favor to the worlds, Viṣṇu will appear in age after age at the cost of his own body.
O Supreme Lord, by my grace, you have assumed forms such as the Fish and others;
for the sake of the world, the teachings of the Vedas and other scriptures were raised up by you.
Having attained equanimity everywhere through the inherent nature of the quality of sattva,
one should be equal toward insects, birds, moths, and so forth, as well as toward human beings.
In whatever way he may grant himself to a devotee,
this very conduct is the means by which awakening into reality is set in motion.
Nevertheless, according to the conduct of the samaya, one's own consort must not be given away to another,
even if the guru has been served by the disciple for a thousand lifetimes.
O beloved, it is certain that this [knowledge] should not be given away even at the cost of one's life, wealth, or kin;
for by a single syllable of it, even Nārada became a spiritual teacher.
O child, by their grace, how could there be anxiety regarding creation?
O God, if all beings, whose nature is Brahman, should depart through this knowledge, [how could there be such concern]?
O Bhairava, tell me: what kind of creation is this, and what purpose could there be here? Are not all [beings] Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Śakra, and Divākara?
"O Bhairava, tell me how there could be a transformation involving decrease or increase.
Having thought thus, O Goddess, I, whose self is the Supreme, contemplated creation.
All the great vidyās, having been cursed, lay upon their beds for seven days;
then, all having assembled, they fell into a mantra-induced sleep, their radiance vanished.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, praise you while overwhelmed by fear:
"O Mother Goddess, Sustainer of the World, Source of the World, Destroyer!"
Cast the shadow of your feet upon my head; render those like me lusterless.
O Goddess of gods, you alone are the creator, and you alone are the cause of its preservation.
14b) For you are indeed the destroyer, and you alone are the source of rebirth;
you alone are the effect, O Goddess of Gods, and you alone are the cause, O Lord.
The distinction between ignorance and knowledge is indeed you alone, for you are their very essence;
you, the Supreme Self, are by your own nature free from the duality of duality and non-duality.
O Lord of the Universe, you alone exist as the supreme power in the form of Sat-Cit-Ānanda; indeed, you alone are the unity of female, male, and neuter.
Indeed, your manifestations arise from you and dissolve back into you alone;
for if they are withdrawn in the very same manner as they were produced by the Great Wisdom, [they are truly yours].
Be gracious; let the deities enter there into the pair of feet, so that everything may proceed according to the movement of the thread by one skilled in its circulation.
A granary, a clod of earth, a leather puppet, and the like are insentient;
likewise, according to your own teaching, Brahmā, Hara, and the others do not possess the nature of Brahman.
"All these painted puppets are capable of both creating and destroying," having said this,
O Lord, all the deities entered his feet.
I shall declare the release from the curse, and you shall become my guru;
that which is the Svapnāvatī vidyā, hidden throughout the three worlds.
O All-pervading Lord, by that very [power] all ignorance is awakened;
she who is the supreme primordial nature (mūlā-prakṛti) embraces everything during the night.
O Lord, having been raised up and brought [there], she formerly dwelt in the middle of a hollow by this very means,
under the guidance of the wise Viśvāmitra.
The goddess Tripurā, the bestower of all prosperity, has been propitiated;
therefore, O Lord, he will certainly become the creator and the destroyer.
Then, even though she was cursed during the Brahmastava, she did not leave her noble lineage;
by the mere act of propitiating you, she continued to live her life elsewhere.
The Mārdinī is the supreme vidyā, highly honored by Nārada;
by abandoning the state of a servant through it, he shall become equal to Viṣṇu.
15a) Considering that to be the Brahman of Sound, he became intent on playing the lute;
through his union with the quality of sattva, he remained in the presence of Viṣṇu.
O Mahādeva, by your grace I have become you;
therefore, O Lord of the World, you alone are asleep within my heart.
O Goddess, you will undoubtedly destroy the previously acquired merit of anyone who does not worship you before the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
Having thus granted that boon, she, the great goddess who was intent on the ultimate goal, fell asleep;
then she, the life-giving one, would be restored to life by the Lord of Conduct (Caryanatha).
Therefore, this supreme knowledge should not be given to just anyone;
rather, through the grace of the path of yoga, it is to be imparted by you through the instruction of the mantra.
"O Lord, by you she was thus deprived of her life.
With such words of grief, anguish, and distress, I have come into your presence.
O Lord of the World, as I remember it again and again, my sorrow is renewed.
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, my heart is worn out by its longing for you;
O Lord, how can you cast me into this cruel, bottomless well of suffering?
She who is this knowledge, the Great Knowledge, Tripura, the Supreme Goddess—you alone are the goddess Mardinī; the supreme Kula is equal for both.
O Mahādevī, I am your own form, consisting of consciousness and the destroyer of the *kula*;
O Caṇḍikā, show me mercy so that I may quickly come to life.
As a heap of cotton in fire, as fire in water, as a master in his own clan,
and as a devotee of Hari on one's head, so is [the sin] struck down by the planet Saturn.
I am unable to remain still for even a moment; O Mother, O Goddess, salutations be unto you!
O Beloved, by your command I shall become your guide as I proceed.
O Goddess of gods, having acquired what knowledge shall I become superior to you?
The illustrious Goddess said:
Arise, O child, O omniscient one! Perform a pacification; for how could there be such a thing as a fire falling from the sky? Do not harbor such thoughts.
Having transcended the power of fire, she exists as the sovereign embodiment of life;
thereafter, she bestows the awakening from sleep upon all sciences.

This supreme two-syllable vidyā, which is as subtle as sleep, hidden and concealed throughout all worlds, is proclaimed as three-syllabled when uttered with its vowels (or, according to another reading, "when spoken with its musical tones").
The awakening [arises] from the union of both;
this is its meaning.

Ākāśa is the letter *ha*, Vahni is *ra*, and Mā is Lakṣmī; by her, who is the nature of the vowel *ī*, there is the breast, and the burden is the *bindu*. Thus, *hrīṃ* is established. Having attained union with both [the letters] beginning with *sva* and the oblations (*āhutīya*), she awakens all vidyās. Therefore...

By reciting [the mantra] for an entire lunar day (*vāra*), there is the awakening of all sciences (*vidyā*). Having encapsulated the *Svapnāvatī* mantra with this [mantra], the five peaks (*pañcakuṭā*) of the *Svapnāvatī* are preceded by the initial syllables.
This knowledge is a great knowledge; even at the end of an aeon, it shall not perish. It will certainly not vanish unexpectedly, O Brahmin, for it is protected by Brahmā himself.
Therefore, my child, what more can I say? Because of your devotion, sorrow will surely cease and liberation will be attained. I shall speak further.
Thus, this seventy-seven-fold knowledge was worshipped by the goddess Satyā;
by the grace of that goddess, she became the wife of Hara.
When the time for ripening has arrived, hope having failed and non-existence being present,
one is rendered distraught by the heat of the fire of thirst.
Taking up the Head-Laughter (Mastakāhasa), it indeed wanders through the three worlds;
O Lord, a Kṛtyā was born from that, on account of the risk of destroying creation.
Then,
having entered those bodies with his thunderbolt,
he reduced them to pieces; having thus divided them into fragments, he cast them down upon the three worlds.
By meditating on the qualities of the Self through that [energy], the body is liberated.
The pair of feet is at Devīkūṭa, and the two thighs are at Uḍḍiyāna.
Kāmarūpa is the great source (mahāyoni) in that region, the navel-center; Jālandhara is the pair of breasts, and Bhairava is at the shoulders and neck.
On the Eastern Mountain, within Kāmarūpa, is Devikāśiras;
it was indeed visited by a twice-born man named Dvijeśa in Kāmarūpa.
By worshipping for a long time with body, mind, and speech, O Goddess,
one attains bliss in a dream by resorting to the source known as Kāmākhya.
Abiding there, he then becomes fully integrated within that gnosis;
assuming the form of a renunciant, he indeed becomes a lord of accomplishments.
Perhaps, having looked upon the young brahmin with a compassionate gaze,
she will be given to him for the sake of creating an obstacle to her own yoga.
Even by that wicked youth, who was always devoid of knowledge,
[this] has been revealed, O child, through the union with all the siddhis.
O Lord of Gods, if this which will come into being at the end of the Mleccha age in due course is kept secret by you, then cause it to be bestowed as the *dīpanī* (the illuminating commentary).

According to the *Tantra* of *Tana*, this Vidyā may occasionally come within the range of a disciple (*gocara*). That which is the illuminator (*dīpanī*) of the *Kula-bhairava* is itself to be accomplished; at the conclusion [of the practice], she becomes the sixteenth [form] of Sundarī.
Having attained the state of the waking consciousness (*jāgrad-daśā*), she too shall become the Goddess.
Alternatively, the seed-syllable of Śakti is preceded by the end of the Śakti-kūṭa.
Then, O Lord, the Goddess shall become the bestower of all accomplishments.
O Mahādeva, this very [teaching] must never be disclosed.
16b) Through the individual application of *tāra*, *māyā*, *rama*, and so forth, [the mantra becomes complete].
Thus, by joining *tāra*, *māyā*, *rama*, and so forth individually at the beginning of the mantra, it becomes the *Sarvavidyā* (All-Knowledge) mantra.
Awakening occurs by means of this; it possesses the seed-syllable like a dream, as was stated at the beginning in the *Śrīkrama-mantranirṇaya*: "O Śrī Mantrīpurasundarī...
I shall now explain the *Dīpanī* [the Illuminator]... [her] disciples and so forth..."
If she is not awakened at the beginning, nor pinned down in the middle,
nor satisfied at the end, this vidyā will not be accomplished.
Therefore, O chariot-like mind, [attain] that which is most difficult to obtain:
the Vidyā of Vāgbhava, consisting of the power of speech, the sequence of illusion,
and the syllable Om (praṇava) as Lakṣmī within the seed-syllable of Speech, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Having thus recited [the mantra], the knower of mantras [should contemplate] the state of the Vāgbhava [mantra] at the end,
with the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava as the essence, through the power of Māyā.
With a concentrated mind, one should worship Mahākūṭa with Svapnāvatī,
as well as Manmatha, Svadhara, Kāma, Ramā, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Then, [there is] Madhumatī, followed by Māyā, Ādi, Carma, and Bījaka; ending and beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava), it is accompanied by the sound "Phaṭ" and manifested through Śiva and Śakti.
This [is] the *avidyā* (nescience) which bestows life;
that fifth, supreme *vidyā* (knowledge) shall then become the bestower of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
This is its meaning:
The *praṇava* is *oṃ*; *lakṣmī* is *śrī*; *vāk* is *aiṃ*; *manmatha* is *klīṃ*; and *bhuvaneśvarī* is *hrīṃ*.
By these [syllables], this is the mantra: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ka e ī la hrīṃ*. 17a)

Oṃ śrī& ai& klī& hrī& hasakala hrīṃ || Oṃ ai& śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ hakahala hrīṃ klīṃ eṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ ka hasala hrīṃ hasa oṃ hrīṃ drīṃ hūṃ phaṭ oṃ hasahakalasa hrīṃ. The meaning is that when this is performed, the five siddhis are attained.
Furthermore, I shall proclaim the supreme [mantras] of the practitioners, which are difficult to obtain:
Māyā-Śrī-Madana and also Śrī-Māyā-Madana.
Śrī is described as being with Madana and Māyā; Śrī is with Madana and Māyā;
and Śrī is with Māyā and Madana—this is declared to be the "Tri-pañcikā" (the three sets of five).
There is no knowledge equal to this to be found in the three worlds;
in the great tantra of Bhairavī, this knowledge is most difficult to obtain.
Accomplished, perfectly pure, peaceful, and the subjugator of the three worlds—
having offered the five peaks and so forth, one should indeed recite the fifth mantra five times.

Having thus placed three seeds each— namely *hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ*, *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, *śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ*, and *hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ*— at the beginning of each of the five peaks (*pañcakūṭa*) and so forth, one should recite; then the fifth [mantra] becomes perfected (*siddha*).
Now I shall declare the life-force of all other vidyās:
the syllables Ramā, Māyā, and Haṃsa-bīja, preceded by Vāgbhava, which are exceedingly difficult to obtain.
The seed-syllable at the end of the *śakti* is "haṃ," and likewise *mahāmāyā* and *ramā*;
one should certainly perform the recitation of the *vidyā* joined with these.
This is its meaning:

One should place *Ramā* (*śrīṃ*), *Māyā* (*hrīṃ*), and the *Haṃsa-bīja* (*haṃsaḥ*) at the beginning of the *Vāgbhava-kūṭa*. At the end of the *Śakti-kūṭa*, however, one should place the *Haṃsa-bīja* (*haṃsaḥ*), *Mahāmāyā* (*hrīṃ*), *Ramā* (*śrīṃ*). Through these seed-syllables situated at the beginning and the end, the awakening of all vidyās occurs.
Joined with the seed-syllable of Ramā, she bestows dharma, liberation, and happiness;
through the syllable Hrīṃ, she is eternal, grants sons, and bestows a multitude of various riches.
17b) By means of the seed-syllable *haṃsa* at night, she bestows various desires;
but liberation, which arises from the utterance of the *praṇava*, is certainly the supreme state, difficult to attain.
This essence has been told; now I shall tell the supreme [essence].

By employing the three seed-syllables *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *haṃsa* at the beginning, and placing *haṃsaḥ*, *krīṃ*, and *śrīṃ* at the end of the *kūṭa* of all the Vidyās, this is the *Sarvaśrīvidyāsudīpinī*.
One should mutter the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] using Tāra, Māyā, Ramā, Kāma, and Vāgbhava;
that same [syllable] reversed, however, is the Kāmabīja conjoined with Nabhaḥ.
That which is joined with Tāra, Vāgbhava, Kāma, Namaḥ, and Māyā is declared to be the essence of consciousness; now I shall describe the supreme [essence].
This is its meaning:

Toya: Oṃ Māyā Hrīṃ Ramā Śrīṃ Kāmaḥ Klīṃ Vāgbhavaḥ Aiṃ. That same [sequence] reversed, beginning with Vāgbhava and joined with Nabha (the letter Ha), is the meaning of Kāmarāja. Tāra: Oṃ Vāgbhavaḥ Aiṃ Kāmaḥ Klīṃ Ramā Śrīṃ Māyā Hrīṃ. By that: Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ.
Eṃ Vāgbhava-kūṭa; Aiṃ Klīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Oṃ Kāma-kūṭa; Oṃ Aiṃ Klīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Śakti-kūṭa. This is the Śrīvidyā-dīpinī. Furthermore:
One should employ the seed-syllable of Vāṇīmāyā-Kamalā, beginning with the Vāgbhava;
then the first of the Vedas (Om), O Lakṣmī, followed by the seed-syllable of Speech (Aiṃ) and thereafter the Manmatha (Klīṃ).
Having first given the *māyā* seed-syllable, one should then utter that which is called the *vāgbhava*.
At the beginning and the end is the *tāra*, with the *māyā* at the conclusion, and in the middle it is conjoined with the *śrībīja*.
At the end of *tāra* (om), the *vāgbhava* and the *kāmabīja* are likewise situated;
having thus pronounced this, one should pronounce the *kāmarāja*.
In the middle of this very vidyā, one should employ Kāma;
[the syllable] Adhara situated within Manmatha, and the Śrībīja within Manmatha.
Having thus joined them in sequence, one should then utter that *śaktikūṭa*.
This is declared to be the *dīpanī* (the illuminator), hidden in all the tantras.
18a) By that [mantra]: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ eṃ oṃ śrīṃ eṃ klīṃ hrīṃ* in the Vāgbhava-kūṭa; *oṃ eṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ* in the Kāmakūṭa; *oṃ aiṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ* in the Śaktikūṭa—this is the Dīpinī. Furthermore:
One should apply the seed-syllable *Tāra* (Om), followed by *Māyā* (Hrīm) and *Haṃ*, at the beginning of the *Vāgbhava* [seed-syllable];
thereafter comes the *Kāma-bīja*, and immediately after that, the *Brahma-bīja*.
The best of practitioners should recite the seed-syllable *haṃsa* at the end of the *śakti*;
this is the *dīpinī* vidyā, and now I shall speak of the supreme one.
Therefore, [the mantra is]: *oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ*, the Vāgbhava and Kāmakūṭa, *oṃ* the Śaktikūṭa, *haṃsaḥ*;

and this is the Śrīvidyādīpinī. Alternatively, having recited the Praṇava, Lakṣmī, Manmatha, Vāgbhava, and Parā, the best of practitioners should utter that which is called the Vāgbhava; namely, the Praṇava and the Vāgbīja.
By means of the *māyā* of Ramā and Manmatha;
having thus recited [the mantra] at that time, one should utter the seed-syllable of Kāma,
followed by the *praṇava*, then Kāma, Ramā, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Thus, having joined them in sequence, one should utter the Śakti-kūṭa;
this is declared to be the essence that bestows all accomplishments.
These are the most secret vidyās, all of which bestow consciousness;
having bestowed any one of them, one should recite the vidyā with a concentrated mind.
At the beginning of the *japa* and at its conclusion, one should recite the words of the Guru in sequence:

"Oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ, Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ" for the *Vāgbhava-kūṭa*; "Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ" for the *Śakti-kūṭa*. This is the *Śrīvidyā-dīpinī*, and thus, from among these [mantras], one should recite whichever is prescribed.

The summary is as follows: having offered [the oblation] in every manner, one should begin the recitation; at the end of the recitation, one should recite in every manner (meaning in all ways). Furthermore:
Furthermore, the specific distinction of the Vidyā of Vāmakeśī is stated again:
[it resides] respectively in the Vāgbhava, the Kāmarāja, and the Śakti-kūṭa.
The "kindling" (*dīpana*) and so forth are taught by means of the *kāmabīja* in its proper sequence (some read "by means of the three seed-syllables" instead).
And thus, in the case of the *vāgbhava* and other *kūṭas*, if there is the imposition of the *kāmabīja*, it serves as the kindling for Vāmakeśvarī.
The meaning is that it comes to be.
In the *Nigamasāranirṇaya* composed by Śrī Ramāramaṇa Devaśarman, the third chapter, which explains the states of *chinna*, *līna*, and *suṣupti*, is now complete.

Thus, although various types of means for accomplishment have been written, nevertheless, since a mantra is not accomplished without the proper disposition (*bhāva*), the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi* is now being written.
In that regard, concerning the Cūḍāmaṇi:
Bhairava said:
O Mother Goddess, Mahāmāyā, who brings about both bondage and liberation! Now I desire to hear the unsurpassed lineage of the gurus.
The Goddess said:
Because the lineage of the gurus is manifold and because of the vastness of the mantras,
and because time itself is beginningless, how could I possibly explain it?
Having failed to know the teacher’s family, one will become lost on the path;
O Mahāvidyā, for one whose path is lost, there is no such scope for the fruit.
If there is no lineage succession among the gurus who have become disciples, then the tantras, mantras, and vidyās are fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
Whether there be twenty men, or even nine, or even three who are asleep,
if they are [awakened] through knowledge, the disciple shall belong to the lineage of the Guru, though his own progeny may have perished.

O Maheśvara, the auspicious and inauspicious nature of one's own lineage should be known as superior to that of the guru's lineage; and the lineage of the bestower of the mantra should be known as even more important than that of one's biological father.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, listen to these teachers everywhere:
first, O Lord of Gods, the giver of mantra is the supreme teacher in all cases.
For I am the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), the essence of all higher and lower gurus;
thus, in all tantras and vidyās, I am myself the one whose form is primordial speech.
Therefore, [I am] in the form of a person; from that [lineage], the succession of my own gurus—
neither they, nor those who are parts of me, nor especially my devotees, [are to be disparaged].
He is the source of all tantras and the bestower of purity everywhere.
Those Brahmins who belong to the Śiva and Āśva [lineages] are also preceptors in all places;
Gaṇeśa and those belonging to the Gāṇapatya [tradition] are considered masters of the Gaṇa-initiation.
O dear one, Śūra, the Śauras, Viṣṇu, and those devoted to Viṣṇu;
the Gurus of the multitude of Vidyās, O God, and likewise the Gurus of the multitude of Siddhas.
I shall briefly describe before you the multitudes of human beings;
the fourfold mantra proclaimed in all tantras and mantras.
Therein, first the Goddess was described; hear now her lineage of gurus:
Mahādevī, Mahākāla, Tripura, and Bhairava.
The gurus of the divine current have been declared; now I shall describe those of the innate current:
Brahmānanda, Pūrṇadeva, Calacitta, and Calācala.
Kumāra, Krodhana, Varada, Smadīyana, Māyā, and Māyāvatī— listen, O beloved, to the multitudes of these Mānavas.
Vimala, Kakara, Bhīmasena,
Sudhākara, Mīna, Gorakṣaka, Bhojadeva, and Prajāpati.
Mūladeva, Antideva, Vighneśvara, and Hutāśana; Samayānanda and Sahaja—these are to be known as the traditional gurus.
Now I shall describe the nine gurus who bestow both seen and unseen fruits:
Ūrdhvakeśa, Vyomakeśa, Nīlakaṇṭha, and Vṛṣadhvaja.
O child, listen with an attentive mind to the divine lineages that bestow success:
Vasiṣṭha, Kūrmanātha, Nīlanātha, and Maheśvara.
Harinātha will speak of the multitudes of men and the true gurus:
Tārāvatī, Bhānumatī, Jayāvidyā, and Mahodarī.
Sukhānanda, Parānanda, Pārijāta, Kuleśvara,
Virūpākṣa, and Pheravī— thus has the Tāriṇī-kula been described.

In the lineage of the Siddhas, the lineage of humans, and the divine lineage, the Supreme Lord— unshakeable, the crown of all, and the bearer of the names and forms of the three-fold embodiment— is established.
Now, O beloved, I shall tell you about Svapnāvatī and the gods:
Parānanda, Pūrṇeśī, Devadevī, and Janārdana.
Pūrṇeśī is the beautiful one; in the *Kāmika* [tantra], she is the uneven oblation. The Hero, endowed with the eastern state of being, is the attractor of those who are attracted.
And when the lineage of Siddhas exists, there is the Goddess, Bhairava, and Candraśekhara. Mā.
Among the multitude of men, the goddess Kalāvatī is full of forgiveness;
Maheśa is named Viṣṇu, and Gaṅgeśa is the leader of those who remember [the Lord].
Kalānanda, Kumārī, and all refined women—
whether they belong to any caste or have reached any stage of life— are all clever.
If a practitioner, disregarding the dignity due to his gurus, [approaches] women who are either young, intoxicated by youth, childless, or without sons;
One should worship Svapnavatī with speech, mind, and even body;
yet one who is possessed of all defects must be abandoned, being a stain upon the lineage.
Therefore, with every effort, one should never do anything unpleasant toward another's wife, nor even toward one's own; for women are portions of me.
Now, my child, I shall describe to you the lineage of the gurus of the sixteen [initiations]:
Ānandanātha, Deva, and likewise Paraprakāśaka.
Beyond that is the god Paraśiva, and beyond that is Paraśakti;
then Kauleśvara, the goddess Śakti, and Akuleśāna—who is he?

O you whose lower lip resembles Durgā, the fourfold Vidyā has been proclaimed;

Bhairava said:
O Great Goddess, you have indicated the conventions of the conduct of the samaya and the very conventions of the state of being; please explain them out of compassion.
