likewise, the Gurus here are of three kinds, as are the Mantras and Deities.
O Mahādeva, the first state is the most excellent, bestowing all prosperity;
the second is middling, and the third is censured by all.

O God, neither through extensive recitation, nor through burnt offerings, nor through bodily austerities and the like, do the yantras and mantras yield fruit without meditative cultivation (bhāva), nor indeed apart from it.

Bhairava said:

it is the foremost of all, skilled in initiating [beings] into the entire expansion of Māyā.
"O Goddess, there exists a cause for the sleep of all beings;
I shall explain it to you, provided that you have come to me as a son."
The Goddess said:
First, the divine state is described; listen with reverence.

and having meditated upon all that, I shall contemplate with a pure mind through yoga.
They were endowed with every noble lineage, born of various castes,
originating from diverse lands, and possessed of both virtue and beauty.

he engaged with them in pleasant conversation, play, curiosity, and so forth.

therefore, it is proclaimed that this continues up to the sixteenth [day].
In that regard, if there is the manifestation of being, that being is considered supreme;
having drunk [the nectar] from the feet up to the crown of the head, one would yet thirst to drink again.
22a) By the beauty of the tip of her forefoot, the moonlight of her toenails— which had shattered the darkness within— would become like the shell of a female tortoise.

The face has the form of a bindu, and beneath that are your two breasts.

having contemplated that form of its creative power within the Kulas and within the Akula.

O Goddess, how should one of noble lineage worship the Supreme Goddess?

Upon his arrival, she should offer a welcome through her playful yoga by means of her own grace;

Having meditated there upon the Kāmakalā, whose complete form consists of the bindu and the other [elements].

standing as the tree of my lineage, I shall nourish my own family.
Therefore, with every effort, one must protect it diligently;
for if, through the conjunction of fortune, there should be an abundance of offspring within one's own lineage.

"O Lord of Gods, there is nothing further to be done with effort; what is the use of these many words? I shall remain within the lineage—of this there is no need for deliberation."

O men, I am not even slightly dear to you because of my talkativeness, my universal hatred, my harsh speech, quarrels and the like, and my frequenting of lowly places.
Through the shattering of the vessel of the cosmic egg, he becomes endowed with that perfection within the living soul;

Bhairava said:

The Goddess said:

O Lord, for those in the fourth stage of life, the state of the Avadhūta is the great asceticism;
therein, through the yoga of my lineage, I am the bestower of gracious liberation.
If it should not be so, my child, listen as I tell you that:
when the absence of knowledge has arisen, one should pray to one's own Kaulikī.

Free from dualities, free from egoism, possessing pure channels, and observant of vows,

in the center, Suṣumnā is declared, and within that is she who possesses a variegated form.

Then, having pierced that mouth with the wind, one should cause it to burst open firmly;
thereafter, the blazing crest of the fever of desire arises from its breath.
Awakened in each wheel, he unites the individual soul (jīvātman) with the Supreme Family;
through that union, it attains eternal immortality.
Having pierced through the sky, the moon and the sun reached the end of the nose,
embracing the great downward-facing lotus by means of the *suṣumṇā*.
The Vyāghuṣṭhānāsikā has reached the middle and is joined with the variegated end;
having pierced upward through the linga, it then reaches the other Puṣkara.
Desiring the jewel of the mind and bestowing liberation,
she remained in the presence of the city, her life-breath restrained by the sight [of him].
One who understands this distinction pierces through it and goes to the supreme state;
though the living being has not seen that realm, it goes outside day after day.
By the measure of the fingers of one's own hand, half of that [distance] is for the upper [part],
twice that is for the time of sexual union, and three times that is for the period outside of eating.
O Goddess, if Bhairava flows upward for half [of the time] for three days,
or indeed if the vital breath flows downward during that same period, he surely abandons the body.
O Lord of Vahuka, having indeed brought about equilibrium within the body,
one should retain the downward-moving breath (apāna) at the opening of the mouth of the Kuṇḍalinī.
Then, having joined the individual soul (jīva) and led it through that which has no beginning or end, and having caused it to undergo coming and going, the human becomes Śiva.
Whatever is drunk or eaten, all that is offered into the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī;
having thus performed the oblation, one attains perfection and is not bound by bondage.
Having disregarded what ought not to be done and his own self-interest for the sake of Kuṇḍalinī, he said:
"O Mother, give me alms; I shall satisfy Kuṇḍalinī."
Having dwelt in the stage of the Avadhūta, one should be intent upon Bhairavānanda.
I am Bhairava, and there is no other; there is no deity superior to me anywhere.
All the acquisition of mantras and tantras has arisen within me, and not otherwise.
I am Śiva, the bliss of Bhairava; I am intoxicated, the leader of the Kula. My limbs are smeared with red sandalwood, and I am adorned with a red loincloth.
Wearing red garlands and garments, he should always be endowed with the [correct] cause;
thus, the mendicant intent on the conduct of Bhairava should wander for alms.
That land where both hatred and its object perish is led by a true lord of the earth; there he is not diminished by sin, nor is he slain by any living being.
In this regard, O Lord, those who perceive [him] through censure for even a moment are ruined;
therefore, he should be honored with effort and must never be treated with contempt.
O Lord of the Gods, whatever desire exists for someone, that action—whether pleasant or unpleasant—is his; other than that, O Lord of the Gods, there is the detailed practice of destruction.
They worship the Great Goddess by the mere sight of the limbs of the Kula;
wherever there may be flowers, incense, betel, and food offerings, that is where she resides.
Having mentally cast that out with the water from the outer [vessel],
O Kuleśvara, one should unite it with oneself in the form of the Goddess.
There is no worship, nor the placement [of mantras], nor final liberation, nor vows and the like;
I am the Full, I am Bhairava, I am eternal bliss, the imperishable.
I am of the nature of the stainless, I am the formless Lord;
I am endowed with all the scriptures and the like, and I have reached the further shore of the meaning of all mantras.
There is no god higher than him— none born in the past, nor shall there be one in the future—
who, being of the nature of bliss, acts for the welfare of all.
One should partake of food such as meat, combined with various fragrant substances, including fish that is free from foul odors, clarified butter, and divine offerings dear to [the deity]. 24b)
One should anoint various parts of the body with fragrant substances such as excellent, pure oil, and with various ointments.
He should cause him to perform a bath for extreme purity, whether subtle or gross,
and adorn him with fragrant flower garlands and ornaments of gold.
Having made his body smooth, naturally sweet, capable of assuming any form at will, enchanting, and auspiciously adorned, he became intent on speaking with gentle words.
Having reflected upon the form of the lineage and having resolved it within the potter,
one should indeed dwell during both day and night, intent upon the sacrificial oblation.
O God, having brought all those women born of the eight classes,
one should indeed contemplate their names and forms according to the sequence of their fragrances.
O Maheśvara, one should perform [this];
for the first Śakti is a twice-born woman whose internal organ is pure,
whose limbs are pure and stainless, who possesses divine fragrance, and who is enchanting.
For that Queen Svapnavatī should employ his mantra there with white flowers, food offerings, and salt mixed with honey.
Having worshipped as before, one should accomplish one's own practice—
that [goddess] who is tawny, blue, and black, whose eyes are auspicious like those of a young deer.
The practitioner, longing for the fragrant, [should avoid] that which has a foul odor.
A woman should be appointed for that [image]; she is proclaimed as the Goddess herself.
One should worship that Goddess with those flowers and with those food offerings.
She should be the third, fair-limbed, with eyes anointed by the fragrance of honey;
that goddess is named Tripurā, and one should worship her with red flowers.
The woman who possesses the scent of rut, slow-moving due to the stumbling of intoxication,
and endowed with the fragrance of raw flesh, is the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
The woman who has the scent of liquor, whose eyes are red and bulging, is proclaimed as Ugratārā; when intoxicated, she is the destroyer of sins.
A woman who has aśvagandhā [on her body] has long shanks and is captivating; she has eyes as tremulous as those of a doe, is mounted upon a horse, and bestows boons.
With the stench of raw flesh in her mouth and a putrid odor from her joints, she has hair that is blue and discolored; with a hideous face, she is Mahonmukhī Durgā.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, filled with various fragrances,
she possessed beautiful teeth, lovely hair, long eyes, and was captivating to the mind.
Skilled in various graceful arts and discerning the treatises of her lineage,
she gazed at the slightly sunken waist marked by the pressure of her husband’s chest.
That goddess, possessing beautiful teeth, shall be the promoter of all undertakings;
she is endowed with these fragrances, whether of various or of a single origin.
Those who are endowed with beauty and fragrance are proclaimed by name;
they must be protected with great effort so that they remain unblemished.
Having himself become known by the name Kāmeśvara and being devoted to desire,
he should perform the root-yoga after first increasing his internal disposition.
If the *mūla-yoga* occurs there, death will happen within seven days;
neither Viṣṇu, nor Hari, nor Śambhu, nor the Goddess, nor even the *Ṣoḍaśī* [can protect].
Neither the conqueror of death (Mṛtyuñjaya), nor the ritual placement (nyāsa), nor even meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) are of avail for him;
O Goddess, when death is destroyed, even the gods have no power over him.
Whether by means of the scripture, the root-yoga, or the method for those bitten by snakes, or even by means of the thunderbolt, the "abhi-jvara," or the power over great diseases;
One dies by that sin; this is the truth, O Lord, most certainly.
Divine activity, however, is manifold, distinguished by the categories of the seen and the unseen.
O Lord of Gods, what more need be said here in particular?
Having concealed her true self through illusion, she assumed the form of her own wife.
Having arrived, she always delights [there], and it certainly does not perish;
therefore, out of a desire for success, one should never do this in one's own country.
Or rather, O Lord of the Gods, why should one fall for the sake of destroying desire,
having taken up the staff of karma and established equality with Śiva?
The Self-born One performed a sevenfold encircling of that body with the thread of the discus for the purpose of binding all beings and protecting them.
"O highly fortunate one, you have been created; let the fierce binding be performed.
Having thus addressed that thread, it was wound seven times around the limb of Śiva.
Having reached the waking state for one-tenth of the duration, one should then recite the mantra of sleep—
the three *praṇavas* encased by the *saṃhāra-prabodhinī*.
This mantra for inducing sleep has been fully explained; it brings about slumber among all living beings.
Having performed this, the Lord himself becomes even more exalted than Maheśa.
If one's family should be fickle, wavering, and greedy for worldly enjoyment, then wings should be fashioned; the wise should never act otherwise.
O fair-limbed one, listen to our words which are the cause of auspiciousness;
having undertaken this task, you must perform what is desired by us.
Having spoken thus and performed their own duty, O Maheśvara, the best of practitioners should neither speak of nor practice the Kula-yoga.
The wife of a hero, the daughter of a hero, and the excellent woman who is the offspring of a hero—
these should not be drawn [as mantras] by practitioners beforehand, as long as their minds have not been agitated.
When that agitation of mind has arisen, whatever fruit results from the root-yoga [is attained].
That fruit arises, O Lord; it is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.
The supreme Maheśvarī herself is the wife of the Hero;
her daughter is indeed the primordial Tripurā, the first among the Kula-vidyās.
Her daughter-in-law is the mistress of the earth, the awakener of all mantras;
whether by right or otherwise, if she is the wife of a hero, she is a guru.
Merely by being seen, he becomes an adept who accomplishes all aims;
provided that, by the power of fortune, a hero’s wife is obtained.
Having brought the ripening of the fruit there, what is not accomplished on this earth?
O Mahādeva, I shall describe the method for the ripening of the fruit, which is honored by all the gods; it must not be disclosed under any circumstances.
O God, seeing the Kṛṣṇa family, the gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras come for the sake of the ripening of the fruit; therefore, one should reflect with great effort.
The dismissal should be performed, along with concealment, the state of being, and the rite of pacification;
according to the appropriate ritual procedure for each, one should make one's own family [of deities] possess its crest-lock.
O Mother, there is no dharma equal to devotion to one’s husband in the three worlds;
the husband is eternally the giver of life, and the husband alone is the supreme refuge.
The husband alone is the Supreme Brahman; the husband is the Lord who surpasses even one's own life-breath.
The husband is the master who embodies all sacred fords; the husband is eternally composed of all that is auspicious.
The husband alone is the great preceptor for all the goddesses;
having arrived, he should sit at her side, and she should remain standing while gazing at his face.
She should be skilled in discerning her husband’s intentions and joyful at the sight of him;
she should give appropriate answers and speak of past events.
That woman who, having abandoned one who embodies all the gods, goes to another man,
will certainly be born as a sow, a donkey, a crow, or a jackal.

Having assumed a body corresponding to the family-wealth of that lineage,
Bhairava, Vaṭuka, and the others [manifest].

having understood the arising [of the result] through the signs.

[one should perform] the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) through yoga for a distance of one cubit (*hasta*).

she brought the ripened fruit in a copper vessel to the great forest.

having performed the Dhenumudrā, one should perform the homa unobserved.

Instantly, honey-sweet success is established in the palm of one's hand, bestowing enjoyment;
the lord of practitioners, possessing a divine nature, becomes equal to Indra among mortals.
O Maheśvara, because you act for the beloved of the gods and because you bestow liberation.
For practitioners who possess knowledge of the *kula*, there is no fault in the felling of the ritual tree;
for the sake of bringing down this fruit, the sower of the fruit [reaps it] at every step.
He creates obstacles everywhere for his own sake and for a specific cause;
likewise, he certainly practices obstruction upon the fruit-bearing tree.
Just as a fruit-bearing tree might sometimes suffer loss through the power of fate, O Lord, so too may it happen for the practitioner; there is no doubt about this.
Whether it be through speech, mind, or even by body, if the fruit-bearing tree is harmed, then the deity perishes; remember this teaching!
O Lord, if the family tree of the practitioner is destroyed for his sake,
our family worship shall continue only so long as its restoration takes place.
Therefore, one's own kinsmen must be avoided with great effort;
for there is no one on this earth who is fit for the performance of this task.
If, in a country situated at a very great distance and devoid of the letters of one's name,
one performs [the rite], it will result in either auspiciousness, an obstacle, or the attainment of the fruit.
In that [practice], the practitioners who are deities of the family are not afflicted by defects;
however, this [method] for accomplishing the fruit may sometimes be predominant in obstacles.
One should never make a conventional agreement regarding the means of accomplishing a result;
for if one acts like a commoner, having merely obtained one's own fruit, [the goal is not achieved].
O Lord of Gods, there is certainly a fruit [of this], and one is surely bound by sin;
therein arises the intoxication of censure—of this there is no doubt.
O Lord, hear from me the fruit of Madhumatī;
from his mouth, the speech that sustains the earth arises like nectar.
Omniscient, the sovereign of all scriptures, and the leader of his lineage,
he enjoys abundant happiness upon the earth as long as the moon and sun endure.
27b) [He was attended] by celestial maidens and apsarases, and by divine gandharvas and cāraṇas,
who were endowed with various graceful charms and skilled in the knowledge of the arts.
With dances and very sweet songs, with various means and elixirs,
and with divine enjoyments that are difficult to obtain— things that produce joy for the sake of immortality.
Having mounted this chariot brought by the hands of celestial maidens,
the Supreme Goddess, her heart longing for the practitioner, approaches with eager anticipation.
Where the god Kāmeśvara has come under the power of thought,
there indeed the celestial maidens constantly go by the thousands.
Having made Indra the protector of his sons, that sinful soul died together with the practitioners;
there, through yoga, he enjoyed manifold pleasures.
O God, having remained on earth for a long time, one shall attain liberation at the end;
this divine state, which brings happiness, has been described to you.
It must not be given to just anyone; O Mahādeva, it should be guarded with great effort even from animals. O Bhairava, listen as the nature of the Hero (vīrabhāva) is described.
Having enjoyed [the fruits] with a mind free from dualities, and having placed the *kalā* within the heart,
he who is joined to the rise of the night-worship is indeed that God.
Taking his own lineage, he himself assumes the form of Bhairava;
the lineage takes the form of Bhairavī, and [this is] the detailed ritual of placement (nyāsa) upon their bodies.
Having performed the entire ritual placement (nyāsa), including that consisting of the nine triangles,
in the midst of a cushion of flowers amidst a profusion of scattered blossoms;
Having written the yantra with family substances (kuladravya) amidst a variety of perfumes,
one should worship the conch after first performing the installation of the water-jar (ghaṭasthāpana).
Having drawn a hexagon on one's left side with the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) in its center,
one should place there a water-pot made of gold or silver, or even one made of barley.
O Lord, one should place a pitcher made of copper, or of earth, or even one devoid of metal, scented with fragrant perfumes, according to the prescribed measure.
28a) One should fully worship the causal substance (*hetu-dravya*) according to the distinctions of the Brahmins and so forth;
having first inscribed the mantra there, whatever [substance] has arisen from one's own *kula*.
Having meditated there upon one's chosen deity, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
then, displaying the *dhenu-mudrā*, one should contemplate that [mantra] as nectar.
Upon seeing the vessel of Arghya, those lords of the Gaṇas indeed dance;
all the Bhairavas dance, and the Mothers and the Gaṇas dance.
All the gods, beginning with Indra, dance, longing for the honey;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others dance, intent on joy.
Having divided the arghya vessel into two parts, one portion should be given to the Guru;
likewise, having given [the other] to the Kula, one should perform the libation for the Deity with the remaining one.
O God, having drunk the essence of the *kula*, adorned with various ornaments,
if the Guru is not personally present, then one should discharge it into water.

O Ānanda, having become possessed of form, one should worship the Supreme Goddess after worshipping her upon the respective yantras according to the procedure prescribed for each specific ritual manual (kalpa).
Having performed the ritual dismissal, one should then employ that essence within one's own lineage;
by drinking the nectar of that drop, I partake of immortality.
By eating the juice of that wheel with honey, one becomes like a tree in full bloom;
by grasping its fruit, O Lord, one ascends the peak of Mount Sumeru.
Merely by embracing the creeper, her body becomes washed with nectar;
when the root-yoga has been performed there, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times.
Then, having taken the sacrificial substance purified by recitation, one should perform the libation;
O Lord, having performed the libation, one should proceed while circumambulating.
Having prostrated and praised him with the hymn prescribed for the ritual manual, one should then please [the deity], saying:
"O God, this Vīra-kula is beautiful and most enchanting."
O Bhairava, in whatever region or family that hero resides,
there shall be no fear of pestilence, nor any fear of the king or similar threats.
There, O Mahādeva, there shall always be auspiciousness that increases wealth and sons; there, prosperity shall remain forever firmly established.
The mantra of Svapnaprabodhinī must certainly be applied with effort at the foot of a tree; then no obstacle will arise.
Even if it is seized through union with another hero, [the result] is not [attained];
however, by the Yoginīs they are worshipped, and they are protected from sin.
Wherever one goes on that day, even to a cremation ground,
the fruit of worship there shall be equal to that of seven days.
When the four-month period has passed there, there shall be no other fruit; "O Lord, [this] would be superior"— thus intent on this thought,
a disturbance arises within me.
Endowed with that portion, the excellent hero shall be well-illuminated;
through enjoyment he attains liberation, and through enjoyment he accomplishes the Kula practice.
Having encountered [this] without cause, O Maheśvara...
there is the fault of thinking "it is red," and there is Māyā which is...
If one sleeps, whatever one does, or whatever one desires...
If one should take [it] after meditating upon all that as having the form of the Kula, one will be happy.
In a solitary, uninhabited place, in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a forest,
in an empty house, or on a riverbank, one should dwell free from attachment.
For heroes, the time for recitation is praised as being at all times;
it should be performed in any place and on any sacred seat (pīṭha), without any doubt.
If a Brahmin should become fallen and devoted solely to family wealth, then [the ritual] must not be performed; rather, the satisfaction of the lineage must be achieved through [other means].
Furthermore, within the *puṣpagarbha*, there is a captivating place of the lineage (kula),
which is the mouth of all the gods and consists of the essence of the arts of great desire.
The horse-loving god Sadāśiva himself is ever present within the flower.
Taking a small amount from that [mixture], one should place sandalwood—or red saffron dye—into the center of the flower; therein resides the essence of Śiva.
One should unite [the self] with the power of Śiva, contemplating their oneness with the intellect;
having worshipped there for a moment and having ascertained the Supreme Goddess.

Having recited [the mantra], that very substance arising from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa)—which is most difficult to obtain—should be known as superior even to nectar; this substance is exceedingly rare.
O Bhairava, where the Aparājita flower, the javā flower,
the red and white karavīra, or the droṇa plant grows;
The Goddess dwells there eternally; my worship is performed in that yantra.
For every single javā flower offered upon a silk cloth, one shall obtain the fruit.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are certainly destroyed in an instant;
O Maheśvarī, it is impossible to describe the greatness of the other [mantra].
The rite of heroic accomplishment (vīrasādhana) must be performed by heroic men;
it may also be performed by divine beings, but not by those who are bound (paśus) or by common, vulgar folk.
It is better to perform the work of a commoner than that of a beast; this is the certain conclusion.
Whatever was previously taught at the proper time, O Śakti, that is the means for accomplishing the mantra.
A hero of great power should prepare collyrium, pills, and so forth;
that which is described as the "piercing" (bhedasara) is the one that exists in every divine hero, in every month.
The *śānta* (peaceful) hero is tranquil, disciplined, sweet, and possessed of refined grace;
the *divya* (divine) hero is generally like a god; and the *vīra* (heroic) hero has an exalted mind.
Whether adorned with magnificent ornaments or smeared with sandalwood paste,
whether concealing his outward appearance or abandoned by his family, O Kulabhairava!
Whether smeared with red sandalwood paste or not a Vaiṣṇava, whether unconsecrated or consecrated, the Lord of the Family is eternally manifest.
One should always remain joyful and content whether met with contempt or honor; whether intent on reviling the deity or even intent on worshipping that very deity.
Delighting in worship there, beneficial, and established in the family-to-family tradition,
endowed with his own true nature, he should move about upon the earth like a god.
The preliminary rite (puraścaryā) must be performed at night within one's own family lineage, and not otherwise;
for just as there is no Vedic ritual for a twice-born man devoid of the Vedas, so too there is no worship of the deity [without this].
O Goddess, just as devotion does not flourish without devotion to Viṣṇu,
so too liberation becomes a mere object of ridicule without the knowledge of Śakti.
Just as one has no entitlement whatsoever to the Tantra without a guru,
so too is a woman deprived of all ritual action when she is without a husband.
Likewise, O Kaula, without the Kula there is no deity, no hero, and no adept;
one is not qualified [for the practice]. Therefore, be devoted to the inner state (bhāva).
How can one who possesses an undisciplined family be an impartial seeker of truth?
Therefore, one should act with such effort that [the family] becomes endowed with discipline.
In the Kuleśāstra, there is no qualification whatsoever for those characterized by existence or non-existence;
therefore, a practitioner who is purified of existence shall become a Kaulika.
The Goddess said:
I shall explain the state of the sacrificial animal (paśubhāva); listen, O dear one, for it is of great benefit.
Having received the initiation of the animal according to the prescribed rule, one should be intent upon that state.
First, one should diligently attain purity regarding the matter at hand;
one should take one's meal while paying homage and not even mentally recollecting a woman.
One should have no greed for another’s wealth, nor should the mind be attached to enjoyments,
whether on the shore of the ocean, on a mountain, in a forest, or in a temple of the gods.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a secluded place, or in a beautiful and holy field,
one should not allow a Śūdra to see [the ritual], and one should keep crookedness far away.
The deities of pure complexion should be meditated upon by those who are well-composed;
one should perform the worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day and practice recitation at the three junctions of the day.
One should never touch the rosary or the yantra at night.
One should not release [the mantra] after eating; one should remain silent during all ritual acts.
Furthermore, the best of practitioners should never approach a woman during the time of the sacred festivals (parvan).
One should worship by personally bringing flowers, incense, and water;
one must avoid sexual intercourse, the suppression of talk concerning it, and assemblies devoted to it.
He should not approach his own wife except during her fertile period, yet he should do so with reverence;
he should have faith in listening to the Purāṇas and be devoted to the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas.
O Supreme Lord, a wise man should not eat betel leaf at night;
whatever has been instructed by the Guru, all that one should perform with diligence.
O Bhairava, having touched one's own kindred flowers and ritual substances,
one becomes pure after three nights by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and by offering praise.
One devoted to the Goddess should not wear red clothing;
furthermore, one should perform the ritual according to the procedure prescribed in the Viṣṇu-mantra.
O heroine honored by heroes, one should not engage in idle chatter; likewise, one should avoid eating mixed food, giving grass first to a cow, and performing the twilight worship at improper times.

O God Bhairava, one devoted to Dharma may perform ritual bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha) and travel to the regions of the sacred seats (pīṭha), yet such a person is merely a beast of two kinds; he is not equal to those who preceded him.
His qualification is for worship, and not for the state of a guru in any way;
nor is there qualification for the former [the guru] regarding worship performed at a sacred site or upon arrival.
But the former should be driven out from his own country by all the Kaulas;
merely by seeing him first, one should perform the rite of beholding the Kula.
O Lord, even a sin such as the killing of a Brahmin is better endured;
I tell you the truth, the absolute truth: in this matter, the mere sight of you [is sufficient].
O Lord of Gods, O Master, although that Self of mine is indeed all-pervading, nevertheless, O Ishvara,
a doubt arises within me at every step.
It is better to abandon one's strength than to destroy one's own family;
it would be better to suffer the censure of one's own family than to cause its prosperity.
Better is the ruin of one's own family, better is the destruction of one's own lineage;
better, through body, mind, or speech, is the downfall of one's own kin.
One should not form a prior intimacy with me for the sake of injuring my body;
among the family scriptures, this is the gravest sin regarding the leader of the clan.

In one's own family, there is great censure; in the family of the Lord of the Family (Kuleśvara), there is the application of supreme yoga. Even greater than that, great sin arises from association with worldly beings (paśu).
In every way, O Kuleśvara, there are two states therein:
existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*vibhāva*), which are established as such.
O God, through the manifestation of two births by means of the state of a bound soul (paśubhāva), that being becomes a hero (vīra); from that, [the state of a divya] arises.
A hero is not born by chance; the hero is a god, the progenitor of beings. There is no doubt regarding the divine hero; he is designated as such.
Existence (*bhāva*), however, is a property of the mind; as for its [presence] in sound, it is...
Therefore, existence should not be [further] discussed; only a mere indication has been provided.
Just as [a thing] arises through the accomplishment of [its causes],
so too is the manifestation and disappearance of existence contemplated by the mind.
O Lord, the one and only Great Being assumes manifoldness through the differentiation of limiting conditions (*upādhi*); thus it is said.
The Lord, the mass of the essence of bliss, the bearer of the supreme form,
He alone is the Self in the form of the gods— the great, partless Lord.
He alone is indeed to be heard, to be reflected upon, and to be meditated upon;
He is the Lord of Gods manifest before one's eyes. He is to be worshipped with various seats, to be proclaimed by the Vedas, and to be contemplated by the mind and other faculties.
This should be meditated upon by those who have attained [the necessary realization] and have been instructed by their guru.
Then, in that very moment, he who is the self of all becomes directly manifest;
for when that God is manifest, O Lord of Gods, the Supreme Lord is manifest.
O God, through various states of being, even that state dissolves therein;
just as a cow, having eaten various kinds of fodder, becomes one with its essence.
O Lord, through the practice of churning milk and other substances, it acquires various forms;
O God, from that [milk] arises grass-juice, and from that, a superior juice.
Therefore, from that comes curd, from that the sacrificial oblation, and from that the emergence of the essence;
that very thing is its cause, it is its effect, and it is obtained as such.
And it is observed, O Mahādeva, that neither effect nor cause exists;
for that [reality] is divided into distinctions through its connection with such states as "being milk" and so forth.
In the very same way, this very self, though born again and again in various forms and wombs, appears divided due to the difference in time.
He is the one who is born, he is the one who dies; he is the one who is bound, he is the one who is liberated;
he is the man, he is the woman, and he is also the neuter; he is the learned one, and he alone is that very same person.
Through union with various meditations, the Lord assumes manifold forms;
yet He is that very Self, one alone, eternal, and consisting of the essence of all.
The unmanifest is indeed known as manifest through its nature;
therefore, it is known by means of the yoga of nature, and never otherwise.
Just as a jar is not perceived when it lacks its connection with "jar-ness," so too,
even though it is being distinguished from others, it does not attain the state of being a distinct entity.
Without me, no distinctions whatsoever can ever arise in the Person—
not through ritual applications, nor through forms of knowledge, nor through sacred revelation, nor through the lineages of gurus.
By nature Brahman is known; by nature the person dissolves;
everything is presided over by nature; by nature the world is desired.
By nature one undergoes differentiation; by nature one may undergo differentiation. (31b) It is better that there be no *prakṛti* at all than that the Supreme Lord be a neuter being.
O Maheśvara, the reality of those two is the object known as "existence" (sara).
The state of equilibrium between the two, however, is the reality of things, the excellent state;
when that is known, this person is himself the very nature of consciousness and wisdom.
O Goddess of gods, the Person, who is changeless and the object of the authority of all the Vedas, becomes manifest; he is the Self, the self-existent Bhava himself.
There are many ways to know the eternal Brahman;
nevertheless, through the application of *prakṛti*, it quickly comes within the range of direct perception.

Just as sea-faring merchants, having taken their ship to various regions and crossed the ocean, enter it again after a long time; so too does one who has practiced yoga emerge from the ocean of worldly existence.
Just as people on the shore take a boat and cross in an instant, O Lord,
so too does one attain Brahman through devotion to Viṣṇu, and even by being absorbed in His nature, O Lord.
If there is no difference in kind (vaijātya) therein, how can that be its cause?
Therefore, those [subsequent moments] have passed beyond [the preceding], for they have indeed attained the status of being causes.
"O child, these are not the causes; primordial nature (prakṛti) is the cause.
The female state is to be known as nature, while the male state is considered the person (puruṣa)."
O Lord Bhairava, knowledge is to be known through the division of the knower and the knowable;
it is like a jar, direct perception, a means of knowledge, or light that colors [an object].
The sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth, do not possess even the slightest degree of non-conceptual [perception].
This concludes the *Nigamasāranirṇaya* composed by Devaśarman, the beloved of Śrī Ramā.
Now, where there is enjoyment (*bhoga*), there is no liberation (*mokṣa*); and where there is liberation, there is no enjoyment.
For one intent on the worship of Śrīsundarī, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are indeed held in the palm of the hand.
Thus, because both [results] are heard through the praise as the fruits [of the practice], and since it serves as the means for both and constitutes a human goal (*puruṣārtha*),
the Sundarī-mantra is first written down.
32a) Here,
although the sixteen-syllable [mantra] holds primacy because it is of the nature of the waking state, nevertheless,
according to the statement: "O Bhadrā, the sixteen-syllable [mantra] indeed consists of the three peaks (trikūṭa) and all [the letters]," the sixteen-syllable [mantra] also contains the three peaks.
First, the mantras of Trikūṭa are written down.
In that regard, it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
Bhūmi, Candra, Śiva, Māyā, Śakti, Kṛṣṇa, Adhva, Mādana,
Arddhacandra, and Bindu— these nine syllables are said to be Meru.

The Meru mountains from which the mantras of Mahātripurasundarī arise are as follows: the letter *la* is the Earth; the letter *sa* is the Moon; the letter *ha* is Śiva; the letter *ī* is Māyā; the letter *a* is Śakti; the letter *ra* is the Path of Kṛṣṇa (Fire); and the letter *ka* is Mādana. These syllables are the Meru mountains of the Sundarī mantras.
The meaning is that within the Sundarī mantras, there is no syllable that exceeds those [specific] syllables. Now, the Kāmarāja.
O fair-faced one, according to one's capacity, there are four syllables in the middle of the *kala*;
the *vāgbhava* consists of five syllables, and then the *kāmarāja* is taught.
O auspicious lady, this six-syllabled Kāmarāja mantra begins with Śivacandra and ends with Śiva, with its eyes closed; it is the enchantment of all.
O Varārohā, the seed-syllable of Śakti, preceded by the Moon (the letter *a*), bestows all siddhis;
its form consists of four syllables, while Tripurā consists of three syllables.
Śakti is the letter *e*; the fourth vowel is the long *ī*, which should be written between the letters *ka* and *la*. Thus, the form is *ka-e-ī-la*, followed by the Māyā-bīja, *hrīṃ*.

If it is asked how [the seed-syllable] is obtained when the seed-syllable of Māyā is not written in the Tantra, [it is replied]: "Sakalā Bhuvaneśānī and Kāmeśī are the supreme seed-syllables; by means of these, I shall specifically declare all the Vidyās. From this, it is obtained.

Now, if it is asked: "Since the entire middle portion of *tūryapārṇa* is prescribed for the *śakti*, how can the middle portion of a *kala* also be prescribed for the *śakti*?"—if this is raised, we say no, because there is a contradiction with another tantra; for instance, in the *Catuḥśatikā*:
Mādana (Kāma-bīja) is below that; Śakti is at its end; Mālinī is the Bindu.
And since it is written that "the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśānī is Aindra, and that becomes Vāgbhava," [it follows].

Regarding "the seed of desire is *moha-mādana*": in the word *mādane*, the letter *ka* [is the first], meaning that which begins with Śiva (ha) and the Moon (sa). At the end of Śiva (*śivānte*) is the letter *ha*; the "end" (*anta*) is the letter *la*. That which has these as its middle and end—[here] there is an elision of the word [itself]—is thus *hasakala hrīṃ*. According to the previous statement, this is the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī everywhere. Now, regarding "in *mādane*, [beginning with] Śiva and the Moon": [this refers to the same sequence].
Thus, how could the presence of *mādana* not exist at the beginning of this *śivacandra*?

Having divided the *śivabīja* threefold according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*naya*), one removes two [units] by means of the first; below the first [remains] the syllable of *mādana*.
One should place the seed-syllables of Indra (L) below Śiva (H) for the state of maintenance (sthiti);
likewise, for dissolution (laya), one should place the fire-syllable (R) below Śiva, according to the scriptural statement: "Fire, the fourth [vowel], and the moon."
According to the reading "the syllable *madana* [is] below the first," it is indeed written as a compound; this is its meaning.

Having written the seed-syllable of Śiva, the letter *ha*, in three ways: two [of these] are preceded by the first [letter], [which is] devoid of the initial *sa*; one is accompanied by the initial *sa*. Having placed the letter *ka*—the syllable of Madana—below the first *ha* and below the *sa*, and having placed the seed-syllable of Indra, the letter *la*, below that *ha*, there is then dissolution (*laya*).
Having placed the letter *ra* and the vowel *ī* at the beginning of the vowels, one should extract the seed-syllable in the middle from below the letter *ha*;
this he calls the "seed of Śakti. The phrase "beginning with the moon" means its nature is that of the digit (*kalā*).

33a) Regarding the statement "therefore, the entire [mantra] is *hrīḥ*": if it is asked how the nature of the *kala*s is obtained since it is not explicitly mentioned in the tantra that sets forth the mantra, [the answer is: because the nature of the *kala*s beginning with *candra* is mentioned in another tantra.
For it is said thus in the Catuḥśatikā:
O Maheśānī, having employed the seed-syllable of Māyā joined with Mādana and Śakra,
and then the seed-syllable of Candra alone, O Varānanā.
One should extract the seed-syllable of Śakti by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra-krama).
Its meaning is as follows:

*Māyā* is *hrīṃ*; *mādana* is the letter *ka*; *Śakra* is the letter *la*; and *candra* is the letter *sa*. Regarding the sequence of dissolution (*saṃhāra-krama*), if it is argued that by the sequence beginning with *candra*—that is, by the sequence of dissolution—the letter *la* is obtained after the letter *sa*, [we reply that] because the term "joined with Śakra" (*śakrasaṃyutam*) functions as an adjective and is therefore subordinate, it is placed first [in the compound]. By this...
The fifteen-syllable mantra known as Trikūṭa-Kāmarāja is called Vidya; such is the direction [of the teaching].
Now, here is the extraction [of the meaning] from that, as it appears in the *Muṇḍamālā*:
This [Vidyā], known as Kāmarājā, was pierced by the Flower-Bowed One (Kāmadeva);
she was formerly worshipped by Śakra and established throughout the worlds.

By him, through the curse of Kāma, Indrāṇī was united with Bhuvaneśī, and thus her deliverance was accomplished; Bhuvaneśī is "hrīṃ. Likewise, O beautiful one, having omitted the Śakti and the fourth [syllable] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, and having placed Śiva and the Moon (the Bindu) at the beginning, this becomes Lopāmudrā. Its meaning is as follows:

Having omitted the power (śakti) of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, which consists of the letter *e* and the fourth vowel *ī*, and having joined it at the beginning with the letters *ha* and *sa* from Śiva and Candra, it becomes Lopaāmudrā.
Therefore, "ha sakala hrīḥ" is the first seed-syllable; [together with the following], these two seed-syllables constitute Kāmarāja.
The seed-syllable, when honored with sixty verses, shall become [accomplished].

The third power of Vidyā, together with the two syllables of form at the beginning of initiation and so forth, becomes Lopa-mudrā as the second. [The third seed-syllable] consists of the first two [syllables] as before. [This is] Brahma-vidyā.
The syllable Raṃ, situated in the center of Śaktimādana, should be made into Śiva; then Vāgbhava follows, and that which begins with Śiva is called Kāmarāja.
[It is] worshipped. The meaning of this is as follows:

One should place Śiva between the two *ka*s, [and] the third seed-syllable preceded by the moon and *ha*. By this, the mantra in its true form—*ka ha e ī la hrīṃ*, *ha ha sa ka ha la hrīṃ*, *sa sa ka la hrīṃ*—becomes worshipped. Otherwise, it begins with Śiva and so forth.

Regarding the word "first" (*ādya*): by this, that which was stated by Devanātha Upādhyāya—that the remaining two seed-syllables exist as they are—is also refuted. Likewise: "O you who are worshipped by the gods, having written the second [syllable] of Lopāmudrā, write the name again, situated in the fourth and fifth [positions]."
Having abandoned these lords of the worlds, one should utter [the mantra] as a single form;
thus the Vidyā, consisting of four peaks, becomes propitiated by Śaṅkara.
This is its meaning.
Having extracted the second [syllable] *lopāmudrā* and having written it as *puṣṭā*,
one abandons *bhuvaneśvarī*, who resides in the fourth and fifth *kūṭas*, upon the attainment of oneness.
She becomes propitiated by Śaṅkara.
Likewise, having written Lopāmudrā and Devī, immediately thereafter,
there shall be the Nandikeśvara-vidyā and the Vaiṣṇavī of the six peaks.
This is its meaning.
From the scriptural statement, "Lopāmudrā is my second," it follows that when Nandikeśvara is made the third,
Lopāmudrā becomes the Vaiṣṇavī consisting of six peaks (ṣaṭkūṭā).
Just as in the Nandikeśvara-vidyā, so too in the vidyā known as Kāmarāja, one should discard the Vāgbhava and Mādana [syllables];
having likewise joined the Moon (the Bindu) in the Kāmarāja, thereafter—
Having abandoned the moon, one should place it in the mouth; this is the Vidyā honored by Nandin.
This is its meaning:

In the first seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the *Vāgbhava* [part] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, one should discard the "intoxicating" letter *ka* and place the "moon" letter *sa*. Thus, it becomes *sa e ī la hrīṃ*. Then, in the *Kāmarāja* [part], having omitted the "moon" seed-syllable *sa*, one should place the "intoxicating" letter *ka* at the beginning. Thus, it becomes *kaha kaha la hrīṃ*; however, this is not done by omitting the "moon."
"One should place the moon with its mark in the mouth"—thus one should cast the *kāma* [syllable] there; O Dakṣiṇāmūrti, that is the third [syllable], which is like the *Kāmarāja*.

Likewise, O Goddess, in the Vāgbhava [Kūṭa], there is *hasa* (ha-sa) preceded by the Moon (i); in the Kāmarāja [Kūṭa], there is *mādana* (ka) situated in the middle of Śiva (ha), accompanied by *śaktikūṭa* (e) and joined with *hasa*.
This Vidyā, known as Candrarādhita, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Its meaning is as follows:

One should make the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja begin with *hasa*; thus, *ha sa ka e ī la hrīṃ* is Kāmarāja. One should make it begin with *candra* (the moon); therefore, the Mādana arises between the two *ha* syllables of Śiva and Śivā;
together with that, *ka pha la hrīṃ* is the Śakti-bīja accompanied by *hasa*; thus, *ha sa sakala*.
"HRĪM"—this [seed-syllable] is worshipped by Candra. Likewise, O Pārvatī, listen to the third [syllable]: the Vāgbhava seed-syllable beginning with HA and ending with ŚIVA, with HA in the middle;
and the Mādana [syllable] in the Kāma-bīja. Listen to the third."
She whose seed-syllable is *hasa* and who is the source of power is worshipped by Kuvera.
This is its meaning:
The meaning is that *vāgbhava* begins with *hasa*, and *mādana* begins with the letter *ha*. Therefore, the connection is as follows:

one should place *ka*—which is preceded by *śiva* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) and situated between *ha* and *sa*—within *mādana*. Thus, the letter *ka*, which resides within the *vidyā* (mantra) beginning with *ha*, should be placed between *ha* and *sa*.

The meaning is that one should perform [this]. Thus, *ha ka sa ha la hrīṃ*—the third seed-syllable of Śakti beginning with *ha*, namely *ha sa sa ka la hrīṃ*—is the Vidyā propitiated by Kubera. Likewise, in the case of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, having omitted the earth [syllable] in the third [position], [the mantra is formed].
O Goddess, place her there below the moon, situated within the seed-syllable of Śakti;
this is the Vidyā worshipped by Indra, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This is its meaning.

In the third seed-syllable of power (*śakti-bīja*) belonging to the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, one removes the letter *la*, representing the earth element, from its stated position and places it below the moon (the vowel *u*) and below the letter *sa*. By this, [the mantra becomes] *sakala hrīṃ*; thus, the final part is as described, while the first two parts are like those of Kāmarāja—this is the summary.
Thus, having explained the *trikūṭa-vidyā*, and since the explanation of the *ṣoḍaśī* depends upon that,
the *ṣoḍaśī* is now written down:
"Now I shall declare that Vidyā, the first of all, which bestows all accomplishments."
She is eternal, composed of the Word-Brahman, and has the nature of sixteen syllables.
A wise person should not practice Śrīvidyā— which is the very nature of the knowledge of Brahman and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation— without the feet of a Guru.
If one should eat [the food] of the yoginīs, he would incur the curse of the glorious Guru. A wise man should not give the sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā to anyone.
"A kingdom may be given, wealth may be given, or even a boon may be granted at any time;
however, success [in this matter] would be destroyed by public disclosure—such is the command issued by Śambhu."
Even at the cost of giving away one's kingdom, or even at the cost of one's own life,
one should give away one's entire empire, as well as sons, friends, and wife.
Even one's own head, together with one's life-breath, should not be given away; yet the sixteen-syllable mantra, when being recited, is remembered as encompassing all forms of speech.
The sixteen-syllable Śrīvidyā is the reality devoid of utterance;
I shall explain this most difficult to attain [mantra] in four ways.
Whichever vidyā has been extracted from the Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra,
each and every one of them is the Ṣoḍaśī-vidyā in its entirety, through the differentiation of its seed-syllables (bīja).
Beginning with Candra and ending with Vāruṇa, and likewise beginning with Śakra individually;
preceded by the left eye, the Bindu, and the Nāda, it consists of the digits (kalās) of the Universal Mother.

By joining [the letters] at the beginning of the *vidyā*, there is the sixteen-fold (*ṣoḍaśī*) form of the waking state. "Candra" (moon) is the letter *sa*; that which begins with it is the letter *ha*.

That which begins with the moon (*candrādya*) is the letter *va*, which is Varuṇa. The end of that is the letter *sa*—this is the meaning. "Accompanied by Śakra and so forth" means as follows: Śakra is the letter *la*; its beginning is the letter *ra*. Together with that, there are two separate syllables.

The form is the left eye, which is the long *īkāra*. It is said that this is joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, and so on; thus, by being joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, the forms become *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*. O God, the application of these two at the beginning of the *vidyā* constitutes the sixteen-syllable *jāgradrūpā-ṣoḍaśī*;
and the *vidyā* here is the *Kāmarāja*.
Arising, waking, awareness, and the constant withdrawal of the mind—these four aspects are established in the waking state; this is the waking [state]. (Guṇa 35b)
O auspicious one, Trikūṭā consists of three peaks alone, while Pañcakūṭā indeed has five; Vaiṣṇavī would have eight peaks, and thus Nārāyaṇī likewise.
By that, this seed...
[the five peaks] become the sixteen-fold Vaiṣṇavī and Nārāyaṇī; she becomes the eight-peak [form]. Of these two, the six-peak Kāminī... [removes] the sin at the end of the mode.

And because it is all-pervasive, it is motionless; for it is directly of the nature of Brahman, having the form of deep sleep. However, the Śāmbhavī [power] has the form of waking due to the application of the single seed-syllable.
Therefore, even in each of those two seeds, there is the Ṣoḍaśī.
At the beginning of wakefulness and other states, the dream-state consists of rajas;
there is delusion month after month, and the mind is fixed upon sense objects.
The fourth digit (*kalā*) is that which is the sixteenth, O Śiva and Śakti.
Adorned with the Vedas and other scriptures, she consists of the nature of Śiva and Śakti;
the meaning of her recollection is [as follows].

The sixteen-fold [vidyā] consisting of five peaks (*pañcakūṭātmikā*) has been described; beginning with *vaya* and so forth, the syllable *oṃ* is used, by which the peaks [are formed], such as the union of Śiva and Śakti, for example: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, which is the Kāmarāja [bīja]. Thus, it exists within its own states of waking, deep sleep, and dreaming.

Thus, three divisions have been described; furthermore, the sixteenth, known as Kāmarāja, becomes threefold by means of the seed-syllable (bīja): having placed the seed-syllable of Kāmarāja before the letter *ā* and above it.
36a) The sixteenth is known as Kāmarājā; she is considered to have been propitiated by Kandarpa. By her grace, even Kāma attained victory over the three worlds.
One who possesses all beauty and auspiciousness should bring [the subject] under control by means of the three-fold [mantra].
This is its meaning.

By placing the seed-syllable of Gopāla, *klīṃ*, to the east of Kāmarāja, the sixteen-syllabled Vidyā worshipped by Kandarpa is written; likewise, when preceded by Māyā (*hrīṃ*), this sixteen-syllabled Vidyā is difficult for all to obtain.
This very [goddess] was propitiated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, since she is the sovereign of the earth;
and by her grace, Kṛṣṇa himself sustains the three qualities (guṇas).
This is its meaning:
If this *māyā* worshipped by Kandarppa, preceded by *hrīṃ* and *rūpā*, becomes [the same as] that worshipped by Śrīkṛṣṇa,

it is not the case that *māyā* is preceded by the *kāmarāja-vidyā*. For, by the statement "but the sixteen-fold [vidyā] in its waking form [is identical] due to the application of the single seed-syllable," non-difference is established.
Likewise, the sixteenfold Vidyā bestows all prosperity;
this Vidyā, propitiated by Lakṣmī, possesses a threefold quality.
The meaning of this is: by whose grace indeed the Vaiṣṇavī Lakṣmī is beloved.

The previously mentioned *Ṣoḍaśī* worshipped by Kandarpya is the *Śrīmata*; it is joined with the seed-syllable *Śrīṃ* and is worshipped by Lakṣmī, but it is not the *Kāmarāja-vidyā*, because that would result in a contradiction regarding the prior classification. Likewise, I shall declare another *Ṣoḍaśī*, which is difficult for all to obtain.
In the beginning of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, the venerable Kāmayoni [is taught] in due order;
by reciting this with devotion, the practitioner attains the state of Lord of Speech. This most secret command is hidden within the seven Tantras.
There shall be no knowledge equal to this;
such is its meaning.
In the previously mentioned Kāmarāja-vidyā and others, the bathing with the waves of *klīṃ aiṃ śrīṃ*— the source of desire and fortune— is performed from the beginning; for Lakṣmī, the source,
has not been propitiated within life itself merely by the practice of this [mantra].

The life-force becomes unimpeded; the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbīja*) is [of the form] *ai*, and the seed-syllable of the *haṃsa* is [of the form] *haṃ*. If the seed-syllable is preceded by the seed-syllable of the pair of dots (*binduyugbīja*), then it is auspicious and becomes worshiped; the seed-syllable of the pair of dots is...

Raḥ. The seed-syllable of Ta... is the great... gati. The meaning is the Kāmarāja-vidyā; if it is preceded by Tāra, then it is remembered as being of such a nature. ... [omitted] ... *Note: Due to the significant amount of illegible characters (indicated by asterisks) in the source text, the translation reflects the recoverable portions of the Sanskrit technical terminology regarding mantra-seeds (bīja), the Kāmarāja-vidyā, and the Tāra-mantra.*

Likewise, Lopāmudrā also possesses a twelvefold nature. Furthermore, according to the scriptural statement that "all Trikūṭās, beginning with Sakalā and Bhadrā, extend up to the sixteenth," it is indeed the case that all [of them] are Trikūṭā.

If it is argued that since [the *ṣoḍaśī*] attains the state of being the sixteenth, how can there be a mention of the object of *lopā*, this is merely a direction for the purpose of demonstrating its most profound secrecy.
Now the Mahāṣoḍaśī is described.
Now, however, I shall proclaim the Sixteenth [Vidyā], which is difficult for all to attain;
by the mere performance of its ritual procedure, one directly realizes Brahman—of this there is no doubt.

That which is characterized as pure, radiant consciousness alone, manifesting from deep sleep up to the waking state, has reached the status of the "remainder" (śeṣatā); it is the fourth state (turyā), the supreme digit.
It is described as being liberated from existence and non-existence, transcending all qualities;
it consists of dispassion, the desire for liberation, meditative absorption, and a pure mind.
What is the reality of existence and non-existence? These are indeed the digits (kalās) of the fourth state (turyā), which is without doors;
by whose grace the Lord Śiva is the all-pervading sovereign of the worlds.
This is the supreme knowledge among all sciences, difficult to find in any treatise;
by its single recitation, millions of great sins are destroyed.
Thousands of ritual baths at sacred fords, hundreds of gifts of elephants, hundreds of thousands of Tulāpuruṣa sacrifices, and hundreds of horse-sacrifices— [all these are equaled by this].
They do not equal it anywhere; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
How much more so when the absolute Brahman is uttered even once?
Thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices, as well as the [merit] of the earth’s life-force,
and pilgrimages to Kāśī and other holy sites numbering three and a half crores— [all these are attained].
They are equal in every respect; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
By the grace of the glorious Guru, I shall explain the supreme [truth] through symbolic terminology.
A wise person who desires his own welfare should protect this [mantra] in every way:

it begins with *Śiva*, ends with *Śānta*, consists of seventy million [recitations], concludes with *Sūkṣma*, and is adorned by eight horses (*aśva*). O Goddess, its right arm is the path of Indra (*śakrayana*), and its left is marked by the digit of the moon (*kalā*).

37b) That which is below the tantra is bliss; it is life (*jīva*), conjoined with the letter *śa* and the letter *ṣa*, and endowed with the mouth (*mukha*). Thus, the fivefold seed-syllable is proclaimed as the bestower of the accomplishment of all aims. It begins with the Vedas and possesses the three qualities (*triguṇa*).

Then one should speak of Ramā, who is served by Kāma; having attained her, she is indeed the supreme among the supreme, the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals, more essential than the essential, the source of the origin of the entire world.
Of this [syllable], the form of the letter *e* is at the end, and the letter *ha* is at the very end.
"Antārakāra" means that very [seed-syllable] which has "ha" as its end; it is thus. "Antaḥ" refers to the letter *śa*.

[The syllable] joined with the seventh letter preceding "śiva" (which is *ha*)—*śiva* being the letter *ha*, and the seventh preceding it being the letter *ra*—and adorned with a *bindu*, is *śrīṃ*. Likewise, *hrīṃ* is the essential form (*svarūpa*). These two are the goddesses of the right arm.

The letter *ka* is the left eye; the letter *ī* is with its own vowel (*svara*). "Klīm" [is formed]; the meaning is that it is joined with the teeth (*da*) and fire (*ra*). Therefore, the remainder is "ai. What is the nature of the tooth? It is the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*). What is that? It is the living soul (*jīva*); that *jīva* is *Kāma*. As it has been said, it is endowed with the face, which is the *visarga*; therefore [it is "ai"].

Having placed these seed-syllables (*bījas*) in sequence before one's self— namely *sauḥ* as the essential form (*svarūpa*), then the beginning of the Vedas which is *oṃ*, then the three-fold *bhuvaneśvarī* which is *hrīṃ*, and then *ramā* which is the essential form of *śrī*; having written [the syllable] *lopāmudrā* (or *kāmarāja*) which is served by *kāma*— and having written this preceding the aforementioned seed-syllables.

One should extract the five seed-syllables according to the sequence of the *pūrvāvaloka*; one should extract them exactly as they were previously extracted in the order ending with *śānta*: namely, Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Aiṃ Sauḥ. (38a)

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ trikūṭā klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ—this is the mantra. And it is also stated in the *Śrīkrama*: "In the *Śrīmāyā*, Madana, Yoni, and Paretāni—place these at the beginning; O Bhuvaneśānī, [place] the *Śrībīja* and the *trikūṭaka*. One should enclose the *ṣaṭkūṭā* with these five syllables: *śrīmāye*."

*Śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *svarūpe*, *madanaḥ*, *klīṃ*, *yoniḥ*, *aiṃ*, *parāsauḥ*, *vedādiḥ*, *praṇavaḥ*, *bhuvaneśānī*, *hrīṃ*, and the seed-syllable of Śrī, *śrīṃ*. Now, having stated that these five syllables are according to the sequence of Śrī, one might ask: "How is the sequence of the Sky (Dyu-krama) obtained? [The answer is found] in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Tantra.
From the vowel [one should proceed]. Therein, having extracted the *kūṭa* from the wheel, one should form an encapsulation (*saṃpuṭa*) with the *mālā*.

Regarding the statement "the Supreme Goddess named Ramā," the author of the *Tantrakaumudī* has written it as a single syntactical unit because the forms *śrīṃ* and *hrīṃ*, which are the nature of the Supreme Goddess named Ramā, are subsequently mentioned. However, in reality...
Regarding the phrase "in the sequence of the eastern gaze," there would indeed be a contradiction with the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra*;

how then can there be conformity to a single textual unity? Due to the difference between the tantras, one must state that there is simply a distinction in the *Ṣoḍaśī*. [The mantra] follows after the *Trikūṭa*:
*Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Aiṃ Sauḥ*—thus it is joined; otherwise, it would be according to the difference between the tantras.

If one does not accept the division of the mantras, then [the sequence] is as follows: *tāra* (the Savior) is "oṃ"; *parā* is "hrīṃ"; *lakṣmī* is "śrīṃ"; *kumārikā* is "aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ"; and *vidyā* is "parā" (the Supreme). In the *māmāya* [mantra], the forms are "śrīṃ" and "hrīṃ".
*Tāra* is "oṃ"; *parā* is "hrīṃ"; *lakṣmī* is "śrīṃ"; *kumārikā* is "aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ"; and *vidyā* is "parā".

*Trikūṭā*, *vyastā*, *vālā*, *klīṃ*, *aiṃ*, *sauḥ*, *śrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *parā*, *hrīṃ*—by means of this awakening through the revelation of the Vedas (*śruti*), the distinction of mantras, which has been accepted as having distinctions, must indeed be expressed; such is the direction [of the teaching].

If it is argued that even in the absence of syntactic unity between the *śruti* and the mantra, a unified syntactical relation (*tantra-ekavākyatā*) is nevertheless appropriate—then there would be a contradiction with the Tantra known as the *Gandharva*. For example: "Lakṣmī, Parā, Madana, Vāgbhava, Śakti, Tāra, Śakti, and Kamalā—these are said to be the Vidyās."
And the Śakti and so forth are applied in reverse order: [the syllable] *śrī* [is] *parā*,
*hrīṃ* is *madana*, *klīṃ* is *vāgbhava*, *aiṃ* is *śakti*, *sauḥ* is *tāraṃ*, *oṃ* is *śakti*, *hrīṃ* is *kamalā*, and *śrīṃ*.
Then, the Vidyā consists of Trikūṭā in reverse order, beginning with Śakti;
thus indeed arises the necessity for this division of the mantra.
He states a hymn of praise:

She who is directly served by hosts of gods and sages, whose infinite forms are the sole essence of saṃsāra, the mother of the three worlds, the source of the arising of dharma and action— she is this venerable Brahman-form, consisting of all qualities yet devoid of [limited] attributes, beyond the senses, and prior to all ignorance.
She who brings benefit to all, who bestows various [blessings], and whose forms are infinite.
Even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of millions of tongues,
one would never be able to describe the sixteen-syllable mantra of Śiva.
From this mantra, thousands of great mantras issue forth,
like sparks that fly from a glowing red-hot iron ball.
This must be practiced together with the Vidyā; it should not be given to just anyone.
Even at the cost of one's life, the sixteen-syllable Turyā should not be bestowed.
Having inscribed the seed-syllable of the Ṣoḍaśī in water for a disciple who is endowed with devotion, devoted to truthful speech, and supreme, the practitioner [should proceed].
Having placed his foot upon the head of the disciple according to the sequence of divine conduct,
[he should recite] one hundred thousand times, or at least ten thousand times, O Gajāntaka.
Having recited the mantra alone in the temple of Śiva, one should reveal it.
Through the auspicious Mantra Purasundarī, success shall be attained; it cannot be otherwise.
Now, her other divisions are described according to the method of the Tantra:
likewise, having established her in the center, one should then abandon the royal [arrangement] and the placement of Lopā.
One should gradually cast away all ignorances through the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Tantra;
then all the divisions become the sixteenth state, the Turyā.
Having understood one of these, that which is to be known remains.

From the middle of the sixteenth [vowel], having abandoned *kāmarāja*, *lopāmudrā*, and *vāsa*, the *sakalā* of the *dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra*—the imposition of the mantra (*mantrāropa*)—becomes the fourfold sixteenth; by this, the *Mantra-kaumudī* [is established].
That which is written by [the author] regarding the *Trikūṭa* alone is because it constitutes the essence of the *Ṣoḍaśī*; thus, the *Ṣoḍaśī* possesses a manifold nature.

In that regard, it is precisely the *Trikūṭa* mentioned in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra* that constitutes its essence. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the specific injunction being rendered meaningless.
Now, another variety is the sixteenfold Turiya.
In the Kulārṇava:
"O Lord, if you are pleased with me, then tell me truly of the *Ṣoḍaśī*;
the venerable *Mahāṣoḍaśī* is hidden by you within the *māyā*, the *kalās*, and so forth."
That which has been kept secret in all tantras, reveal it to me now.
Īśvara said:
Listen to this secret Great Vidyā, which is difficult even for gods and asuras to obtain:
Śiva, Śakti, Kāma, Earth, and then Punaḥ.
The Sun, the Moon, and likewise Kāma; then I am he, and Vāsava;
and the third is Parākāma—these are the thousand-eyed ones.
The Supreme Goddess is always joined with the Heart-lines (hṛllekhās) below;
from the piercing [of those lines], Bhuvaneśvarī is the sound (nāda) consisting of Indra (Śakra), the left eye (vāmākṣi), and Ka. 39b)
If the supreme fire is beyond you both, O eye, and the triad of Bindu and Nāda;
O Maheśānī, one should offer it at the beginning; thus one becomes the illustrious Mahāṣoḍaśī.
O Deveśī, by mere knowledge of this, one leads death itself to the state of deathlessness.
The meaning.

Śiva is the letter *ha*, Śakti is the letter *sa*, Kāma is the letter *ka*, and Earth is the letter *la*. Then Ravi is the letter *ha*, Candra is the letter *sa*, Kāma is the letter *ka*, Haṃsa is the letter *ha*, and Vāsava is the letter *la*. Then Parā is the letter *sa*, Kāma is the letter *ka*, and Sahasranayana is the letter *la*. These are the letters at the ends [of the mantras].

Endowed with the *hṛllekhā* (the heart-line), which is *hrīṃ*, the first syllable of the *lopāmudrā* mantra thus becomes *hrīṃ*. Below this, the *parameśvarī* is *hrīṃ*. At the beginning of this mantra, from the "mouth" (*tuṇḍa*)—that is, from the letter *ka*—comes *śakra*, which is the letter *la*; the "left eye" is *ikāra*; and it is joined with the *anusvāra* and so forth. By that [it becomes *klīṃ*].

*Klīm* is Bhuvaneśvarī; *hrīm* is the supreme, the cause of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), higher than the highest, whose form is essence (*rasa*). [The word] *yasyāt* is a Vedic usage where the syllables *para-pada* and *sa* are elided. *Agni* is the letter *ra*; *vāmākṣi* is the long vowel *ī*;
and there are the *bindu* and *nāda*. Thus, *śrīm* is formed. This is the placement of these three seed-syllables (*bīja*) at the beginning.
The Śrī Mahāṣoḍaśī; by this [mantra] *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ lopāmudrā hrīṃ*, there are many varieties of the Ṣoḍaśī, such as the Aparā, the Turīyā, and the Mahāṣoḍaśī.
Now, the fifth [section] on the mantras, from the Śrīkrama Saṃhitā.
One should then recite *kāma*, *śakti*, and *māyā*, followed by the seed-syllable of Indra (*indrabīja*),
which is conjoined with space (*viyat*) and fire (*vahni*), and endowed with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*.
The *vāgbhava* seed-syllable is said to be the *kūṭa* (peak syllable) adorned with the fourth vowel.
Its meaning is desire; the letter *ka* [is the first part].

The letter *ka* is Śakti; *e* is Māyā; *la* is the seed-syllable of Indra; *ha* is Viyat (Space); *ra* is Vahni (Fire); the Bindu is the Anusvāra; and the fourth vowel is the long *ī*. Thus, *ka-e-ī-la-hrīṃ* is the first *kūṭa*, known by the name Vāgbhava.
After that follows the power of space (viyacchakti), then the fire of Kula (kulavahni) in the process of manifestation;
this is conjoined with my own vowel-sound (mayā-svara), endowed with the resonance (nāda), the point (bindu), and the digit (kalā).
I shall now declare the celebrated seed-syllable (*bīja*), which has arisen and is very difficult to obtain.
It is celebrated as *Madhumatī*. *Viyat* is the letter *ha*; *Śakti* is the letter *sa*; *Kala* is the letter whose nature is *kala*;
*Nakula* is the letter *ha*; *Vahni* is the letter *ra*; *Māyā* is the vowel, the long *ī*; and the *Bindu* is the *Anusvāra*. Thus, it is *hasakala*.
"Hrīṃ" is the second seed-syllable.
Likewise, O Goddess, having extracted "viyat," then "kāma" and "vyoma" thereafter;
O auspicious one, the supreme seed-syllable of Śakra—listen further, O beloved.
Mahāmāyā is thereafter called Svapnāvatī.

Viyat is the letter *ha*, Kāma is the letter *ka*, Vyoma is the letter *ha*, Śakrabīja is the letter *la*, and Mahāmāyā is *hrīṃ*. Thus, for this [mantra] *ha-śa-la-hrīṃ*, the name is likewise Svapnāvatī.
The *mādana* (the letter *ka*), the seed-syllable of Śiva (*ha*), and then the wind (*ya*);
after that the seed-syllable of Indra (*la*), and then the seed-syllable of Śiva (*ha*) together with fire (*ra*).
O Goddess, O beloved, hear this seed-syllable of Śakti, known as Kāmarāja, which is conjoined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the Bindu and Nāda.
The letter *ka* is the *mādana* (the intoxicating one); the letter *ha* is the seed-syllable of Śiva; the letter *ya* is *anila* (wind); the letter *la* is the seed-syllable of Indra;

the letter *ha* is the seed-syllable of Śiva, joined with *repha* (the letter *ra*) and the fourth vowel in its long form, *ī*; and the *bindu* is the *anusvāra*. Thus, *ka-ha-ya-la-hrīṃ*—this is the name of Kāmarāja. Likewise, the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu...
O Great Goddess, O Maheśvarī, one should subsequently recite the Śakti-māyā mantra, which bestows the fruit of all desires, [beginning with] "Kāmamindram.
Regarding the creation and destruction previously described by Brahmā to me as occurring within Time:
whether in a distant land or even in a wilderness, when a conflict with an enemy has broken out;
In battle or even upon the ocean,
she— having become manifest before the practitioner— shall protect him from all calamities;
or the Goddess, the supreme mind, is seen by the practitioner in a dream.
I bow to her whose splendor resembles the reflection of vermilion, who is clothed in the garments of waves, who is known as ten million suns as red as the Bandhūka flower,
who is adorned with the fivefold sciences, and who is designated as possessing the five types of marks.
And through devotion, it is equal to the secret [teachings] that are difficult for others to obtain.
Having treated it like union with one's mother, one should keep it secret;
accomplish the vidyā as it has been proclaimed in due order.
The Goddess said: Thus, in the Śrīkrama.
The entire form of knowledge has been told to you out of devotion;
that which is called Brahmavidyā has been illuminated by me.
The Lord said:
And once it has been revealed, O Goddess of gods, humans, rākṣasas, and kinnaras will become bestowers of siddhi; how then shall my sovereignty come to pass?
The Goddess said:
O Goddess of gods, I shall perform the renunciation of life, the dissolution into the divine and the Brahman,
and the destruction of all things; there is no doubt that this must be done.
The Lord said:
O Pārvatī, according to the sacred tradition (āgama), if you were to reveal this great imperishable Brahma-vidyā, then your spiritual attainment (siddhi) would be lost.
Listen, O Goddess of the Gods, to that Vidyā which is endowed with Kāmendra, [to be attained] by one desiring liberation through Mahātripurasundarī.
O auspicious lady, thus is the triad of seed-syllables, the essence of the Vidyā, adorned with the fourth vowel through the differentiation of the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*.
The application of Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja,
and Śakti to the principle (tattva) grants enjoyment for those who possess honeyed [wisdom], and when liberated, bestows absolute liberation (kaivalya).
O Goddess, whatever knowledge is established when joined with these syllables, its accomplishment will be achieved within a month; this should be known with certainty, O Goddess.
This is its meaning.

The syllable *ka* is Indra; the syllable *la* is the fourth long vowel, *ī*. Thus, *klīṃ klīṃ klīṃ*—these three constitute the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja. Or else, it refers to another [Vidyā] consisting of three peaks (*trikūṭā*). For this very reason, whichever Vidyā is joined with these syllables, its accomplishment (*siddhi*) shall occur within a month; such is the meaning.
He states another tantra in the Śrīkrama:
O Śakra, [the syllable] *mādana* (ma) is joined with *māyā* (ī) and the nasal drop (*nādabindu*).
In that very place, it should be understood separately according to the division of the peak-syllables (*kūṭa*).
O best of goddesses, when one has thus recited the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti-kūṭa, life is produced therein.
It must be guarded with extreme care and protected with great effort;
it is difficult to find in all the worlds and has been revealed in the Śrīkramas.
This is its meaning.

The letter *ka* is *mādana*, the letter *la* is *śakra*, and the letter *ī* is *māyā*; thus, by means of *klīm*, through the division of the three peaks (*trikuṭa*), when applied at the beginning of the three peaks, it becomes most secret and one's life is preserved—this is the general direction.
41b) Others have not been written here because they were omitted out of fear;
now, the sequence of worship is written down in brief.
The morning ritual in the Tantra, according to the Jñānārṇava.
O Goddess of gods, having risen at dawn and meditated upon the Guru with [mantras],
the knower of mantras, O Goddess, should perform the twilight prayers, the ritual bath, and other rites according to the rules.

Because of this statement, the necessity of saluting the Guru in the morning and the sequence for doing so are as follows: having meditated upon the Guru at the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasradala*) within the body— which possesses six faces— one should bathe the body with the water from his feet and then offer salutation.
As in the case of a mantra:
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye was opened for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, using the collyrium-stick of knowledge.
Having thus prostrated to the Goddess and meditated according to the instruction, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, three hundred times, or a thousand times.
O Goddess of gods, having risen at dawn and remaining upon his bed,
one should meditate on the Goddess within one's own heart and recite [her mantra] one hundred and eight times.

"One should recite [the mantra] three hundred times daily, or one thousand and eight," according to the scriptural injunction. Thereafter, the disciple who serves the Guru should perform the morning twilight ritual (*prātaḥ-sandhyā*). Having joined the water with the sacred sites (*tīrtha*) using the root mantra, he should cast it upon the ground with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass and sprinkle it seven times over his head.
Having taken water in the left hand, one should [perform the rite] with the mudrā by means of the right hand.
Again, having thrown that [water] with the left hand, they sprinkle the vessel upon the head;
then, having drawn that water back through the *iḍā*, the karma is washed away once more.
One should cause that water to fall upon the stone in sequence with the Astra mantra;
for this is indeed the Arghya-offering, the destroyer of all sins.
Then, having recited the Gāyatrī, one should offer [the water];
according to the Tantric view, one should invoke the three holy waters (tīrtha) onto the ground with a blade of kuśa grass.

Having sprinkled [the vessel] seven times with the root mantra, one should sprinkle the head. Taking that water in the left hand, one should cast it upon the crown of the head with the *tattva-mudrā* using the right hand; then, drawing that water in through the left nostril, one should wash the interior [of the channels], and finally expel that water through the right [nostril] while reciting the *astra-mantra*, "phaṭ."

One should cast [the offerings] into wood or stone with the mantra. Then, having satiated them with: "May the Gurus of the Divine Current (divyaugha) be satisfied," likewise "may the Gurus of the Siddha Current (siddhaugha) be satisfied," and likewise "may the Gurus of the Human Current (mānaugha) be satisfied"; and having satiated [her] three times with: "Oṃ, may the glorious Akṣobhya-mātṛ with her retinue be satisfied," one should recite the Gāyatrī. Oṃ Tripurasundari...

"Vimahe Kāmeśvarī, dhīmahi, tannaḥ Klīne pracodayāt. Having thus recited this Gāyatrī as many times as possible, one should offer arghya to the Sun. Having offered the arghya with the mantra: "Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ, to Mārtaṇḍa Bhairava, together with the Śakti Prakāśa, this arghya, namaḥ," one should perform the bath. As it has been said:
In the Jñānārṇava.
Or else, O Goddess, with the root-mantra or again with the Sūrya-mantra;
the Sūrya-mantra is the syllable Śiva (Ś) situated in fire (R), adorned with the left eye (Ū).
One should then utter the word *haṃsa*, which is pervaded by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*.
O Goddess, with this mantra one should offer the *argha* oblation to the Sun.
