The seed-syllable of Śiva is *ha*, and fire is *ra*; thus, *hrīṃ* and *haṃsaḥ*. Having visualized the Śrīcakra in the water and performed the extraction of the assembly (*melāpakarṣa*), one should invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) from the solar orb using the *aṅkuśa* mudrā.

With that water, regarding it as milk, one should satisfy the Goddess along with her retinue according to one's capacity, and [sprinkle it] upon the head with the root mantra using the *kumbha* mudrā.
The summary is: one should bathe after sprinkling water three times.
This has been stated in the Jñānārṇava:
Then the wise one should perform the rite of bathing; having consecrated water three times with the root mantra, he should pour it over his own head while holding it in his cupped hands.
O Supreme Goddess, one should scatter [the water] three times, and having sipped water (ācamya), one should offer libations (tarpayet).
Thus it is said in the Jñānārṇava.
After the ritual bath and the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), having arrived at the sacrificial hall or the temple, well-adorned and radiant,

one should draw a wheel on the ground with vermilion powder, or likewise with saffron powder upon entering the earth in a mountain or forest. Alternatively, it may be drawn in many ways using gold, silver, or copper.

Since sitting upon a seat is necessary, that too should be done with the seed-syllable of another [deity] and preceded by *dhāra*. Having written the word *śaktyām*, one should write *kamalāsana* (lotus-seat). One should extract the word *namaḥ* ending in *ṅe* (dative case) and recite the mantra of the seat.
The meaning is that, having worshipped with "Parā Hrīṃ, tena Hrīṃ, Ādhāraśaktaye Kramatvā Savāya Namaḥ," one should sit there and draw the Śrīcakra.

Thus, in the *Yāmala*: "The point (bindu), the triangle, the eight-cornered [figure], the ten-cornered, the pair, that which is joined with the fourteen-cornered, the eight-petaled, and the sixteen-spoked, along with the three circles and the earth, and the three 'Loves' (madana)—this is declared to be the Śrīcakra-rāja of the Supreme Deity. Therefore, while the Śrīcakra consists of nine principles (*tattva*), Māyā is not among them.
O sinless one, I shall explain to you the ninefold reality of the wheel:
the first is the origin of the gods, and the second is the sixteen-spoked [wheel], and so forth.
The sequence of writing has been omitted due to the bulk of the text; it is to be understood from the teacher’s oral instruction—this is the direction [of the method].
Now, the ritual procedure according to the Vārāhī Tantra.
First, one should contemplate one's own guru on the right cheek;
one should prostrate to Gaṇeśvara and the supreme guru upon the crown of the head.
One should contemplate the deity within the heart and then perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
With that [mantra], one should offer salutations: "Guṃ, salutations to the Gurus" on the right side of the cheek; "Gaṃ, salutations to Gaṇeśa" at the crest-lock (*śikhā*);
and "Salutations to the Supreme Gurus" at the heart. Having prostrated with "Salutations to Tripurasundarī," one performs the general water offering (*sāmānyārgha*).
Having first performed the ritual installation, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
In the Jñānārṇava:
Having prepared his own square maṇḍala on the left side,
he should place the yantrikā there and deposit the conch shell upon it.
Having filled [the vessel] with pure water, one should worship it with the causal mantra;
having worshipped the six limbs there, O Śiva, this is the general *argha*.
Having laid out a square mandala on the left side and fashioned a triangle therein, having placed the yantra upon it,
and having filled a conch with water there and worshipped the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) there,
and having recited the root mantra eight times there, one should sprinkle everything with that water and perform the installation of the special arghya offering (viśeṣārgha).
Likewise, in the Tantra:
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the characteristics of the poison-offering (viṣārgha).
Between the self and the Śrīcakra, there should be a square mandala.
The preceptor, ending with the earth-born [mantra], should pour water from the general arghya vessel and place the yantrikā there, conjoined with the half-syllable of the fire-corner.
One should worship the mandala there, consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a hexagon;
having then meditated upon the fire therein, one should worship that which consists of the Yantra.
As before, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Trikūṭā situated in the center;
there, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Trikūṭa within the eight peaks.
Repeating [the mantra] twice, one should worship the six limbs within the six corners;
one should place the vessel in the form of the Sun and draw the yantra as before.
O Śivā, one should worship the Trikuṭa among all the combined, individual, and composite [mantras];
especially, O Śivā, having fully filled the moon with the substance.
Having drawn the yantra as before, one should worship that which is situated in the middle of the three peaks;
there, O Śivā, one should worship the triangle with the three peaks.

One should worship the supreme diagram, which begins with 'a', is enriched with three lines, and contains 'ha' and 'kṣa' within it, by repeating it twice; one should then worship the six limbs in the six corners.
Beginning with the seat of the Self, one should worship with bliss;
the wise one should then worship the Root-Vidyā, which consists of sixteen syllables, as the Supreme.
Manifesting therein, he becomes directly composed of Brahman;
with that, he should sprinkle himself, as well as the materials for worship.

Having drawn a square on the ground with the general offering water (*sāmānyārghya*) and a triangle situated within it, and having placed there the small diagram (*yantrikā*) in the form of fire, one should contemplate therein a triangle, a circle, and a hexagon; then, having worshipped it with the mantra: "Obeisance to the Fire-maṇḍala, whose self is pervaded by the ten digits (*kalā*)."

Having worshipped with the *trikūṭa* [mantra] and having repeated it twice, one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in the six corners. Here, because there is no specific mention, the meaning is that it is the root mantra; however, in the *Kauladīpikā*, it says:
"Having placed the *argha* vessel, which has been washed three times and is the form of the Sun, [one should worship] the twelve digits (*kalā*) that pervade the Self."

Having established it as before, one should fill that arghya vessel with water for the arghya offering and worship there with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the moon-earringed one, whose self is pervaded by the sixteen kalās. Then, having inscribed the mantra there as before, [one should proceed].

44a) Therein, having meditated upon the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa* in the center of the triangle, and the sixteen syllables beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *tha* on the three lines, one should worship as before. Therein, the seat and so forth [should be offered] with the mantra to be recited.

Having worshipped the group of four, one should worship the root-mantra as before; there, reciting the root-mantra eight times and forming the *dhenumudrā* with the syllable *vaṃ*, as well as the *yonimudrā*, one should protect [the area] with the *astra-mantra*, sprinkle everything with that water, and contemplate everything as consisting of the mantra (*vidyāmaya*).
Now follows the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Likewise, having worshipped Ānanda, one should then terrify the spirits;
having recited the root mantra, the binding of the directions and the bursting [of obstacles] occurs, and not otherwise.
Facing [the deity] and having bowed down, one should then perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*);
thus concludes the worship of Ānandabhairava according to the written tradition.
As for the mantra: ||
Śiva, Candra, the end of Mātṛkā, Kāla, Śakra, and the first of the fires (Agni), along with Vāyu joined with the left ear (the letter U) and Bindu, [form the syllable *auṃ*]. This is Ādinī.
Having uttered this seed-syllable, likewise Ānandabhairava ending in *ṅ*,
joined with the crest-mantra (*śikhā-mantra*), one should again write down the seed-syllable.
Having abandoned the moon, one should direct it toward the quarters; one should join the ear with the eye.
*Sudhā* for the Goddess, then *vauṣaṭ*: this is Ānandabhairava.

Śiva is the letter *ha*, Candra is the letter *sa*, Mātṛkānta is the letter *kṣa*, Kāla is the letter *ma*, Śakrādya is the letter *va*, Śakra is the letter *la*, Vahni is the letter *ra*, and Vāyu is the letter *ya*. Vāmakarṇa is the letter *ū*, along with Bindu and Nāda. Thus, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *hasakṣama varayūṃ*. Then, [the name] ending in the dative case...
"Ānanda bhairavaṃ śiśā mantraḥ vauṣaṭ. Following that, after the previous seed-syllable (44b),
one should write the seed-syllable in the same manner as "ānanda bhairavāya vauṣaṭ," omitting the moon (the *m* bindu), and first perform the conjunction (*saṃkuryāt*).
Placing [the drop] on the left ear and the left eye with the mantra "To Sudhādevī, Vauṣaṭ," one [worships] with Ānandabhairava.
Together with that, using the mantra "KṢA MA VA RA YA ĪṂ, To Sudhādevī, Vauṣaṭ," one should worship Ānandabhairava.
Then, having performed the protection against spirits (bhūtamivāraṇa) with the root mantra, as well as the binding of the directions (digbandhana) and the ritual piercing (sphoṭana).

Having formed the *kacakacchapikā* mudrā by taking a flower with the thumb and ring finger and placing it on the left side of the belly, one should contemplate the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) residing within the belly, reflecting upon that sinful person situated therein.
The murder of a Brahmin is its head, the theft of gold its two arms,
association with such a person its pair of feet, and every minor sin its limbs and members.

One who has committed the drinking of liquor should be depicted with a heart; one who has violated the teacher's bed with two hips; and one who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka) with pride and blood-red eyes.

In the north, one should contemplate the sinful Piṅgalākṣa, who holds a trident and is terrifying; then, one should visualize the seed-syllable situated at the mūlādhāra in the form of a flame of a lamp.
Drawing [the breath] in with the *praṇava*, the wise one should lead it to the *dvādaśānta*;
by means of the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*), the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) situated within the body, together with their sins, [are purified].
Having dried it with the fire-seed (RAṂ), one should burn it along with the sin;
then, having rendered the life-force immortal as if freed from sin, one should live on.
O Goddess of gods, make it firm with the earthly [seed-syllable] and the water-seed.
Because of this statement.

From the *mūlādhāra*, one should unite the light consisting of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by means of the syllable *oṃ* and the mantra *haṃsaḥ*, using the *haṃsa* residing in the lotus (*puṣkara*). According to the *Surasā* [tradition], one should do so with this mantra; or else, having led [the soul] to the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*) in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasradalakamala*) by means of this mantra, and having taken up the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) along with the flower, one should place it upon the head at the *mūlādhāra*.
One should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
Then, with the wind [element], generated from the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, one should thoroughly cleanse the body; [then] with the fire [element], generated from the seed-syllable *raṃ*...

Having visualized the body as burnt by the fire arising from the big toe of the right foot, one should imagine oneself born again from a rain of nectar produced by the seed-syllable *vaṃ*. Then, having made it firm with the earth-seed syllable *laṃ*, one should contemplate the form of the Goddess. Thereafter, [one should contemplate] the transcendent principles (*tattvas*) and the individual soul (*jīvātman*) with the mantra *so'ham*.

One should invoke [the deity] into its respective place with the mantra: "ĀṂ SOHAṂ MITI. This is the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, which is to be recited according to the specific ritual procedure (*mukhavṛtta*), as indicated by the writing: "HASA and the reverse."

Alternatively, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) in the form of three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) by means of the three seed-syllables. Although the placement of the *mātṛkā* letters (*mātṛkānyāsa*) is not explicitly mentioned here, nevertheless, according to the statement: "The recitation and so forth of all mantras should be performed without the placement of the letters;
one should know that [the rite] is fruitless if done otherwise; therefore, one should first place the letters," it must be done prior [to the main practice].
The ritual placement of the script (lipinyāsa).
And so it is said:
In the lotus of the hatred [direction] (west), one should place the sixteen vowels on the petals;
in the heart-lotus, one should place the twelve consonants beginning with *ka* on the twelve petals.
One should place the ten letters beginning with *ḍa* in the ten-petaled lotus at the navel;
and one should place the six letters beginning with *va* in the six-petaled lotus situated in the middle of the *liṅga*.
One should place the four vowels on the four petals of the *ādhāra*;
O Śivā, one should place *ha* and *kṣa* on the two-petaled lotus located between the eyebrows.
Having thus performed the internal placement of the *mātṛkā*, one should perform the placement for all the limbs:
on the head, the face, the eyes, and the ears, O Pārvatī.
One should place [the syllables] on the nose, throat, lips, and teeth, as well as on the head and face;
likewise, O Śivā, at the ends, middle, and tips of the pair of hands and feet.
Likewise, one should place [the syllables] in order on both sides, at the navel, and in the abdomen;
such is the rule for its fingers.
One should place the ring finger in the middle of the forehead for the circular face;
the index, middle, and ring fingers, along with the thumb, are for the two eyes.
One should place the thumbs on the two ears; the little fingers and thumbs on the two nostrils; the middle fingers and thumbs on the two eyes; and the middle fingers on the two lips.
Placing the ring finger between the two teeth,
the middle finger on the head, the ring finger in the mouth, the middle finger in the hand, and likewise on the feet and the two sides.
One should place those [fingers]—the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger—on the back;
all of them, together with the thumbs, one should place on the region of the navel and in the belly.
The palm [of the hand] is applied to the heart, and all [the fingers] to the region of the armpits;
first the palm is placed on the heart, and likewise the palms are applied to the hands, the belly, and the mouth.
These mudrās of the Mātṛkās have thus been proclaimed in their proper order;
for him who performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) without knowing them, that placement shall be fruitless.
Thus, one should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa in this sequence.

Having remembered that for this mantra Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Tripurasundarī is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of desired goals, one should perform the salutations: "Obeisance to the seer Dakṣiṇāmūrti on the head;
obeisance to the Anuṣṭubh meter on the mouth; obeisance to the deity Tripurasundarī on the heart."
Now, in the Vārāhītantra:
The seer is Śambhu, the seed-syllable is Śiva, and the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is known as Sundarī, whom one should employ for the attainment of desire and liberation.
According to this statement, Śambhu is also the seer (ṛṣi) here.
The *vidyā* beginning with the middle finger and ending at the palms effects purification of the hands;
O Śivā, by repeating it twice over the fingers, it effects purification of the hands.
46a) As with a mantra: ||
Having uttered the first, which is Vāgbhava, and the second, which is Kāmarāja,
and the third of the Kumārī, she is Tripurā, O Supreme Goddess.
Now, the formal application.
The first is the syllable A, the second is Ā, and the third of the maiden is SAUḤ.
This has been stated in another tantra:
The first, the second, the syllable above, Tripureśī, and the final great one;
by that, "aṃ madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ" (salutation to the two middle fingers).

Āṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers; Sauḥ, salutation to the two little fingers; Aṃ, salutation to the two thumbs; Āṃ, salutation to the two index fingers; Sauḥ, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands. Having thus performed the placement (vinyāsa), one should place the fourfold seat (āsana-catuṣka).
As for the mantra: ||
Having set aside the first [mantra] of Tripureśī, one should surround Bhuvaneśī;
with this [latter], one should offer the seat for the self and perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) of Tripureśī.

Having omitted the primordial seed-syllable (*ādibīja*) of the three-eyed Bālā, one should surround Bhuvaneśī with *hrīṃ*. Thus, with "hrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ, obeisance to the seat of the Self" (*ātmāsanāya namaḥ*), one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) at the feet; having thus performed the fourfold placement on the feet, the shanks, the knees, and the genitals, according to the *Surasā* [Tantra].
O Maheśānī, if Tripureśī is situated within the three seed-syllables,
know that the Goddess seated upon the wheel-throne is Tripuravāsinī.
When Tripureśī consists of the three seed-syllables enriched with the letter *ha*,

then [the mantra] *haiṃ hklīṃ hsauṃḥ cakrāya namaḥ* is for the seat of the wheel (*cakrāsana*) on the two shanks. Likewise, Tripureśī Maheśānī is in the Vāgbhava and Kāmarāja [syllables], while the third [syllable] is of the nature of Śiva, conjoined with Śiva and the Moon.

This Śrī Tripurā, seated upon all mantras, is the auspicious Tripureśī Bālā; O Śiva, she resides in her first syllable (Vāgbhava) and her second syllable (Kāmarāja), which are joined with the Moon (the Bindu); and in her third seed-syllable, which is joined with Śiva alone, she becomes seated upon all thrones—Śiva being the syllable *Ha*.
46b) The letter *sa* is the moon; with it, [one recites] *hklaiḥ*, *hsklīḥ*, *hkauḥ*, and *sarvāsanāya namaḥ* on the two knees. Likewise,
O Daughter of the Mountain, for those seated upon the Ātman-seat, having abandoned the third [seat] and superimposed the power of the Self, there arises the Sādhyasiddha-seat.

The meaning is that for the seed-syllables situated on the seat of the Self (*ātmasana*), one should omit the third seed-syllable, which is mobile in nature (*calamātmaka*), and instead provide the seed-syllable *vlu*. Thus, [the mantra] becomes: *hrīṃ klīṃ vluṃ sādhyasiddhāsanāya ye namaḥ*. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the four seats upon the *liṅga*, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by repeating the *Vālā* mantra twice.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa). As it has been said:
Then one should perform protection by means of the previously mentioned family-vidyā,
employing the application of the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) along with the recitation of salutations.

With these [mantras], one should place the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*) upon the respective limbs: *aiṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *klīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *sauḥ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *aiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *hūṃ*; *klīṃ* to the eyes (*netra*), *vauṣaṭ*; *sauḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. Thus one should assign them to those limbs. Likewise: *aiṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*, and so forth, in sequence beginning with the thumb.

Placing [the hand] at the palm of the other, having performed the triple clapping of the hands (*tālatraya*) and the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) and so forth, and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) seven or five times with the root mantra, one should meditate upon the sixteen-syllable [mantra] in the form of a stream of incense flowing from the throat to the head. As it has been said:

For the sake of attaining perfection, the wise one should place the pervasive form [of the deity] and contemplate it in its entirety within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), possessing a radiance like that of the sun.
One should meditate on her as flowing nectar, sixteen-fold, bestowing great serenity;
then, with her left hand, that divine beauty, holding a staff, should whirl it about.
One should cast the tongue of the enemy, which is the Mahāmudrā, at the base of one's feet.
As in the case of Daṇḍinī:
Having formed the entire tarjanī [mudrā], one should whirl it; it becomes the daṇḍinī.
47a) One should employ the *ripujihvāṅkā* mudrā at the time of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), having pressed the surface of the earth with the inner fist formed by the thumbs.
Now, the placement (nyāsa) of Vaśinī and the others, as described in the Jñānārṇava:
One should install the Vaśinī Mātṛkā, endowed with the eight seed-syllables;
at the end of the letter 'a', one should write the seed-syllable 'ra-vala' according to its sequence.
O Śivā, O radiant Goddess, one should place Vaśinī, the deity of speech, who consists of the *bindu* and *nāda*, upon the left ear which is enriched with beauty.
The letter *a* is the sixteen vowels; at their end is *rava-lūṃ*. The left ear is the letter *ū*; thus, on the head is *aṃ āṃ*, and so forth.
After the sixteen vowels, [one places] *rava-lūṃ vāśinī vāgbhavāyai namaḥ*.
Likewise:
O Maheśānī, at the end of the *ka*-group [consonants], one should utter the supreme seed-syllable of Kāmeśī,
which ascends to the peak of Meru, and then worship Vāgdevī.

At the end of the *ka*-group is *Kāmeśī*, whose seed-syllable is *kala hrīṃ*; [with] *tenakaṃ* five times and *kala hrīṃ*, one should worship *Mā Kāmeśvarī Vāgdevatāyai namaḥ* on the forehead. Likewise, at the end of the group is the syllable *dhānta* (the letter *na*) joined with the fourth vowel (*ī*), which is possessed of *lakṣmī*.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship Modinī, the deity of speech.
At the end of the *ca*-group is the letter *dh*, which is joined with *na*; *nīra* is the letter *va*, and *kṣmā* is the letter *la*. The fourth vowel is the long *ī*.
Thus, *caṃ na valī modinī vāgdevatāyai namaḥ*—likewise, [this mantra] is placed between the eyebrows.
O Maheśvarī, at the end of the *ṭa*-group is the seed-syllable of Vāyu (*ya*), situated upon Indra (*la*), enriched by the moon (*u*) of the left ear (*ṛ*) and the *bindu*.
By this, [the syllable] is *ṭaṃ* 5 *yluṃ*. [The mantra is: "Salutation to Vimalā, the Goddess of Speech.
Here, the seed-syllable of Vāyu is the letter *ya*; Indra is the letter *la*; the left ear is the vowel *ū*; likewise, at the end of the *ṭa*-group is [the letter] *ja*, enriched by Agni (*ra*).
Adorned with a left eye,
marked with the *bindu* and *nāda*, one should worship the seed-syllable of the goddess of speech, Maruṇī.

By that [the letter] Ja; the fire [Ra] with the letter Repha; the short vowel I; by that [the syllable] Jam. "Salutation to Aruṇī, the goddess of speech"—thus [one should meditate] in the heart. Likewise, at the end of the Pavarga [the letter] Va; Vyoman [Ha]; the earth [La]; the fire [Ra] with the number [of its position] in the alphabet (the third). * * *?
Joined with its own vowel and ending in the Bindu, [one attains] the Mother, O Victor.
The labial class (*pa-varga*) is well-known; *vya* is the cause of delusion; the Moon is the letter *sa*; the Earth is the letter *la*; Water is the letter *va*.
From that, Fire and Number (three) in reverse order is the letter *ya*; by that, *yaṃ*.

At the end of the *ya*-group, one should worship the goddess Sarveśī, who is joined with the letter at the end of the *ja*-group (*ña*), the letter *ṛ*, the letter *ma*, the letter *ra*, the letter *ra*, the letter *va* (wind), and enriched by *māyā* (the long vowel *ū*). [Thus: *ña* is the letter *ṛ*; *kāla* is the letter *ma*; *repha* is the letter *ra*;
*vāyu* is the letter *va*; *māyā* is the long vowel *ū*. Therefore: *yaṃ 4 ṛ ma na yūṃ*—Sarveśī.

Salutation to the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā) in the Foundation (*ādhāra*). Likewise, one should worship Kāmavahni and Tūrya. O Maheśānī, [the seed-syllables] *nyaṃ* and those for the accomplishment of all aims (*sarvārthasiddhi*) are the long vowel *ī*; by that, [is formed] *śaṃ*... [Kaulinī].
Regarding the baths, it is stated therein that [the mantra consists of] the head, the forehead, the middle of the brows... [omitted].
Now, concerning the first... he says why the letter *ca* should not be there:
"In another Tantra (*tantrāntare*), one should extract the letter *ra* first; below that, [one should place the letter] ending in a curve."

Because it is written [thus]. (48a) Now, if it is asked: "How is the letter *ya* obtained, given the statement that 'the victorious seed arises from water and is the destroyer of fire'?"—if so, [it is not so].

If it is asked, "How is the letter *ū* obtained from the *Śrīkrama*, given that it states 'Nalī, Soma, Śakra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu,' and from the *Kaulinī-bīja*, given that it is heard as 'Māyā, Svara, Svara'?"—the answer is:
"It is because of the understanding from the *Śrīkrama* that 'the seventh [vowel] conjoined with the sixth vowel is the most excellent *kuṭa*. This is the general direction.
Then one should perform the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa), by which one becomes Śiva through direct realization;
[as stated] in the Vāmakeśvaratantra.
The first assignment is Gaṇeśa, and the second is considered to be by the planets;
the third should be by the lunar mansions, and the fourth by the Yoginīs.
The fifth [stage] is declared by means of the zodiac signs (rāśi), and the sixth is said to be by means of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
Thus is the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body; it is to be worshipped by all yogis.
In this world, those who are the objects of one's placement (nyāsa)—namely, one's father, mother, and other elders—are worthy of worship;
he alone is worthy of worship by all, for he is himself the Supreme Lord.
O Pārvatī, if one bows down to anyone who is devoid of the sixfold imposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa),
he shall soon meet death and fall into hell.
Vighneśvara and likewise Śrī, Vighnarāja and likewise Kriyā,
Vināyaka and likewise Tuṣṭi, together with Śānti and the supreme Śiva.
Vighnakṛt is endowed with nourishment, Vighnakṛt is Sarasvatī;
Vighnarāj is joined with delight, and Gaṇanāyaka is rich in intelligence.
Ekadanta, Kānti, Dvidanta, the husband of Kāminī,
Gajavaktra, Mohinī, and then Nirañjanaja.
O beloved, [the sequence is] Kaparda, Hṛtī, Ātīvrā, Dīrghavaktra,
then Svāminī, followed by Nandā, Aṃ, Karṣa, and Ṛṇau.
And Vṛṣadhvaja is conjoined with Svarasagaṇanātha;
thereafter, Kāmarūpīyikā is joined with Pañcāṅgajendra and Śubhā.
Sūryakarṇa was with Jayinī, and the three-eyed one was joined with Satyā.
Then there is Lambodara, Vighneśī, she whose nature is Great Bliss (Mahānanda),
the fourfold form, the bestower of desires, and thereafter she who is joined with Sadāśiva.
Then there were Mada-vihvalā and Āmoda-vikaṭā; likewise Durmukha, Pūrṇā, Sumukha, and Bhūtimat.
Likewise, Pramoda is a Bhūmi; Ekapāda is Satī;
Dvijihva joined with Ramā; and Mānuṣī is formed with the vowels.
Afterwards, O Daughter of the Mountain, there are Vīra along with Makaradhvaja,
Ṣaṇmukha, Vivarṇā, Varada, and likewise Bhrūkūṭī.
On the left is the deity Lajjā;
after that is Vaktratuṇḍa, followed by Dīrghaghonānvita, and then Dviraṇḍaka, the wielder of the bow.
The army leader is liberated from the night-walker; the village chief is joined with the night.
Darkness is united with moonlight, and the stainless one possesses the radiance of the moon.

Then follow *mattavāhana* (the letter *ma*), *lolacūḍatī* (the letter *la*), two *capala* syllables (*ca* and *pa*), *kṣaṇā* (the letter *kṣa*), *svantarukṣmā* (the letter *sma*), and finally the six-dot (*ṣaḍbindu*) conjoined with the *bhaga* (the letter *ha*).
Caṇḍī, endowed with supernatural power (ṛddhi), Khaḍī, and Bhagamālī—
this is an alternative reading. Also Varaṇya, Śubhagā, Vṛṣaketu, and likewise Śiva.
Bhakṣapriya and Durgā, Meghanāda and Kāminī;
Gaṇeśa and Kālakuṇḍala, [and] Prahāriṇī.
O Goddess, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) with the letters of the Mātṛkā, and thereafter one should perform the placement of the planets (grahanyāsa).
One should place the Mothers in the locations of the Mātṛkā according to the sequence: "Aṃ, obeisance to Vighneśvara together with Śrī" on the forehead, and so forth.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should place Mercury with the *ṭa*-group on the heart, Jupiter with the *ta*-group above the heart,
and Venus on the throat with the *pa*-group.
O fair-faced one, one should thus place Saturn with the [first] group on the navel, Rāhu with the [second] group on the mouth,
and Ketu with two hundred thousand [units] on the feet.
Then, having recited "aṃ āṃ" sixteen times followed by "sūryāya grahāya," one should place [the mantras] in the aforementioned locations in that sequence.
Then one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the host of constellations, which brings happiness:
two by two, and likewise two by two, with Rohiṇī joined with a pair of pairs.
One by one, and likewise in pairs, ending with Puṣpā;

by this [method], the fourteen vowels from Aśvinī to Puṣpā are assigned: for some [deities] there is a pair at the beginning, for some a pair, and for some a single [vowel]. Thus, "aṃ āṃ aśvinyai namaḥ" [is recited] on the forehead and other locations.
One should place [the mantras]:
first on the forehead, then on the left and right ears.
O Goddess of the gods, one should likewise place [the mantras] in sequence at the nose-tip and the throat.
Having placed Kapuṣpa and Khaga, as well as Sarpika,
on the right shoulder with the two syllables Ghaṃ, and Maghā on the second shoulder.
O Dear One, one should place the constellation Pūrvaphalgunī, conjoined with the letter *cha*,
on the right elbow, and Uttaraphalgunī on the left elbow.
One should place the hand joined with the letters *ṛ* and *ña* at the right wrist-joint;
and one should place the *citrā* [finger] joined with *ṭa* and *ṭha* at the left wrist-joint, O Śivā.
O Śivā, one should likewise place the root [syllable] with the letter *pha* on the left hip;
then, one should place Pūrvāṣāḍhā with the letter *va* on the right thigh.
With the syllable *bha*, one should place Uttarāṣāḍhā on the left thigh;
immediately after that, with the syllable *ma*, one should place Śravaṇā joined [with it] on the right knee.
One should place Dhaniṣṭhā, situated in the letter Ya, on the left knee;
then, O Goddess Śivā, one should place Śatabhiṣā with the letter La.
One should place the syllable *ga* on the right shank, followed by *pa* and *ū* of Pūrvabhādrapadā;
then, having placed the syllable *va*, one should place *śa* in sequence on the left shank.
49b) O Goddess, one should place Sahā upon the right foot of Uttarābhādrapadā; then, with the letter *kṣa*, followed by the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the visarga (*sarga*), one places Revatī.
Having first assigned [the letters] starting from the left, one should perform the Yoginī-nyāsa.
One should assign them in sequence as follows: "Aṃ aḥ, to the two forms consisting of the Bindu and Sarga, obeisance to the ninety."
Now follows the placement (nyāsa) of the Yoginīs.
O Dear One, the two seed-syllables Ḍāṃ and Ḍīṃ are in the middle; Svāḥ is for the sake of the Kalahas.
Likewise, Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Śākinī, and Hākinī—these Yoginīs grant immeasurable accomplishments.
Meditating on the moon in the left ear, one should likewise say: "Homage to Ḍākinī here.
At the end of the vowels, however, the two words "kṣara kṣa" should be performed.
Having placed [the syllables] in the pure region of the throat, O Śivā;
having thus [placed them] in the throat—*aṃ āṃ*—within the interval of the sixteen vowels: *ḍāṃ ḍīṃ ḍūṃ*, obeisance to Ḍākinī! Protect, protect!

The mantra is "to the self of the skin. Having uttered the two seed-syllables *ḍāṃ* and *ḍīṃ*, [one considers] the *ḍa-kalā*s of these [deities], Ḍākinī and the others. [Regarding] the moon-point (*bindu*), the resonance (*nāda*), and the half-moon: in the left ear, that is, in the vowel *ū*, there is *ḍūm* and so forth; [and] *vāṃ*, *vīṃ*.

The seed-syllables (*bījas*) are thus: *syā* and so forth; likewise, for the names, there is no dispute. Furthermore, the two letters *ka* and *ṭha* belong to Rākinī, while the syllables beginning with *ṭa* follow in sequence. As before, the seed-syllable is joined [to these], and one should speak of the sixfold nature of the *bhaga*.

One should place *kraṃ svaṃ* immediately after the twelve syllables, followed by *rāṃ rīṃ ruṃ rākiṇyai namaḥ rakṣa rakṣa asṛgātmane*, and so forth, in sequence, according to the prescribed locations. Likewise,
one should subsequently place [the mantras] in the Anāhata [cakra] using the vowels beginning with *u* and the consonants beginning with *pha*.
And likewise, O Goddess, Lākinī, whose nature is flesh, resides in Manipūraka.
Having likewise placed Kākinī at the Svādhiṣṭhāna with the syllables *vala* and *varṇa*,
whose nature is fat (*medas*), one should place Śākinī with the syllables *yaśa* and *varṇa*.
One should place the bone, as previously mentioned, preceded by the seed-syllable.
Likewise, O Great Goddess, one should place the syllable *hakṣa*, which is white in color, as Marjā Hākinī between the eyebrows; this is known as the Yoginī-nyāsa.

Having written the aforementioned syllables by this method, and having written "Ḍāṃ Ḍīṃ" and so forth, one should write the names and the letters joined with the sixth vowel and the *bindu*; then, having written in sequence "Ḍākinyai namaḥ" and so forth, and finally having written the two words "rakṣa," one should recite "tvagātmanaḥ" and so forth.
Now, the placement of the zodiac signs (rāśinyāsa).

Likewise, O Goddess praised by the gods, one should then perform the placement of the syllables (rāśinyāsa), which provides complete protection for men; one should place them starting with the letter 'a' in groups of four.
One should place a ram on the right ankle, and then a bull with its snout; one should place the knees with the two signs of Gemini, and then the testicles with Taurus.
With two [consonants] one forms a crab on the belly; with two, a lion on the shoulder;
and with the anusvāra, visarga, and the *śa*-group [of consonants], a maiden.
O you who are honored by heroes, one should place [the letter] *śa* on the right side of the head;
likewise, on the left side of the head, one should place the *ka*-group, which serves as the counterpart to the scale.
Likewise, O Śivā, one should place Vṛścika upon the shoulder with the *ca*-group;
and likewise, O Śivā, one should place Dhanvin upon the belly with the *ṭa*-group.
One should place the *makara* with its own [corresponding] syllable on the two testicles in sequence;
likewise, one should place *vumpha* with the *pa*-group on the left knee.
With the *ya*-group and the letter *kṣa*, one should place [the seed-syllable] for Pisces on the left ankle.

With this [mantra], beginning with "aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ, obeisance to Aries," one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in the aforementioned locations in sequence, starting with the right ankle. Then, one should place the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*) in order using the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Kāmarūpa is the great pīṭha, and Vārāṇasī is likewise a pīṭha;
Nepāla is also a pīṭha, as well as Ṛddhana.
Likewise, Parasthita and Pīṭha; after that, Vasthira is considered next.
Then follows the great seat (mahāpīṭha) Pūrṇaśaila, and after that, Nicutva.
The sacred seat (pīṭha) of Āmrātakeśvara, and after that Ekāmra;
Kailāsa, Bhṛgukedāra, and then the seat of Candrapura;
likewise the Śrīpīṭha and Iṅkāra, which is considered the supreme seat in Jālandhara.
Likewise, Mālava is a pīṭha, as is Kalānta;
Gokarṇa is a great pīṭha, as indeed is Mārukeśvara.
Aṭṭahāsa, Viraja, Rājagṛha, Mahāyudha, Pīṭha, and Kolā are proclaimed; immediately following is Malāpura.
The great seat of Vāmeśvara, [the goddess] Antakī,
the seat of Ujjayinī, and the one named Citrākṣī.
The seat of Hastināpura, Uḍīśa, Raviyogaka,
the seat of Ṣaṣṭhīśa, and likewise Māyāpura Maheśvara.
Mahendra, Vāmana, and Hiraṇyapura as well.

The seat consisting of Mahālakṣmī is Uḍḍiyāna; beyond that, one should perform the placement [of mantras] in the locations of the Mātṛkās in sequence, beginning with "Oṃ, salutation to the seat of Kāmarūpa" on the forehead, and so forth.
O Goddess, you are eternally praised as the essential nature of the Mātṛkā vowels.
The Mātṛkā [is located] in the sixfold face (*ṣadvaktra*); it bestows all prosperity in due order.
Therein, first is the primary Vidyā; again... (51a).
Kāmeśvarī is well-known, and likewise Bhagamālinī;
Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and Vindhyavāsinī as well.
Vajreśvarī, Dūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī,
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā.
Jvālāmālinī and Vitrā—these are proclaimed as the fifteen [Nityās].
These are the Nityās; at the mouth [of the face], "Oṃ, obeisance to Mahātripurasundarī."
Thus, one should place [the mantras] on the forehead and so forth in the prescribed order.

Likewise, one should then perform the placement of stability (*sthiti-nyāsa*) with the sixteen syllables of the Śrīvidyā: on the five fingers of both hands, at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), on the face, and in the heart. Having thus performed the placement, O Daughter of the Mountain, one should place one [syllable] from the navel down to the feet, and thereafter the syllable *ḍā* from the throat up to the left side.
Having performed one placement from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) down to the throat, [one should perform another] on the two feet.
Having placed [the mantras] upon the fingers, this ritual placement (nyāsa) brings about stability;
likewise,
it is performed on the head, forehead, heart, mouth, tongue, feet, and the sattvic [faculties].
One should place the sixteen syllables in the mouth and in the locations of the vowels in sequence;
one should perform the pervasive Goraka [mudrā] and then practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Thus, many varieties of *nyāsa* have been recorded in the tantras, but they are omitted here for fear of excessive prolixity. Even so, the necessity of performing the sixfold *nyāsa* (ṣoḍhānyāsa) is established by this; the summary is that one should perform *prāṇāyāma* after having performed the pervasive (*vyāpaka*) *nyāsa* in seven or five ways. Likewise:
The body [of practice] for breath control (prāṇāyāma), performed according to rule and conjoined with mudrās, is proclaimed to have nine limbs:
Kṣobhaṇā, Drāvaṇā, Ākarṣaṇā, Vaśyā, Unmādanā, Mahāṅkuśā,
Khecarī, Bījā, and Yonimudrā.
Likewise, in the Jñānārṇava:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the great internal sacrifice:
let [the breath] enter the subtlest [channel], from the root up to the aperture of Brahmā.
It was composed of the mass of rays from the rising sun and the splendor of ten million lightning bolts.
He possesses the radiance of ten million moons and consists of the singular light of the three worlds.
One should meditate upon the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of all things without exception,
O Goddess, in such a way that the mind becomes unwavering.
Having thus performed the internal sacrifice, one should perform the external sacrifice.
Thus it is said.
The meaning is that the external sacrifice must take place immediately after the internal sacrifice.
Now, meditation.
Then [he beheld] the Goddess, who resembles a lotus, reddened by the rays of the rising sun,
like the hibiscus flower, and akin to the interior of saffron.
Resembling a swarm of dark bees, she possessed curved locks of hair and earrings.
The Supreme Goddess has a face resembling a fresh, rosy orb;
she possesses a soft fillet upon her forehead,
shaped like the bow Pināka and beautifully tawny.
Her eyes were undulating with the playful movement of the waves of bliss.
I bow to the Supreme Goddess, whose radiant earrings shimmer with a mass of throbbing rays,
and whose expansive orb of face has surpassed the circle of the moon.
Her nose was perfectly defined by the lines of creation fashioned by Viśvakarman;
her lips were red like a small copper mirror and resembled nectar.
My tongue, as it speaks, shines like an island of jewels, while my rows of teeth gleam with the reddish luster of pomegranate seeds. It illuminates the entire world.
She is endowed with sweetness that is gentle and exceedingly sweet, like an ocean of the essence of nectar;
she is beautifully adorned with a waist marked by three folds.
The Great Goddess, with a neck like a conch shell, possesses arms as graceful as lotus stalks;
her delicate lotus-hands have the appearance of a cluster of red lotuses.
The sky was covered by the radiance of the nails of his lotus-like hands.
She is endowed with a creeper-like necklace of pearls, possesses lofty breasts,
and is beautifully adorned at her waist, which is marked by the three folds.
She was adorned with the flowing river of loveliness,
her waist graced by a girdle fashioned from endless jewels, and she possessed shapely hips.
The Goddess, whose hips are like the orb of the moon, whose line of hair is like a supreme goad on an elephant,
and whose limbs are as delicate as the graceful pillars of a plantain tree.
Adorned with a pair of shanks like plantain trees of loveliness, her two feet possessed hidden ankles, and the soles of her feet surpassed tortoises in beauty.
Her slender, long fingers were radiant with moon-like nails,
and her lotus feet were rubbed by the crest-jewels on the heads of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Her continuous stream of luster resembles a hundred moons and smiles with radiance;
she surpasses vermilion in her redness and the yellow lotus in her golden hue.
She is clothed in red garments, with noose and goad raised in her hands;
she is draped in red cloth and adorned with red ornaments.
She has four arms and three eyes, holds five arrows and a bow,
and her mouth is filled with betel-leaf mixed with camphor.
Her body is intensely red with saffron and abundant with great musk;
she is enriched with all the attire of love and adorned with every ornament.
To the Goddess who generates joy for the world, who brings delight to the world,
who consists of all the gods, and who dwells in the midst of the Kadamba forest.
One should contemplate [the breath] as it gradually emerges from the opening of the channel-pouch;
having thus meditated upon this supreme [state] through the sequence of the moving channels and pouches.
Having arrived at the center of the wheel, [one should act] with the three-part mudrā.
One should contemplate the Goddess established there, dwelling within the Śrī-pīṭha.
The invocation mantra according to the Tantra.
The Bhairavīrāmanta, endowed with the *sṛṣṭi* (creation) [mantra], is the *vidyā* of the Goddess’s vehicle; this is seen from the following: *aiṃ ha sakala ra īṃ ha sa ra auṃ*.
Having uttered the root mantra (*mūla*), [one says]: "O Mahātripurasundarī, who dwells within the great lotus forest, come! I invoke you!"

O Mother, O Supreme Goddess, whose form is absolute bliss, who art devoted to the welfare of all beings—by these [mantras], O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, grant Your presence in this great maṇḍala! Come here! Stay here! Be present here! Be firmly established here! [Having done so, one should perform] the six limbs upon the body of one's own deity with the mantra of the six limbs.
Having performed the placement [of mantras], the three claps, the binding of the directions,
and the sealing, one should display the respective mudrās.
Thus it has been said:
The seals (*mudrā*) of Mahātripura [are to be performed] with such-and-such a seal;
for it is heard [in scripture] that "O fortunate one, having invoked [the deity] with the Vidyā, one should perform prostration," and this refers to the Root Vidyā (*mūlavidyā*).
From the *Darśana*: "One should display the mudrās there; one should worship in three ways by means of the parvan rites. Now, the mudrās for the invocation and so forth are as follows:
Having joined the palms with both hands, one should place the two thumbs at the root joints of the ring fingers; this is the mudrā known as Vahanī.
O Śivā, this ring should be worn with its face turned downwards.
The *sannidhāpanī* [mudrā] consists of the joining of the fists with the thumbs raised.
Another, with the thumb inserted, is considered the "awakening" (saṃbodhanī) mudrā. || 4 ||
The two hands with palms turned upward and fists joined are considered the *sammukhīkaraṇī* mudrā. || 5 ||
The placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the body of the deity is the act of making it resonant with the *kakalī* sound.
The fist formed with the left hand, with the index finger extended long and pointing downward—
this is the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*, considered by the wise to be the *amitā*.
Then, for a moment, [perform] the mudrās and so forth, beginning with the agitation [mudrā].
Likewise, having placed the middle fingers together and raised the little fingers and thumbs,
one should position the two index fingers like staffs above the middle fingers and the ring fingers.
This, however, is the first mudrā, which causes the agitation of all. || 1 ||
O Supreme Goddess, when the middle fingers of this very same mudrā are made to be strong, it then becomes the "All-Enthraller."
O Supreme Goddess, the middle and index fingers, as well as the little and ring fingers, are equal; the two middle fingers take the form of a hook.
This is the Ākarṣaṇī mudrā, which draws in the three worlds. || 3 ||
Having formed the hands into the hollowed-cup gesture (*puṭākāra*), the two index fingers are made into hooks;
then, having turned them in successive order, the two middle fingers follow beneath them.
In that sequence, O Goddess of Gods, having joined the two— the little finger and the ring finger— make all the fingers firmly pressed together from the region of the tips of the thumbs.
O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā is considered to be the bringer of all subjugation. || 4 ||
Having placed the two hands face-to-face, with the middle fingers positioned between the two little fingers, the ring fingers straight,
and the two index fingers outside of them.
Then, with the two thumbs shaped like staffs and the tips of the middle fingers at the nail-base—
this mudrā is named Mādinī, which brings delight to all women.
Having made her two nostrils into the shape of a hook,
one should apply them in sequence by means of the index fingers, as if piercing them.
This is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all activities.
O Maheśānī, having placed the left arm on the right side and the right [arm] on all sides, one should join and rotate the two hands.
O Goddess, by that sequence, the little finger and the ring finger form the mudrā;
they are pressed down by the two index fingers, with the left middle finger positioned above the fire [middle finger].
O Maheśānī, one should even cause the two thumbs to be joined with the palms;
thus this is known as the Khecarī Mudrā, considered the most excellent of all.
O beloved, having turned the two hands over, they should be formed into the shape of a half-moon;
then, one should join the pair of index fingers with the pair of thumbs simultaneously.
One should place the two middle fingers pressed down beneath the little fingers;
likewise, one should join the two ring fingers at the very bottom.
This is the Seed-Seal (*bījamudrā*), which swiftly brings about all accomplishments: having placed the two middle joints of the nose below in the shape of a hook,
one should likewise apply the two index fingers in that same sequence.
This is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all activities.
O Maheśānī, having placed the left arm on the right side and the right [arm] on all sides, one should rotate both hands.
O Goddess, by that same sequence, the little finger and the ring finger [are joined];
the two index fingers press down upon the middle finger of the upper left hand.
O Maheśānī, one should cause the two thumbs to be pressed even with force;
thus, this mudrā, known by the name Sasvarī, is considered the most excellent of all.
Having turned the two hands over, O beloved, when they have been formed into crescent moons,
one should then simultaneously join the pair of index fingers with the pair of thumbs.
One should apply the two little fingers below; likewise, one should join the two bent middle fingers, and all [the fingers] at the very bottom with the two ring fingers.
O Yama, this seed-syllable mudrā shall swiftly bring about all accomplishments. || 8 ||
Having made the two middle fingers curved and positioned above the index fingers,
the ring fingers should likewise be placed between them, as should the little fingers.
Joining all [the fingers] together in one place and pressing them with the thumbs—
this is the first mudrā, known as the Yoni-mudrā.
Having turned the two hands over, one should make the two thumbs even;
having placed the two ring fingers inside, the two index fingers should be made curved.
O Maheśvarī, one should employ the little finger in its own place;
this is declared to be the "Three-Parted" (trikhaṇḍā) mudrā for the ritual of the seed-syllable of Tripurā.
In this very [state], there is the dissolution of the individual soul (jīvanyāsa).

The *jīvanyāsa* mantra should be sought in the section concerning Viṣṇu. Then, at the end of the root mantra, one should perform libation three times with the *argha* water, saying: "I satiate Mahātripurasundarī along with her retinue. This is because no specific mantra has been mentioned. Likewise:
One should properly offer perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth to the Goddess.

By this, there is a connection at the end of the root mantra with "aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ"; thus, according to the sequence of pairs, the seed-syllables consisting of Māyā and Lakṣmī [are employed]. Then: "I offer water for the feet (pādya) to the delicious [Goddess] Mahātripurasundarī."
One should offer the water for the feet and the other items. As it has been said:
"Saying 'I present the water for the feet,' one should arrange the water for the feet and the rest.
Likewise:
Having worshipped the Supreme Deity with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*),

one should again offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) three times while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*); such is the direction [of the teaching] according to the Tantras, that after worship there is a further offering of libations.
At this time, O Goddess, one should worship the Nityā of the lunar day.

O fair-faced goddess, one should worship the deities beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Vicitrā, who take the form of the lunar days (tithis) from the first day of the fortnight up to the full moon.
One should worship the circle of lunar days (*tithi-maṇḍala*) during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), beginning with Vicitrā and ending with Kāmeśvarī, O excellent lady.

Therefore, during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), one should meditate on [the goddesses] beginning with Kāmeśvarī, while during the dark fortnight, one should worship those beginning with Vicitrā and ending with Kāmeśvarī; such is the rule regarding their colors and positions therein.
One should contemplate the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ṛ* on the southern line;
then, on the eastern line, the five long vowels beginning with *ā*.
Having drawn [the diagram], one should then write the powers (śakti) and so forth along the northern line;
one should worship the sixteen measures ending with the anusvāra, and the sixteenth in the visarga.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship the sixteen Nityās in counter-clockwise order.
By this [method], having inscribed the five short vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *ḷ* on the southern line,
having written the five vowels beginning with *ā* and ending with *ḹ* on the eastern line, and [having done so] on the northern line...

Having written the vowels beginning with *śakti* (a) and so forth, ending with the nasal (*anusvāra*), one should worship the Nityās therein in a counter-clockwise direction; one should then worship the sixteenth [vowel], the Visarga.
Now, the constant measures.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme Nityā-maṇḍala:
one should utter Vālā, Tāra, and at the end of the two [syllables], say "Kāmeśvari."
In the phrase *icchākāmaphalaprāpte*, one should utter the word *pade*;
thereafter, one should say *sarvavaśam*, followed by the phrase *karisarvajagat*.
At the end of the agitation, one should speak; one should write three *hūṃ* syllables on the hand.
Having written the five *vāmās*, one [attains] the maiden through the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
55a) O Śivā, this eternal Kāmeśvarī has been described here as an incidental matter.
Therefore: Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Oṃ Namaḥ Kāmeśvari, O bestower of the fruits of desire and will, Sarva Sarva!
One should worship with the mantra: *vaśaṅkari sarvajagatkṣobhaṇakara hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ vlūṃ saḥ sauḥ klīṃ aiṃ aṃ kāmeśvarī-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. || 1 ||
One should write the Vāgbhava syllable at the end of the word "bhaga," followed by "bhage bhagini. Then one should write "bhage devi," and at the end of "bhaga," "bhagamālini bhagāvahe."
Bhaga, guhya, bhage, prānte, yoniprānte, bhagāṅkite, nipātini, and sarvānte; then Bhagavaśaṅkari.
Then the form of the *bhaga* (vulva) should be drawn, with eyes like blue lotuses;
one should always draw it as moist at the edges of the *bhaga*, according to its true nature, or indeed in all its aspects.
"Bring my vulvas here; grant them and draw them!
O Retas, O Suretas, O Blessed One, O Wet One, O Wet One, O Liquid One! Then [he spoke].
Moisten and dissolve all beings in vain, O Mistress of the Yoni!
Make yourself possessed of the yoni, and cause agitation and destruction everywhere.
One should utter "Satyaṃ Bhageśvari," followed by the Vāgbhava mantra, *vlaṃ*, *jaṃ*, and so forth; then *bhauṃ*, *vlaṃ*, *sauṃ*, *vlaṃ*, *haiṃ*, *hūṃ*, and thereafter *ahaṃ klinne*.
"Bring all the vulvas under my control," and at the end of "Hara," the syllable consisting of *vala* (the seed-syllable of Śrī).
Having drawn Bhuvaneśī, this is the Vidyā known as Bhagamālinī.

By that [mantra]: *aiṃ bhagabhage bhagini bhage devi bhagabhagamālini bhagāvahe bhaga guhye bhagayoni bhagani pātini sarvabhagavaśaṅkari bhagarūpe nitya klinne bhagasvarūpe sarvabhagāni me ānaya varade rete surete bhaga klinne klinna drave*.

55b) O Mistress of the *bhaga*, moisten and dissolve all sentient beings in vain! O Mistress of the *bhaga*, you who know the *bhaga* yourself, agitate fear in all sentient beings! Aiṃ vlaṃ jaṃ vlaṃ bhaum vlaṃ sāṃ vlaṃ ca haiṃ hūṃ.
And with "ca ha klīnne sarvāṇi bhagāni meva samānaya śrīṃ hara vlaṃ hrīṃ bhagamālini śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi," one should perform worship.
Likewise, having uttered the seed-syllable of the other, [the mantra] is "ni *? kli * *? da *?
ve"; these mantras ending with the wife of Agni (svāhā) are eternally called "klinne yamī" (O you who are ever-moist). || 3 ||
With that [mantra], one should worship, saying: "I worship the venerable pādukā. Likewise, having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then utter the pair of goads (aṅkuśa).
O Goddess, one should draw the syllable whose nature is contemplation in the center of that.
Each [syllable] is endowed with the fourteen vowels and individually marked with the bindu.

The seed-syllable consisting of the letter *bha*, its own form (*svarūpa*) and its class (*varga*), the letter *cha* and *ja*, the form of the vowel *ṛ*, fire which is the letter *ra*, the fourteenth vowel which is *au*, and the wife of fire which is *svāhā*; by means of these: *oṃ kroḍa kroḍa kroḍa svāhā*—this is Bheruṇḍā. 4.
Likewise, having written "parām" and then "vindhya-antavāsinyai namaḥ," this eight-syllable mantra belongs to the Great Goddess; Vindhyavāsinī is its presiding deity.
Parāvī hrīṃ, by that hrīṃ, obeisance to Vindhyavāsinī; [obeisance] to Vindhyavāsinī. || 5 ||
One should draw her as eternally moist and perpetually flowing, with a star upon her face;
at the end of *hṛllekhā* and ending in *pharaṃ*, one should write the seed-syllable of the wheel (*cakrabīja*) like a visarga.
The fourteen-syllable Vidyā-mantra is the goddess Vajreśvarī.
Its meaning is: "Nityaklinnā, flowing with intoxication. [This refers to] the previously mentioned mantra of Nityaklinnā.
Having written the vocative ending in *svāhā* at the end, one should place it around its mouth. At the beginning is the *tāra*, the syllable *oṃ*;
then *hṛllekhā*, *hrīṃ*; the essence of *phara*, *phreṃ*; and the lunar seed-syllable, the letter *sa* joined with the *visarga*. Thus: *oṃ hrīṃ phreṃ saḥ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā vajreśvarīm*.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Parā, joined with "Śivadūtī" and the dative suffix "ṅe," this mantra ending with "hṛt" (namaḥ), O Goddess, is Śivadūtī, the bestower of prosperity.

The seed-syllable of Parā is *hrīṃ*; with that, one should write "Salutation to Śivadūtī" (*hrīṃ śivadūtyai namaḥ*) for Śivadūtī. Likewise, having uttered the syllable *oṃ* as the seed-syllable, one should write the armor (*kavaca*). Having written *khe ca chai kṣaṃ*, one should also write the female seed-syllable (*strībīja*).
The syllable *huṃ*, *kṣa*, and the supreme weapon (*astra*)—this is the Tvaritā Vidyā.

The supreme *hrīṃ*, the armor (*kavaca*) *hūṃ*, the female seed-syllable (*strībīja*) *strīṃ*, and the weapon *phaṭ*—by means of these, [one recites]: *oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ kheca dakṣa strī hūṃ kṣe hrīṃ phaṭ* for Tvaritā.
One should enclose Bhairavī with the *vāla* syllables; likewise, the five arrows are pure, and Nityā becomes the syllable of Śakra.
With that [mantra]: Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Uralakahasa Aiṃ, Uralakahasa Īṃ, Uralakahasa Auṃḥ; Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Drāṃ Drīṃ Klīṃ Vluṃ Saḥ Vimalāṃ. || 9 ||
By that [mantra]—drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ vlū saḥ—one [attains] Nityā. || 10 ||
The Praṇava, the syllable consisting of Bhuvaneśānī and Pha-reṃ, and the second [syllable] consisting of Vlūṃ; then the goad of Bhuvaneśī.
Having extracted the word *nitya*, one should join it with *mada* and *dravām*;
[these are] the armor (*kavaca*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the *nīlapatākinī* vidyā.
The Praṇava (Oṃ), O Bhuvaneśānī, Hrīṃ, Phareṃ as the essence, Phreṃ Vlaṃ the goad, Kroṃ,
Nityamada Drave Hūṃ Kroṃ, [and] the one with the banner of the blue [lotus].
O Goddess, this Vidyā, which possesses the voice of Śakra and consists of the Bindu and Nāda, shall be Vijayā.
The syllable *va* is vomited; *kāla* is *ma*; *śakra* is *ra*.
Likewise,
O Goddess, one should write the seed-syllable of Dāra conjoined with Candra and Vāruṇa; then, one should write Sarvamaṅgalā ending in the dative case.
Within the heart [is] Sarvamaṅgalā.
The Moon is the letter *sa*, the one belonging to Varuṇa; the seed-syllable of Tārā is the syllable *oṃ*. By that, [it becomes] *khāṃ*—*namaḥ sarvamaṅgalāyai sarvamaṅgalām* || 13 ||
And [the word] "Goddess," having been uttered twice, at the very end [is followed by] "O you who effect the withdrawal of all beings."
Having inscribed [the mantra] in *jātavedasi*, one should ignite the pair of words;
one should write the couplet "jvalati prajvala" and the three *hūṃ* syllables.
The mantra consists of the three fire-seeds (RAṂ), followed by the armor (HŪṂ) and weapon (PHAṬ) syllables, and concludes with SVĀHĀ.
O Great Goddess, this is the supreme Nityā Jvālāmālinikā.
Therefore: Oṃ, homage! O Blessed One, Goddess garlanded with flames, Goddess who destroys all beings, O Jātavedasī!
Blaze, blaze, blaze! Flare up, flare up! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! Raṃ raṃ raṃ! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Jvālāmālinī || 14 ||
Ending with the *ka*-group and ending with the vowels, conjoined with the vowel of Indra (the letter *i*),
and pervaded by the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*— such is the wonderfully diverse Supreme Goddess.

The letter *ca* is at the end of the *ka*-group; the end of the vowels is the *kṣāra* (the letter *kṣa*). The vowel of Śakra is the letter *au*. With that, one should worship with the mantra: "I worship the variegated *śrīpādukā*, *ka auṃ*. || 15 ||

Then, one should worship with the root mantra, saying: "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Mahātripurasundarī. As it has been said [in the scripture]: "Furthermore, for the sake of attaining good fortune, one should worship the Goddess Śrī Tripurā."

In the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), however, one should worship [the goddesses] beginning with Vicitrā and ending with Kāmeśvarī; then, in the corners starting from the northwest (vāyavya), one should worship, saying:

"Salutation to the Supreme Gurus (paraguru)," "Salutation to the Higher-Lower Gurus (parāparaguru)," "Salutation to the Supreme Gurus," "Salutation to the Preceptor Gurus (parameṣṭhigurubhyaḥ)," "Salutation to the Highest Gurus (paramagurubhyaḥ)," and "Salutation to one's own Gurus (svagurubhyaḥ)."
This has been stated in the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
One should worship the six gurus starting from Vāyu (the northwest) and ending with Īśa (the northeast);
then, having honored the triad beginning with Gara, one should worship the triad beginning with Parameṣṭhin.
This is the lineage of gurus for all ordinary disciples and teachers.
Now follows the worship of the Tradition (Āmnāya).
Likewise, one should worship the Eastern Tradition (pūrvāmnāya) in the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa-cakra,
and one should worship the Southern Tradition (dakṣiṇāmnāya) in the Sarvarakṣākara-cakra.
O Goddess, one should worship the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya) within the middle wheel;
O Mistress of the Gods, one should worship the Kubera Tradition (Kuverāmnāya) within the nine wheels.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the lion-throne in the center of the Vaindava;
likewise,
[one should worship] the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa and other wheels, since no specific [location] has been mentioned for them.
One should worship Śrīvidyā and the others.
Likewise, in the Tantra:
Śrīvidyā, as well as Lakṣmī and Mahālakṣmī,
along with Triśakti— all these being joined together, they are proclaimed as the five Lakṣmīs.
Śrīvidyā, Parā Jyotis, Para Niṣkala Śāmbhavī,
Ajapā, and Mātṛkā— these are declared to be the five sheaths (pañcakośas).
Śrīvidyā, Tvaritā, Pārijāteśvarī,
Trikūṭā, and Vāneśī— these are known as the five Kalpalatās.
The Mistress of the Seat of the Nectar of Śrīvidyā, Sudhā, Śrī, Amṛteśvarī,
and the one renowned as Annapūrṇā— these five are considered to be the bestowers of desires.
Śrīvidyā, Bindulakṣmī, Mātaṅgī, Bhuvaneśvarī, and Vārāhī are proclaimed; these are declared to be the five jewels.

With this— *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, "I worship the sandals of Śrīvidyā"— one should worship. O Goddess of beautiful countenance, having joined the seed-syllables consisting of Māyā and Lakṣmī with the Vāgbhava and the others in their proper order, one should worship them all sequentially.
By this, the appearance of the three seeds is shown when no specific distinction is stated.

"O Maheśvarī, in the Cakrarāja, the place of worship for Śrīvidyā, I worship the Pādukā, the mother of all auspiciousness. Having recited this, one should then worship Koṣā and the others within the supreme light; for it is stated thus: "One should worship the Pādukā within the Bindu or in the treasury (koṣa)."

The connection "I worship" applies everywhere. Likewise, O Goddess, one should worship the vision of the letters within the parts (*aṃśi*) as belonging to the Bindu above Śiva; [one should worship] the supreme wheel, O Parameśvarī, and one should worship it, O Goddess, in the earthen liṅga (*bhūliṅga*), for the aforementioned vision is the most excellent.
O Goddess, one should worship the Vaiṣṇava vision of the Cakra.

One should worship the wheel of emanation (*sṛṣṭicakra*) according to its characteristics, and having fully honored the wheel of persistence (*sthiticakra*), one should [follow] the supreme Buddhist view.
Having thus worshipped the entirety [of the deity], one should worship Śrīvidyā all around.
One should again offer libations three times while bowing with the *mudrā*.
As for that *mudrā*: "This is declared to be the *tatvamudrā*, formed by the thumb and the ring finger."

The mantra is: at the end of the root [mantra], "I satisfy [Name]," and it is said that one should employ the injunction for the libation (tarpaṇa) by saying "I satisfy" at the end of the mantra. Likewise, O Goddess, one should offer [the oblation] with the mudrā known as Jñāna.
Having propitiated [the deity] with all ritual services, one should display the mudrās in their proper sequence.
Now follows the limb-worship (aṅgapūjā).

The ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the mantra in the intermediate corners beginning with Agni and Īśa, as well as in the center and the cardinal directions, because no specific mantra has been mentioned. Thus it is said:
"The worship of the limbs is performed in the corners of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu, as well as in the center and the cardinal directions," likewise in the *Trailokyamohana-cakra*.
One should worship the manifest Yoginī.
In the square with four doors, the Yoginīs are the bestowers of success (*siddhi*).
One should worship Animā on the right side at the western door.
And one should worship Mahimā at the eastern gate and Śivā at the northern gate.
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the accomplishment of mastery (īśitva-siddhi) at the southern gate;
the accomplishment of control (vaśitva-siddhi) in the northwest, and irresistible will (prākāmya) in the northeast corner of Śiva.
O Supreme Goddess, the desire for the enjoyment of fire is in the eastern part, while in the south-west are attainment, accomplishment, and the fulfillment of all desires.
O Supreme Goddess, they should be known in the form of an upward and downward sequence.

Having worshipped with "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to the Trailokyamohana Cakra," one should worship in order at the southern part of the western door with: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the Animā Siddhi. Thus one should worship in sequence.
Likewise, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Aindrī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
and then Vārāhī as the sixth; Cāmuṇḍā shall be the seventh.
And likewise Aṣṭamī and Lakṣmī; "in the sequence beginning from the west" means that they are placed on the second line starting from the west.

As for what was written by Devanātha— that [the sequence] beginning with Asitāṅga and Bhairava applies even in Yoga because it is stated in the Bālātantra and because of the Surasa-stavarāja— we do not understand the purpose of that, since it would result in an excessive burden of ritual procedure when writing down the sequence prescribed in the Pañcamī-tantra.

58b) With this [mantra], one should worship in sequence: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Brāhmī. Likewise, on the third line [are] Kṣobhaṇā, Drāvaṇā, Ākarṣiṇī, Unmādinī, Mahāṅkuśā, and Khecarī.

One should worship the three sections known as the *vīja-yoni* in sequence. With the five arrows, one forms the five mudrās; the imperishable [syllable] consists of the letters *ka*, *ra*, and *ma*. First is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Rudrabhairavī, followed by the syllable beginning with *śi* (Śiva).
O Goddess, the Vāgbhava [syllable] alone, along with the fourfold sequence.

With the five arrows—*drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *vlaṃ*, *saḥ*—which are its own forms, [one attains] that which consists of the hand (*karāmātmakam*). *Krāṃ* is its own form. Of Rudrabhairavī, the first is *ha-sa-ra-aiṃ*. With Śiva as the direction, at the end of the letter *ha* is the letter *sa*; *hayaṃ* is its own form, and *vāgbhava* is the syllable *aiṃ*. These seed-syllables (*bījāni*) are each [to be applied] at the beginning of the *kṣobhaṇā* and other mudrās.

Having offered the sandals, one should worship with the mantra "I worship. Since no specific instruction is given for the *trikhaṇḍā* [mudrā], one should worship the three seed-syllables—*aiṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ*—on the left side, and then as before from the northwest (vāyavya) onwards. Having thus worshipped these, one should worship the supreme *cakreśī*, Tripurā.
One should display the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā at the moment of the lotus.
With this [mantra], one should worship with the words: "I worship the sandals of Tripurācakreśī, Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ. Likewise, one should then worship the Sarvāśāpūraka-cakra, which has sixteen spokes.
There, on the sixteen-spoked wheel, one should worship these [deities] endowed with the sixteen vowels, starting from the west and proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction (vāmāvartana).
Thus it has been said:
O Goddess, [I worship] Kāmākarṣiṇī, as well as Buddhyākarṣiṇī,
Ahaṅkārākarṣiṇī, and the one whose form is the attraction of sound (Śabdākarṣaṇarūpiṇī).
She whose form is the attraction of touch, and she who possesses the form of attracting form;
she whose form is the attraction of taste, and she who effects the attraction of fragrance.
She who has the form of attracting thought and she who has the form of attracting fortitude.
She who has the form of attracting mindfulness, likewise she who attracts names,
she who has the form of attracting seed-syllables, and she who effects the attraction of the self.
Likewise, Amṛtākarṣiṇī and Śarīrākarṣiṇī,
endowed with the vowels, are located on the sixteen-spoked wheel in reverse order starting from the west.
O Goddess, one should worship the eternal Kalā, the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī), Tripureśvarī.
With this [mantra], one should worship in sequence, saying: "I worship the venerable sandals of Vāmākarṣiṇī: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṃ."
Then, one should worship with the mantra: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ cakreśī tripureśvarī pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. Likewise, having displayed the Sarvavidrāviṇī mudrā, one should offer [the oblation].
One should worship the eight [deities] possessing the luster of gold in the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa cakra.
One should worship Anaṅgakusumā in the east with the *ka*-group,
and likewise Anaṅgamekhalā in the south with the *ca*-group.
After "Anaṅga Madanam," [place] the *ṭa*-group in the west;
after that, the *ta*-group in the north, followed by "Anaṅgamadanāturām."
In the southeast corner, one should worship Anaṅgā Rekhā with the *pa*-group of consonants;
and in the southwest, one should worship Anaṅgavegā with the *ya*-group of consonants.
One should worship Anaṅgāṅkuśā in the northwest with the group of letters beginning with Śa;
likewise, Anaṅgamālinī is to be worshipped in the northeast with the group of letters beginning with La.
Then, O Goddess, one should worship Tripurasundarī as the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī);
and, O you who are praised by the gods, one should display the Sarvākarṣaṇa mudrā.

With this [mantra], one should worship in the order starting from the east: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ anaṅgakusumāṃ śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; then, in reverse order, one should worship with: *cakreśvarīṃ tripurasundarīṃ śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.

59b) Then, having worshipped the Wheel that bestows all good fortune (*sarvasaubhāgyada-cakra*), there, upon its fourteen spokes, just as there is the power (*śakti*) that agitates all (*sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī*), so too is the one that subdues all (*sarvavidrāvinī*).
The power that attracts all, as well as the one that brings delight to all;
the power that deludes all, and the one that causes the immobilization of all.
The power that subdues all, likewise the power that brings all under control,
and the power that delights in all objects— this is the ninth Supreme Goddess.
She is the one who intoxicates all beings, the further accomplisher of all purposes,
the perfection of all prosperity, and likewise composed of all mantras.
And on the fourteen-spoked [wheel], Śakti resides, who brings about the destruction of all dualities;
she is in the wheel that bestows all auspiciousness, starting from the west and proceeding in reverse order.
O Goddess of gods, having worshipped by way of the left path, [one attains] the Cakreśvarī who bestows all perfections,
the supreme resident of Tripura, the granter of success.

Having worshipped [her] and displayed the *vaśya* mudrā, one should offer [the oblation]. By this [method], starting from the west and proceeding counter-clockwise (*vāmāvarta*), one worships with: "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of EṂ HŪṂ ŚRĪṂ Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī. Then, having worshipped: "AṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ Cakreśī Siddhikarī Tripuravāsinī Pādukāṃ..."

Thinking "I worship," one should perform the worship. Then, having fully worshipped the ten-spoked wheel which accomplishes all aims, [one should praise] the Goddess who bestows all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*), as well as the Goddess who bestows all prosperity (*sarvasampat*),
the Goddess who makes everything dear (*sarvapriyaṃkarī*), and the Goddess who brings about all auspiciousness (*sarvamaṅgalakāriṇī*).
She fulfills all desires and liberates one from all suffering.
The goddess who pacifies all death, who wards off all obstacles,
who is beautiful in every limb, and who bestows all prosperity.
One should worship in sequence on the ten-spoked wheel in reverse order, beginning from the west;
one should worship Tripurā, the Goddess Śrī, the Mistress of the Wheel who bestows success.
Having displayed the *sarvānmādana* mudrā, one should offer [the worship] with this:
in reverse order starting from the west, *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, the venerable sandals (*śrīpādukā*) that bestow all accomplishments.

Having worshipped with "I worship," one should worship with: *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, "I worship the *Śrīpādukā* of Cakreśī, the bestower of success. Then, having fully worshipped the inner ten-spoked wheel (*antardaśāra*) which effects all protection, [one worships] with: "The omniscient one, the all-powerful, the bestower of all sovereignty."
The Goddess consists of all-knowledge, she is the destroyer of all diseases,
her essential nature is the support of all, and likewise she is the remover of all sins.
The Goddess consists of all bliss, her very nature is universal protection;
she grants the fruits of all desired objects and bestows all prosperity.
One should worship in the reverse order, starting from the west, in the rows and corners;
O Goddess, one should worship Sarvajñā in front, and then Mālinī as the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśī).

Having displayed the Great Hook (Mahāṅkuśā) Mahāmudrā, one should offer [the oblation]. Having worshipped with "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the Omniscient One (Sarvajñā)," proceeding in reverse order from the west and so forth, one should then worship with: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of Tripuramālinī, the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī)."
Then, having worshipped the eight-spoked wheel that removes all diseases, one should worship in sequence the secret Yoginīs, O Goddess, Vaśinī and the others, as well as the Siddhis,
starting from the west and proceeding in reverse order, according to the previously mentioned method.
Having worshipped Cakreśī, the bestower of supernatural powers, one should gradually show Khecarī.

Having worshipped the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī by means of the seed-syllables mentioned for the ritual placement (nyāsa) in reverse order starting from the west, one should worship [the central deity] with: "I worship the venerable sandals of Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrī Tripurā Siddhidā, the Mistress of the Wheel."
Then, having worshipped the wheel that bestows all accomplishments, which is known as the supreme-secret, one should fully worship the Yoginīs.
Having recited the five arrows, O Great Goddess, one should worship the deities of the arrows— Kāma, Kāmeśvarī, Māyā, and the one called Jambhana.

With this [mantra], one should worship with "Oṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ vlūṃ saḥ, obeisance to Jambhana Kāmeśvara-vāna" and likewise with "Obeisance to Kāmeśvarī-vāna. In the western direction, one should likewise worship the second bow, which consists of the syllable *dha*, as the Bow of Desire (*kāmacāpa*).
One should worship the deities of the bow, beginning with the one called Mohanā, who presides over desire.

With this [mantra], "Oṃ Dhaṃ, salutation to the bow of Kāmeśvara for the purpose of delusion," and likewise, "Salutation to the bow of Kāmeśvarī," one should worship in the northern direction. Similarly, O Bhuvaneśānī, there is a second pair of nooses that brings others under control.
The drawing-in of the three worlds by Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśī is dear [to them].
One should worship the fourth pillar, the goad (*aṅkuśa*) of the Goddess.

In the eastern direction, one should worship with: "Oṃ Āṃ, obeisance to Kāmeśvara, the lord of desire, for the sake of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*)," and likewise, "Obeisance to Kāmeśvarī’s noose (*pāśa*"). In the southern direction, [one should worship] with: "Kroṃ, obeisance to Kāmeśvara’s goad (*aṅkuśa*) for the sake of immobilization (*stambhana*)."

One should worship with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Goad of the Lord of Desire, obeisance," and likewise worship in the four directions in sequence starting from the west. Similarly, one should worship Kāmeśvarī, the Mudrā-Śakti, in front with the first *kūṭa*.
And with the second peak, one should likewise worship the one called Vajra and Vaiṣṇavī.
Having worshipped [her] in the south-eastern corner, one should not worship the third [deity];
[one should worship] Bhagamālā, the power of the universe (viśvaśakti), in the north, and Viśvamātṛkā.
One should worship Cakreśvarī and Ambikā, and Kāmeśī in front.
By this [method], one should worship with the Vāgbhava-kūṭa in the eastern corner, saying: "I worship the Śrī-pādukā of Kāmeśvarī.
One should worship with the Kāmarāja-kūṭa in the southern corner, saying: "I worship the Śrī-pādukā of Vajreśvarī."
With the *śaktikūṭa*, one should worship in the northern corner with the mantra: "I worship the venerable sandals of Bhagamālā.
Then, having worshipped with: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Tripurāmbikā Vajreśvarī."

One should display the seed-syllable mudrā. Then, having worshipped the entire wheel consisting of universal bliss within the bindu, one should worship that which is the nature of all vidyās, the form of all deities, and composed of all things, by uttering the three kūṭas.
And that very Cakreśvarī, the Great Tripurasundarī,
the Śrīvidyā of sixteen syllables, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should worship with offerings, such as food, fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice grains;
furthermore, one should offer libations three times with the root mantra.
Having displayed the *yoni-mudrā*, one should display the *artha-mudrās* in succession with pure,
fragrant substances produced from the sap of trees.
One should fumigate the Supreme Goddess with incense made from the ten ingredients and others; around the altar and the mandala, lamps filled with ghee should be lit.
One should also heat lamps made of camphor and filled with oil;
then, having offered incense and lamps, one should perform the libation as before, O Śivā.
O you who are worshipped by heroes, one should perform the *ārātrika* rite according to the rules,
offering food consisting of the six flavors, accompanied by honey, incense, and other offerings.
One should perform the rite of the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) for Saṃkalpaparameśānī;
