according to the root mantra, one should offer five oblations accompanied by the vital breaths (prāṇas).

The daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) for the six limbs is declared to consist of six oblations. Having recited the root mantra, one should offer the five-fold [oblations] in sequence— namely *prāṇāya svāhā* and so forth— to *apāna*, *samāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *grāsamudrā*, and then [offer] with the six-limbed mantra.
One should offer six oblations. Then,
having sat upon a beautiful seat, one should thereafter draw a square mandala in its center on the left side, O Dear One.
Then one should worship the mandala, which is a triangle within a circle and fully blossomed.
At the end of the pervasive [mantra], for the mandala, one should utter the Vāgbhava [syllable] ending with the Heart [mantra] and Parā.
O beloved, having placed the worshipful maṇḍala in the mouth, one should recite the mantra.

The Vāgbhava is the syllable *aiṃ*, and Parā is *hrīṃ*; having placed [the word] "heart-salutation" (*hṛn-namaḥ*) at the beginning—that is, having placed the Vāgbhava and Parā first—it means: *aiṃ hrīṃ vyāpakamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*.
Thus one should worship, and then recite [the mantra] according to one's capacity.
O you who are the protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us;
O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, may success be mine through your grace.
Thus one should offer the recitation (japa) to the Goddess. [From] the Vārāhī-tantra.
One should worship during the Mahāmatsava, at the Pavitra rite, and on the eighth day of the bright fortnight;
one should not worship by way of the left-hand path (vāmamārga), nor should one worship with improper conduct.
Afterwards, one should worship Animā at the location of the Bindu,
Kāmakalā in the third part, Brāhmī in the [third] part, and Sundarī in the fourth.
One should worship Ākarṣiṇī on the fifth petal and Kāmeśvarī on the sixth;
Bhairuṇḍā on the eight-petaled [lotus] and Kuleśvarī on the sixteen-spoked [wheel].
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
this alone should be done daily, but one should abandon it during birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka).
One who is endowed with devotion must certainly recite the mantra;
even when performing the daily rites while counting on the fingers, one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*).
One should not recite [mantras] for Viṣṇu at night; however, in the Śrīkrama, there is no fault in doing so for the Śākta or the Śaiva.
Whether one is completely free from disease, or pure, or even impure.
Whether at the improper time or the proper time, may I always be a performer of worship;
for I am devoted to yoga with a mind focused on You, O Lord.
With a heart satisfied by that, he shall become my practitioner;
whether he be a husband or a king, there is no other who is my worshiper.
62a) Now, the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
In whatever location a *liṅga* may be situated, it should face westward;
it may be self-manifested (*svayambhuva*), fashioned from bamboo, made of fruit or root, or established in water.
O you of virtuous vows, whether at a western sacred site or another,
in the fields of power, at the Ganges, at a river, or on a mountain peak.
O Goddess, being gracious, one should worship the Vidyā in pure places;
likewise, [one may offer] the fruit of the *vāna* tree established by the demon Bāṇa, along with meat, water, roots, and so forth.
Thus.

Staying there, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; then the Goddess herself will appear in her true form, [accompanied] by a rosary of pearls, rudrākṣas, lotus seeds, crystals, and udbhava beads.
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) with beads made of rubies, *padmarāgas*, and the like.

We maintain that where a recitation of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) is prescribed, this constitutes the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*); however, where a recitation of two hundred thousand or more is heard, we say that it is for optional purposes (*kāmya*) intended for greater fruit. For this very reason, [it is said that] by two hundred thousand [recitations], sins of seven lifetimes [are destroyed].
It has been stated that there are other modes as well; however, other methods have not been described here for fear of making the book too voluminous—this is the general direction.
Now the *jīvanī* is written.
As it is stated in the Śrīkramasaṃhitā: "O God, listen to how the Vidyās born of the Kula may become endowed with life on earth through Mahātripurasundarī. Just as...
O Goddess, the syllable *śrīṃ* comes first, and immediately after that, *krīṃ* and *klīṃ*.
"Haiṃ Haiṃ Kala Hrīṃ Sauḥ Sakala Hrīṃ"—
then one should recite "Klīṃ Klīṃ," O Goddess, and below that the syllable Hrīṃ as well as Śrīṃ.
This is the life-giving Vidyā of all, joined with all the cakras.
In the same manner, one should offer the bali-oblation before the image with a concentrated mind;
then, on the right side of the Goddess, one should perform the recitation of the Jīvanī mantra.
Having offered the blood of goats, one should then worship Kālikā.

By this [method], at the time of the installation (pratiṣṭhā) of a yantra or an image, the recitation of the Jīvanī-mantra must be performed during the rite of infusing life (jīvanyāsa); it should also be performed at the time of worship with greater frequency. The mantra is clearly manifest; as for the visualization (dhyāna), it is as follows:

62b) She holds a sword and a musta-grass, has a fierce countenance, and is adorned with a tiger skin; she wears red garments, possesses a formidable form, has four arms, and bestows boons while holding a sword, a trident, and a skull-cup.
One with a sharp nose.
Now, the mantra of Kālasundarī is [found] in the Śrīkramasaṃhitā.
A wise person should not recite [the mantra] joined with Krodhīśa and Ananta, accompanied by Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā, followed by Krodhī and Ananta.
One should then recite Pinākī, Sūkṣmā, Krodhī, and Ananta;
below that, one should recite Anila, Bhautika, and the Praṇava.

This is the Vidyā, the Great Vidyā, endowed with the Great Cakra. Krodhīśa is the letter *ka*; the end is the letter *ā*. Krodhī is the letter *ka*; Ananta is the letter *ā*. Pinākī is the letter *la*; Sūkṣmā is the letter *i*. Krodhī is the letter *ka*; Ananta is the letter *ā*. Anila is the letter *ya*; Bhautika is the letter *ai*.
The *praṇava* is the syllable *oṃ*; by that, [the mantra] is "Oṃ, to Kālī. Likewise, the second is called the South; beyond that are the West and the North.
She is the Goddess Mahākālī, the beautiful one who is beyond time (*nāmakālika*).
The goddess seated upon the great lotus throne is the bringer of great life;
having restored the image to life, one should sprinkle it with blood by means of this [mantra].
Listen indeed to the Great Meditation, O you who are the embodiment of supreme power—
the Goddess who resembles a dark blue cloud and possesses the luster of a blue girdle.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with red garlands;
holding a sword and a trident in her left hands, and a discus and a goad in her right hands.
With a moon disc upon her head and seated upon a sun disc,
she is clothed in red garments and anointed with red perfumes.

The best of practitioners should meditate upon Goddess Dahā in such a form: adorned with the foot of Śiva, who is [the source] of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others; possessed of intoxicated youth, seated upon a corpse, and pressing against a linga.
O Goddess, having worshipped the Supreme Sovereign with this vidyā,
one should then, having beheld the footprint in the circle, worship the image of Caṇḍikā.
O Goddess, with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, the practitioner, with a steady mind,
should place the *nirmālya* upon his head, and having offered praise and prostration, he should dismiss [the deity].
By this, it follows that this [Vidyā] also possesses the status of an independent Vidyā; its name is Kālasundarī, and its worship and so forth are like those of Sundarī—this is the summary.
Thus ends this chapter concerning the preliminary rites of meditation and worship for the mantra of Sundarī, composed by Devaśarman, the beloved of Śrī Ramā, in his *Nigamasāranirṇaya*.
She who bestows [grace upon] the ankles,
she who is blessed with great beauty, she who destroys great death,
the Goddess who embodies all sacred fords, and she who bestows mountains of molten gold.
The sun-sound is the letter *ai*; the end of the vowels is the letter *kṣa*. The earth... Bhṛgu; likewise Dakṣiṇāmūrti. By that [is meant] the beginning with Āditya and the middle;
the middle, the very middle, that which is final, Ambā... and likewise. Furthermore:

That itself would quickly become [the mantra]. O Tripureśānī, the nine-syllable [mantra] and the ten-syllable life-force (prāṇa) [mantra]: "The first of the first" refers to the previously mentioned three-syllable mantra; the first syllable is repeated twice in the middle, and after that, the final [syllable]...
Having repeated the first syllable three times— namely *aiṃ aiṃ klīṃ hlīṃ klīṃ hūṃ*—
and having performed the mantra ending with *Sundarī* in the morning,
one should offer flowers and perform the rites beginning with *śama* (tranquility) during the state of the sacrifice.
O Goddess of the gods, [perform] the placement (*nyāsa*)... the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the Vāgbhava [kalā].
One should infer the *śakti* of this [mantra] from the third [syllable].
By this, one should remember: "The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the meter (*chandas*) is *paṅkti*; the deity (*devatā*) is Vālātripurā;

the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *vāgbhava* (AIM); the power (*śakti*) is *hsauḥ*; and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of desired success. Having thus remembered, [one applies it to] the head, face, and so forth.
One should place the sages, meters, deities, and so forth within the heart. Having placed [the mantra] from the navel down to the feet,
and another from the throat up to the head, one should then sequentially place the three-syllable mantra from the head down to the throat.

Thus, by means of the sound of the three syllables, the armor (kavaca) is characterized by the three peaks, as is seen in the case of Bhairavī and others. Likewise, O Śivā, one should know that the triple seed-syllable (tribīja) is to be deposited in the palm of the left hand, likewise in the palm of the right hand, and in the hollow formed by joining both hands together.
Likewise,
one should place the three seed-syllables in sequence upon the head, the support, and the heart;
thus, one should place the three seed-syllables in order upon the aforementioned locations.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the five weapons in sequence upon the five fingers,
from the thumb to the little finger, in their proper order.
It is said that "drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ vlaṃ" is the mantra by which the Moon becomes possessed of creation.
O Goddess of the gods, O Pārvatī, hear the names of the five arrows:
Kṣobhaṇa, Drāvaṇa, O Goddess, and likewise the one known as Karṣaṇa.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the stages of subjugation and intoxication have thus been described.

With this, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the thumb and the other fingers in sequence, saying "drāṃ" for agitation and "namaḥ" for the subsequent stages. The letter *sa* (sakāra) is the moon, possessing both the inherent *sarga* (visarga) and the explicit *visarga*; therefore, "saḥ" is stated as the authority for the four *cāṇas*.
In the Jñānārṇava.
Having written two *kha* syllables situated in fire (*ra*) in sequence,
it is adorned with a mouth-circle, an eye, and a left [circle].

O Vārānanī, these two arrows have been proclaimed: the one consisting of the letter *ma* joined with the earth (*la*) and enriched by the fourth vowel and the bindu, which is the form of sound (*nāda*). 65b)
The letter *pha* joined with *śakra* (the letter *i*) and adorned with the left ear (the vowel *u*).
"Endowed with *bindu* and *nāda*, etc. [This means: the letter *tha* (the end of the dental series) is *da*; *vahni* (fire) is *ra*; the "mouth-circle" (*mukhavṛtta*) is the vowel *ā*;

the "left eye" is the vowel *ī*; *mādana* (delighter) is *ka*; "earth" is *la*; the fourth vowel is *ī*; the "end of *pha*" (*phānta*) is *va*; *śakra* (Indra) is *la*; and the "left ear" is the vowel *ū*. Thus, [the seed-syllables are] *drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *klīṃ*, and *vlūṃ*.
The Kāmas should be known in that very place; hear their names, O Supreme Goddess: Parā-bīja, Madhyavāṇa, and Vāgbhava.

Then one should place the fourth arrow, the female seed-syllable (*strībīja*), and that sequence in order: the supreme seed-syllable *krīṃ*, the middle arrow *klīṃ*, the *vāgbhava* syllable *aiṃ*, the fourth arrow *vlūṃ*, the female seed-syllable *strīṃ*,
and likewise those known as Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja.
O Maheśānī, the fifth [seed-syllable] is proclaimed as Mīnaketu (the Fish-bannered one).

With that, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the thumb and the other fingers in sequence, saying: *hrīṃ kāmāya namaḥ*. Likewise, having repeated the root-mantra twice, one should also perform it upon the palms of all the fingers; thus, the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is accomplished.

One should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa. By means of that, having performed the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) nyāsa in sequence—starting from the thumbs and ending at the palms, and starting from the heart and so forth—with "aiṃ hṛdayāya" and the rest, one should then perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa as taught in the Sundarī-mantra.
After that, one should perform the Vidyā-nyāsa with the three seed-syllables (bījas) in order, O Śivā.
First, one should place [the mantras] on the hands— at the wrists, the palms, and the fingers—
and having placed them on the right and left, [one places them] on the armpits, the elbows, and the palms.
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should likewise place [the seed-syllables] on the right and left [sides] and on the two feet;
thereafter, one should place the Liṅga at the end of the Nāda in the heart.
66a) O Goddess of the gods, one should place [the mantras] upon these limbs in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Upon these three sets of three limbs thus mentioned, one should sequentially place the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the order of withdrawal. Thus, by way of the sequence of withdrawal.
The meaning is "in reverse order.
Then, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) marked with the *yoni* [mudrā] using the three seed-syllables (*bījas*),
again upon the two ears, the chin, the two temples, and the mouth.
Having placed [the mantras] in the two eyes, the two nostrils, the pair of arms, and the heart-lotus;
and then in the two elbows, the two sides of the abdomen, the two knees, the secret organ, and the head.
One should sequentially place the three seed-syllables known as the "nine wombs" (navayoni) on the two feet, the secret place, the two sides, the heart, the two breasts, and the throat.

Having spoken thus, one should perform the placement of the nine *yonis* by repeating the *vidyā* three times in sequence with the nine seed-syllables (*bījas*) in the aforementioned locations; likewise,
O Goddess, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in sequence by repeating it twice.
In the Śailasaṃbhava [tantra], by the number three, one, ten, three, and two.
According to this statement, one should perform what is to be done at the appropriate time;
thus it is said.
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and then place the arrows and the [five] desires (kāmāḥ) in sequence upon the forehead,
throat, navel, and the root-support (mūlādhāra).

By this, it is meant that one should place the previously mentioned arrows and the *kāmās* on the forehead and other locations. Then, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, one should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). This [placement] occurs first, followed by the *mātṛkā*; thereafter follows the hand-placement (*karanyāsa*). Likewise, other optional placements (*kāmyanyāsa*) found in other tantras should also be understood accordingly.
Likewise, in the Jñānārṇava:
Having thus cast off the body and being concentrated in mind,
he, filled with bliss from the mass of supreme joy, should meditate in due order.
Then, having performed the internal sacrifice (antaryajana), one should perform the external worship (vāhyapūjā).
Seated there facing the east, one should arrange the grand sacrificial diagram (yantrodāra).
One should draw a straight line from Īśāna to Agni.
The preceptor, having drawn lines from the tip of that [line] toward the east starting from the northeast, and having unified them at the supreme Śiva in the southeast,
[proceeds].
The form shaped like a triangle is declared to consist of two powers;
one should draw a measuring-staff at the front portion of the tip of the first power.
O Supreme Goddess, draw two lines from the corners toward the northwest and southwest;
from their tips, draw them forward to the east.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, this shall be the letter *va* with its tip pointing east.
This King of Wheels (cakrarāja) shall consist of nine distinct wombs (yoni);
it should be drawn on the exterior as a circle resembling the full moon.
One should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with its center as the ascendant, endowed with eight knots;
one should form the knots by enclosing them between two *praṇavas*.
O Śivā, having drawn eight tridents,
one should draw a square adorned with four beautiful gates, which always bestows all bliss.
O Goddess of the gods, having inscribed the syllables *haṃ sauḥ* upon the triangle,
one should inscribe the left-hand seed-syllable in the middle of the eight-cornered [figure].
O Goddess of the Gods, having drawn eight petals starting from the west and proceeding clockwise, one should write the sixteen vowels, divided into pairs of pairs.
O Supreme Goddess, one should write the seven groups of letters beginning with 'ka' at the locations of the knots; O Supreme Goddess, [one should place them] in the center as well.
The letter *kṣa* should be joined as the eighth; the remaining letters are to be written in sequence.
However, in the eight root [syllables], they should be written starting from the fifth in order.
O Supreme Goddess, one should write the Mātṛkā-vṛtta on the exterior; O Maheśānī, within the square, one should write the Mātṛkā with the Kāma-bīja inserted within it.
Having drawn the yantra on a plate made of gold, silver, or other materials, one should worship it;
or [one may worship] upon the ground or on a sandalwood pedestal using saffron and red sandalwood.
Or else, with vermilion powder, musk, and saffron water.
O Goddess of the gods, having drawn the yantra, one should arrange the articles of worship.
In the Vārāhī Tantra.
Likewise, one should place a vessel of honey in front and a vessel of milk on the right;
then, one should set down two vessels filled with guggulu resin on the left and the right.
One should utter the word "Tripurā" followed by the syllable "ṅa"; then one should recite the word "vidmahe," and after saying "Bhairavyai," one should then say "dhīmahi."
One should utter "tanno devī" and then say "padaṃ coktā pracodayāt.
This Gāyatrī is known as Traipurī; one should extract it by means of the vowel *rā* and so forth.
"Ending with the fourth case" means [the word] *vāk*. One should purify the sacrificial materials with water from *kuśa* grass over which this has been recited;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the Goddess.
May she enter from the base of the body up to the aperture of Brahmā, becoming exceedingly subtle—
her pure hair adorned with flowers, possessing the playful beauty of wandering bees.
She was radiant with a pearl-streak adorned by a bee hovering at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
her forehead marked with a jewel-tilaka set upon that pearl-streak, and she was brilliant with a crown.
She is adorned with a crown featuring a crescent moon and enriched with pure pearls and gems;
she is graced by three eyes that possess the playful beauty of wandering bees.
Supreme, adorned with a crown of great jewels as radiant as the sun,
and beautified by ornaments of shimmering white pearls.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, and leaf-patterned ornaments, she surpasses the nectar of immortality with her shimmering luster;
she is resplendent in pure garments as white as the spray of the Ganges and camphor.
Her vine-like arms shine like creepers of white sandalwood;
she is radiant with the luster of jewels set in her glittering ornaments, such as the *kaṅkāla* and others.
Adorned with foot-lotuses shaped like coral sprouts,
she was embellished with anklets of pearls resembling a garland of stars.
O fair-faced one, with her left hand she does not hold a book with one [finger], but with the other she bestows boons upon the practitioners with the gesture of fearlessness.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, who bestows boons, holding a rosary and the gesture of granting boons (varada) respectively in her two right hands, the giver of universal prosperity and speech.
One should meditate upon Śivā as serene and white as a jasmine flower or the moon;
having thus visualized her and worshipped her with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual placement of the *argha* water.
Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), one should first worship the radiant Goddess Ravi;
then the twelve goddesses: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Ambikā, and Icchā, and so forth.
Jñānā, Kriyā, Kubjikā, Vibhī, Viṣaghnikā, Bhūcarī, and Ānandā— O Goddess, these are the twelve Śaktis.
O fair-faced one, the twelve [deities] beginning with the East should be worshipped all around;
having worshipped them, O Goddess of gods, one should worship the Pretasiṃhāsana in the center.

With this, one should worship in order, proceeding clockwise starting from the east, with the mantra "Oṃ vāmāyai namaḥ. Thereafter, one should worship the Pretasiṃhāsana (the lion-throne of the deceased),
which is the seed-syllable situated in the center of the wheel, the great abode of Sadāśiva.
The mantra for the preta-padmāsana ends in "ṅe" and concludes with "namaḥ"; it is proclaimed as "muru."

O Parameśvarī, the seed-syllable situated in the center of the wheel of Mahāśiva’s Kulārṇava is *hasauḥ*; with that, the mantra is: *hklauḥ sadāśiva-mahāpreta-padmāsanāya namaḥ*. Having thus invoked her into the center of the wheel, one should satisfy Kulasundarī.
By this [method], the invocation and so forth—
along with the invocation and other rites written down right there— are performed; likewise, one should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with ritual offerings (upacāras) and ornaments.
Having established [the deity] through this [channel], and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the vital breath (*jīva*) and so forth,
one should invite [the deity] and satisfy it with the water of the *argha* offering.
The meaning is that one should then worship with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet;
one should properly assign the six limbs to the body and thoroughly satisfy Śivā.
Afterwards, O Śivā, one should perform the worship of the retinue, and first, the protection of the limbs with this six-limbed mantra;
having worshipped the six limbs with this six-limbed mantra, one should perform the worship of the Guru. As it has been said:
"Immediately after the worship of the Guru, one should worship the Supreme Guru."
Likewise, one should worship one's own Guru within the space between the corner and the center of the Yoni.

By this [means], one should perform the worship consisting of the Guru within the space between the central and side-yonis; then, one should display the special mudrā. Just as that which is called the "yoni," when projected into the heart, becomes the agitator of the three worlds, so too, O Supreme Goddess, that which is situated in the mouth is named the "melter" of the three worlds.
O Great Goddess, when stationed between the eyebrows, she becomes the attractor of the three worlds.
O Great Goddess, she who resides in the forehead is the subduer of the three worlds;
she herself, when situated in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), is considered the bringer of joy to all.
The Goddess, consisting of the five mudrās, should display the yoni-mudrā;
thereafter, O Adrijā, the six-limbed enclosure [should be placed] all around the seat.
One should worship [the deities] in the southeast, northeast, northwest, and in the center, as well as in the cardinal directions around the pedestal—

that is, all around the pedestal. Likewise, one should worship Rati in the front corner (southeast), Priti in the rear corner (northwest), Manobhavā in the right corner (southwest), and then worship the arrows in the left corner (northeast).
One should worship with these jewels in this sequence, saying "Namaḥ. Thus, the place for the worship of Bāṇa has been described in the Jñānārṇava.
O Goddess, one should worship two arrows in the north, two in the southern direction,
and one in front, worshipping the five arrows in this very sequence.
O Goddess, one should likewise worship the five objects of desire in order, beginning with the first;
O Mistress of the Gods, one should worship them in sequence within the eight wombs.

With this [mantra], one should worship in sequence: "Obeisance to Anaṅgakusumā in the [first] womb," and so forth; likewise, thereafter, one should worship Brāhmī and the others, according to the distinction of pairs and pairs, O fair-faced one, within the eight petals.
Likewise, O Śivā, [worship] Asitāṅga, Brāhmī, Ruṇṛuṇṛu, and Māheśvarī.
Caṇḍa and Kaumālikā, Krodhīśa and Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Unmatta and Vārāhī, Māhendrī and Kapālīn.
O Maheśānī, one should worship Bhīṣaṇa, Cāmuṇḍā, and Saṃhāra as the eighth;
one should fully worship these pairs along with Mahālakṣmī.
Then one should worship the seats (pīṭhas) in the sequence beginning from the west.
By this [method], one should worship on the eight petals in the sequence beginning from the west with: "Oṃ, salutation to Brāhmī together with Asitāṅga.
Then one should worship the seats.
Kāmarūpa, Malaya, and then Kolagiri;
Kulāntaka, Caivānta, and after that Jālandhara.
Uḍḍiyāna, Devakūṭa, and Pīṣṭanta, proceeding step by step;
these should be worshipped at the roots of the knots in sequence, beginning from the west.
There, at the bases of the knots, one should worship in order starting from the west with "Obeisance to Kāmarūpa" and so forth,
surrounding the trident within the four mandalas of the Mātṛkās, O Goddess;
the ten Bhairavas are to be worshipped, O Śivā, in sequence starting from the west.
And likewise the Vetāla Hetuka, Tripurāntaka in their midst,
Agnijihva, Kālānta, and immediately after Kapālin.
One should worship Ekapāda, Bhīmarūpa, Malaya, and Hāṭakeśvara;
with the mantra "Namaḥ to Hetuka" and so forth in sequence, one should worship within the circular maṇḍala surrounding the trident.
In the square [maṇḍala], one should duly honor the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Likewise,
having uttered the seed-syllable *kṣauṃ*, one should say "Salutation to Vaṭuka"; and having uttered the seed-syllable *yāṃ*, one should likewise say "Salutation to the Yoginīs."
Having uttered the seed-syllable *kṣāṃ*, one should say "homage to Kṣatrapāla";
likewise, having uttered the seed-syllable *gaṃ*, one should utter the name of Gaṇapati.
Those ending in *ṅ* [the locative case] are to be worshipped in sequence in the directions beginning with the west.

By this, the meaning is that the word "Gaṇapati" should be in the dative case (*caturthī*) ending in *ṅ* and ending in *namaḥ*. Likewise, O Supreme Goddess, they are to be worshipped in the intermediate directions of the square in sequence starting from the northwest (*vāyavya*), as will be described, O Maheśvarī.
O Śivā, O beautiful lady, one should worship the Vasus, the twelve Ādityas, and the Rudras, as well as all the elemental beings (bhūtas), in due order.

By this [method], one should perform worship with the plural form in the dative case in the corners starting from the northwest; having thus performed the worship, one should fully honor the Goddess of the Gods with the ritual offerings (*upacāras*). Thus it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
One should properly diffuse the incense while recollecting the root mantra in one's heart:
"This excellent fragrance, rich in scent, is produced from the sap of the lord of plants."
May this incense, which is to be smelled by all the gods, be accepted;
it is brilliantly luminous, of great splendor, and dispels darkness everywhere.
"Let this lamp, which is light both external and internal, be accepted;
likewise, O Supreme Goddess, this lamp-mantra exists."
One should perform the Ārātrika rite, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires;
one should draw a beautiful eight-petaled lotus with saffron.
Having fashioned a beautiful form of the moon, one should place a single lamp upon the auspicious mole in its center,
and lamps upon the eight petals.
O Maheśānī, having consecrated it with the mantra of Ratneśvarī thereafter,
O Parameśvarī, one should then write the Śrī-bīja and the Parā-bīja.
O Śivā, following the [syllables] *ga* and *sau*, which possess the power of accumulation (*caya*), there are then the syllables situated in Indra (*i*) in sequence;
these are joined with the left ear (*vāmakarṇa*) and adorned with *nāda* and *bindu*.
O beautiful one, these five seed-syllables are the five jewels;
when the first seed-syllable is reversed, it becomes the nine-syllabled Ratneśī mantra beginning with *yaṃ*.

The seed-syllable of Śrī is *śrīṃ*, *parā* is *hrīṃ*, Indra is the letter *la*, and the left ear is the vowel *ū*. With the preceding seed-syllables *śrīṃ* and *hrīṃ* in their essential form, one consecrates [the offering] with this mantra: *śrīṃ hrīṃ glūṃ mlūṃ plūṃ vlūṃ llūṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*.
Having thus worshipped it with the root mantra, one then performs the *ārātrika* ceremony.
One should perform the waving of lights (*nīrājana*). Then, O Great Goddess, having lifted the vessel again and again up to the top of the head nine times, one should then perform the *nīrājana*.
O Sovereign of all the wheels, O Goddess whose form consists of nine petals,
accept this divine *ārātrika*, O Supreme Goddess!
O Goddess, in the Nīrājana rite, Manu is manifested at the end of the Vidyā.

With this, having offered the nightly oblation with the mantra beginning "samasta-cakra" at the end of the root mantra, one should perform the Cakramudrā: [placing] the little finger of the right hand inside the thumb of the left hand.
O Goddess, one should cast the little finger, the fetus, the left bean, and the [other] six according to their respective conjunctions;
this is declared to be the Cakra-mudrā.
Having performed the ārātrika rite, one should present the food offering (naivedya).
O Supreme Goddess, accept this drop of exquisitely prepared supreme food contained in a golden vessel, endowed with the five types of grains and the six flavors.
O Supreme Goddess, at the conclusion of the Vidyā, the mantra for the food offering (naivedya) has been proclaimed;
having then sprinkled [the offering], one should perform the worship of the God.

The meaning is that one should offer the *bali* immediately after the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Likewise, O Goddess of Gods, one should perform five oblations (*āhuti*) in succession with the root mantra:
for the vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
One should know this to be the essential nature of the five oblations.

Six oblations are offered in the six limbs; this is declared to be the daily fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*). Having offered five oblations in sequence with this root mantra, beginning with "To Prāṇa, svāhā," and so forth—

One should offer oblations for the six limbs with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*). Then, having recited [the mantra] as much as possible and offered the recitation with the verse beginning "The secret, most secret... (*guhyātiguhyeti*), one should take the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) with the *saṃhāramudrā* and consume it according to the prescribed manner. Thus.
Having performed the ritual for the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), one should carry out the ritual for the offering of oblations (balidāna).
In the corners beginning with the northeast, there should be a set of four mandalas.
O Goddess, fearless, one should draw the Śrīcakra, which is a triangle within the void;
or else, one should draw a single mandala on the left side.

The meaning is this: having prepared either four mandalas or one, one should draw a triangle around the Śrīcakra; likewise, O Daughter of the Mountain, one should worship Vaṭuka and the others with the previously mentioned mantras.

Having worshipped with the previous mantra, "kṣauṃ vaṭukāya namaḥ," and so forth, one should offer the *bali* offering with the following mantra: "Come, come, O son of the Goddess! O Lord Vaṭuka! O you with tawny matted locks! O you radiant with a mass of matted hair! O three-eyed one!"
And Jvālāmukha, at the very end, destroy, destroy all obstacles!
The mantra of Vaṭuka is proclaimed as follows: preceded by the word "Hṛh" and the two words "Baliṃ gṛhṇa," followed by the wife of Vahni (Svāhā). It is accompanied by all ritual offerings.

The mantra is: *Vahnijāyā* (the wife of fire) is *svāhā*. With that [mantra]: "Come, come, O Goddess! O Son Vaṭukanātha! O you whose body is radiant with tawny matted locks! O you whose eyes are the face of knowledge! Destroy, destroy all obstacles!
Accept, accept the offering (*bali*) together with all ritual services, svāhā! Thus: *Yāṃ yoginībhyaḥ namaḥ*.
May the goddesses, who have set foot upon the fields (*kṣetra*), seats (*pīṭha*), and secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), and who are not pleased by mere flowers, incense, and the like,

but are always gratified by us through the rite of the auspicious *bali* offering— may those goddesses, who are worthy of worship by the Lord of Gods, protect us. At the end of this [mantra], O Great Goddess, is the seed-syllable *yām*, followed by *yoginī*.
After "svāhā" and at the end of all the castes (varṇas), one should write the word "yoginī."
Having drawn the armor (kavaca) and the weapon (astra), one should again write the wife of fire (svāhā).
O Goddess, with this mantra, one should offer the oblation (bali) to the Yoginīs.

One should offer the *yoginī* bali with the mantra: *kavacaṃ hūṃ astram phaṭ vahnijāyā svāhā*, [followed by] *tena yāṃ yoginībhyaḥ svāhā yoginī hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Likewise, one should again write the letter *kṣa* conjoined with the six long vowels; then again, the word *kṣatra*, *pāla*, and incense, lamps, and so forth.
One should write it together with the *vali*. Having written it, one should then say: "Gṛhṇa gṛhṇa" (Seize, seize!).
O beautiful one, this mantra of Kṣetrapāla is endowed with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*). With that—namely, "Kṣāṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ"—one should worship him, [and then recite] "Kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣuṃ..."

One should offer the bali-oblation with the mantra "svāhā. Likewise, having written "gūṃ" three times, one should utter "Gaṇapati" ending in the letter ṅa (i.e., Gaṇapataye). After the word "vara," one should add "varada," and after "sarva," one should write "jana."
Having been told, "Do not come," she took the offering in two ways, O supreme one.
One should offer the oblation (bali) to Gaṇapa with the mantra beginning with "Vahni...";
the oblation to Vaṭuka should be made with the left thumb and ring finger.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Gaṇapati with the mantra: "gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ, O Gaṇapati, grant your favor; bring all things to me in peace;
accept, accept the bali—svāhā!"
71a) Now, the *valimudrā*.

That same gesture, when joined with the right thumb, is called the Vaṭuka-mudrā for the Yoginīs. Likewise: "One should join the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger in the shape of a vulva; first, having formed a left fist, make the index finger strong."
O Goddess, with this mudrā one should offer the bali-oblation to Kṣatrapāla;
likewise, place the fingers in the fists so that they stand like staffs.
The elephant-tusk *mahāmudrā* shall be the offering for Gaṇapati;
beyond this, it should be investigated in other tantras.
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*), it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and offer oblations (homa) equal to a tenth part of that number, O Śivā. This is sufficient; further elaboration is unnecessary. The sense is that wherever a higher number is heard [in the scriptures], there the fruit is greater.
Now, the mantras of Bhairavī. Since the mantra of Bhairavī is also composed of the [mantra of] Bālā, she is presented before Bālā. Thus it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
O Great Goddess, tell me how that supreme Tripurā is seated upon five lion-thrones, and how the lion-throne comes to be.
Śiva and Candra situated in Vahni, followed by Vāgbhava;
likewise, O Goddess, Kāmabīja, then Śiva and Candra joined together.
The seed-syllable of the Earth (La), enriched by Fire (Ra)—listen to this third [syllable], O Beloved!
O Supreme Goddess, it is that of the Virgin (Kumārī), excluding the emission of the Bindu.
O Śivā, the goddess Tripurā Bhairavī is the bestower of great liberation.
The syllable *ha* is Śiva, the syllable *sa* is the Moon, and the syllable *ra* is Fire; thus, the Vāgbhava seed-syllable is *aiṃ*. The Kāma-bīja is *klīṃ*.
The meaning is that the syllables *ha* and *sa* are conjoined with Śiva and the Moon. Situated in the middle of those is the seed-syllable of Earth (*la*).

The letter *la* is fire (*vahni*), and the letter *ra* is its fuel (*tadāḍhya*); joined with that, it attains the status of an independent syllable. Thus, *hasakalara īṃ* is established. Having written the third seed-syllable of power (*śakti-bīja*) belonging to the Virgin (*kumārī*), one should omit the visarga and make it possess the bindu; what kind [of syllable]? It is endowed with Śiva and the Moon (*śivacandrānvita*). Having thus performed the six limbs (*anuṣaḍga*), [the mantra is complete].
They extract the third seed-syllable as *hasauṃ*. As for the question, "How is there the abandonment of the *visarga* in that third seed-syllable of Bhairavī, which bestows prosperity?
[the answer is: O beautiful goddess, having removed the *bindu*, one should then place the *visarga*.

If it is argued that in this [verse] the abandonment of the *bindu* alone is heard, we say no; for here the interpretation is justified by a fixed syntactic connection (*vyavasthitānvaya*) according to which one should "discard the *sarga* and insert the *bindu*. That is not so, because it would result in the occurrence of four seed-syllables at the end, the presence of a disjointed connection (*anusaṃgāvattir vyavahitānvayāvatti*), and the third [syllable] of the Virgin (*kumāryāstārtīyaṃ sauḥ*). In that regard:

In this case, due to the connection with *śivacandra*, there is the occurrence of four syllables including *sa* and *sau*; furthermore, two other obstacles are evident: the statement regarding the sublation of the *visarga* and its existence.
The mind is in the *sāvadhānī*. Or, as in the illustration of the crescent moon of creation (*sargendukhaṇḍa*), O Goddess, we [state] that the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) is likewise;

here, just as the *vāgbhava* of the Virgin (Kumārī) resides in Śiva-Candra, so too does the seed-syllable of desire of the Virgin reside in Śiva-Candra. However, this is the distinction: the earth-seed-syllable (*pṛthvībīja*) resides within the seed-syllable of desire.

Then, having placed the third [syllable] of Kumārī, which is enriched with fire (va) and conjoined with Śiva and the Moon (sa), one should extract it; whether omitting the *sarga* (visarga) of the lunar [syllable], or else omitting the non-*sarga* lunar [syllable]—having abandoned the lunar [syllable], that is, the letter *sa* belonging to the Moon (*indu*)—it is the *sasarga* residing within the seed-syllable of Śakti: *asa*.
The meaning is that one should extract [the mantra] after discarding what is enclosed by "Śivacandra" and so forth.

(72a) Now, if it is asked: "In the phrase 'having discarded the creation' (*sasargaṃ hitvā*), why should the creation (*sarga*) not also be subject to abandonment in some cases?"—it is because [the context refers to] only one [instance].
Because in the Tantra, there would otherwise result a division of the mantra; therefore, it is only the abandonment of the letter *sa*—whether situated before the vowel or after it—that occurs.

For this very reason, the final seed-syllable (*bīja*) consists of three letters. Consequently, there is no grammatical attachment (*anuṣaṅga*), and the connection is fixed once the nasal dot (*bindu*) is omitted. Thus, in the instruction "one should then project the emission (*visarga*)," it is indeed the *visarga* alone [that is intended].

Because it is the nature of a gift (*prāpānika*). For this very reason, in the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*), specifically in the extraction of the second seed-syllable, it is said: "It is the bestower of prosperity for Bhairavī; that indeed is the *Kāmarāja*, and it is the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva.
Therefore, within the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva, there exists the state of the *visarga* (emission) and its form as three phonemes. For this same reason, it is the remover of curses (*śāpoddhāra*).

It is stated in the *Sārasamuccaya*: "By whom this Vidyā was previously cursed by the Goddess as being illusory (*māyā*), by him it has been rendered lifeless. This Vidyā is the original source; it has been described by me and must be understood in every way by those who desire spiritual perfection (*siddhi*). Therefore, even from childhood, the seed of Śiva and Śakti has been deposited by Śambhu."

Above those two former seeds, there is Akula above Parā; in the middle is Dahana, O Mādhava. From that point on, it became worshipped. The seed-syllable of Śiva-Śakti is in the form of *hasa* above the two former seeds;
beyond that is Parā, the letter *sa*; above that is Akula, the letter *ha*; in the middle is Kāmarāja; and below is Dahana, the letter *ra*.
By this, the entire family of Manu is indicated.
Likewise,
O Śivā, I shall describe her meditation, which bestows great prosperity:
she has the brilliance of a thousand suns of copper-red hue, and her matted locks flash like the autumnal moon.
Her eyes gleaming with the jewels of her crown, in which pearls were reflected;
adorned with a garland of severed heads dripping with the mud of blood.
She is rich with the longing of her three eyes, considered to have a face like the full moon,
and possesses high, firm breasts like fish adorned by a shining garland of pearls.
Clad in red garments, her form intoxicated with youth,
she holds a book in both left hands and a rosary in her right.

O you of excellent vows, one should first perform the placement of mantras (nyāsa), worship, and other rites for the maiden herself, while constantly recollecting her who is intent on granting boons and possesses great splendor.
Likewise, the first seed-syllable is Vāgbhava, endowed with Jīva and Prāṇa;
the second seed-syllable extracted is Sakalā Bhuvaneśānī.

O Maheśānī, the Vidyā that deludes the three worlds consists of the syllable *jī* (the individual soul), followed by *pra* (vital breath), situated in *va* (fire), adorned with the vowel *i* (Indra), and enriched with the *visarga*.
Consciousness is the name Bhairavī; it is the awareness within the unmoving Śiva.

The letter *sa* is the individual soul (*jīva*), the letter *ha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the letter *ai* is the Vāgbhava-bīja. Together with that, *aiṃ* is the Mistress of the World (*Bhuvaneśānī*) who abides in all the letters and is complete. *Hrīṃ*—therefore, *sakalahrīṃ* [is the mantra] consisting of the individual soul, the vital breath, and fire.
The letter *au* is known as having the sound of Śakra; therefore, *hasara auḥ*.
Now, meditation.
She possesses the radiant form of the rising sun, adorned with various ornaments,
and is endowed with a crown shining with the moon and [other] celestial beings.
She eternally holds a noose and a goad, carries a skull-cup in her left hand,
is enriched with the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and possesses full, elevated, and firm breasts.
Having meditated thus, O Śivā, one should worship the Goddess seated upon the lion-throne;
then, performing a double repetition, one should assign the six limbs according to the characteristics of all the limbs.
O fair-faced one, I shall now describe the yantra of this goddess, which fascinates the three worlds:
it consists of a triangle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and a corpse.
One should draw the mandala as four-cornered with four gates;
there, one should worship the Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, on the outside as before.
One should worship the goddess Rati and the others, as well as the deity, as before.
O lady of beautiful countenance, O daughter of the mountain, Kāma dwells in front of the god to the left, while Candra is in the southern corner; worship the other [deities] as before.
One should worship Ḍākinī, Śākinī, Kākinī, Lākinī, Rākiṇī, and Hākinī, starting from the west and proceeding in order.
The *sārasa* and *śukamegha* [melodies] are likewise dependent on others;
furthermore, the *apāṅga*, *bhrūvilāsa*, and *bhārahāra* [melodies] are as before.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, she who is seated upon the eastern lion-throne has been described. Likewise, the two seed-syllables (bījas) of this very Vidyā have been proclaimed;
at the end of those, O Supreme Goddess, [are the words]: "O Ever-Moist One, O You whose essence is the flow of intoxication."
The third [syllable] of this very [mantra] belongs to Rudra, O Supreme Goddess.

The meaning is that after the two seed-syllables of this Bhairavī of Consciousness, one should write "nityaklinne madadrave" and then extract the final seed-syllable. For this very reason, it has been said:
O Goddess, in the case of meditation, worship, and so forth, they are indeed consciousness as before;
however, O sinless one, there is a distinction regarding the triangle, which I shall now explain.
In the order of the front corners, Nityakinnā, who is dripping with the flow of intoxication,
having been released from the eastern lion-throne, [the text] speaks of the southern lion-throne in the Jñānārṇava.

O Śivā, the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] consists of Śiva (S) and Candra (M) situated on Mādana (R), followed by the letter Vānta (H) joined with Vahni (R), pierced by Śakti (I), and enriched by Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā.
The seed-syllable of Kāmarāja is indeed that of Sampatpradā Bhairavī,
while Sadāśiva is the seed-syllable of Mahāsiṃhāsana.
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, on this lion-throne to the right:
*śiva* (ha) and *candra* (sa) form the syllable *ha*; *mādana* (ka) is the letter *ka*; *vānta* (la) is the letter *la*; *vahni* (ra) is the letter *ra*; and *śakti* (e) is the letter *e*.
Thus, by *hasakala aiṃ*, the remaining two [syllables] belong to the Bestower of Prosperity (*sampatpradā*).
She possesses the brilliance of a thousand rising suns, has the moon as her crest-jewel, and is three-eyed;
she is beautiful with various ornaments and is the destroyer of all enemies.
She wears a garland of severed heads dripping with blood and is clothed in red garments.
Having meditated thus, O Great Goddess, one should touch the worship-maṇḍala:
a triangle, O Goddess, a hexagon, a circle, and an eight-petaled lotus.
O wide-eyed one, this triple-city machine consists of the circle of the earth,
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Kālī.
One should worship Kalāḍhyā, Valāḍhyā, and likewise Vikaraṇī;
one should then attain the state of Sarvabhūtapramathanī.
Likewise, having worshipped Damanī accompanied by the word *manonmanī*,
one should utter Bhuvaneśvarī in the *aghora*, *vāgbhava*, and *ghora* [syllables].
One should perform protection for the Rākṣasas in places that are indeed most terrible.
O Śivā, one should write this Vidyā, joined with the seed-syllable of the Goddess who is the Mistress of All, consisting of thirty-three syllables. It has been declared thus.
O Goddess, with this mantra one should then worship the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*).

Having worshipped all [the goddesses] beginning with Vāmā and ending with Manonmanadamanī by means of this [same] mantra, one should worship the lion-throne with this mantra. O Goddess, the seed-syllable is *hrīṃ*; by that [is worshipped] Aghorā in the Vāgbhava [kūṭa].

"O Bhuvaneśvarī, most terrible of the terrible, protect us, protect us from all sides, O Sovereign of all! Hrīṃ! Thus, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the guardians of the earth, the directions, and the worlds, together with their weapons, and the Supreme Goddess upon the second throne.
Having left the southern lion-throne, they ascended the western lion-throne.
In the Jñānārṇava.
O Goddess of the Gods, having extracted the seed-syllables of Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī,
and Kākinī from the pair [of syllables], one should join them with the moon and the sun.
The first [syllable] is joined with the syllable Aiṃ, while the other is adorned with the syllable Iṃ.
O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, one should write the third seed-syllable endowed with the sound of Śakra,
pervaded by the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā.
O Great Goddess, this vidyā resides on the western seat.
Ḍākinī is the syllable *ḍa*, Rākinī is *ra*, Lākinī is *la*, and Kākinī is *ka*.
Having formed these seed-syllables (*bīja*) above the moon and sun—that is, above the syllables *sa* and *ha*—one should extract them in the form of the three peaks (*kūṭatraya*).

Therein, the first is the syllable *aiṃ* joined with *ḍa-ra-la-ka-sa-ha*, thus: *aiṃ ḍaralakasaha*. Another is adorned with the syllable *īṃ*, thus: *īṃ ḍaralakasaha*, conjoined with the vowels of Indra (*śakra*). O Goddess, the third is the vowel *au* (the syllable of Indra), conjoined with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth, thus: *auḥ ḍaralakasaha*. The third [mantra] is "born of the mountain" (*śailasaṃbhava*), as it is not explicitly stated otherwise.
Since two *bindus* have fallen from the two previous seeds, the third seed here is also seen to possess the *visarga*; as it has been said:
"The other pair is endowed with *bindu* and *nāda*, while the last one possesses the *visarga*. And thus is the visualization.
O Goddess, she possesses the luster of an *indragopa* insect, resembling the color of hibiscus and saffron;
she is beautiful with a garland of severed heads, possessing a radiance like that of the rising sun.
Her breasts are full and elevated, shaped like golden jars;
she holds a noose, a goad, a book, and likewise a rosary.
Having meditated thus, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the Goddess with mental offerings,
having performed the six-limbed ritual by repeating [the mantra] twice.
O lady of excellent hips, one should draw her yantra as a triangle with its interior hollowed out;
outside that, one should then draw an eight-petaled lotus and subsequently a twelve-petaled one.
One should draw a mandala that is square and has four gates;
one should worship Bhairavī daily according to the procedure previously described.
The six syllables of this very vidyā are situated in their proper sequence.
"O mature woman, speak [the letters] in reverse; this is the vidyā that bestows both enjoyment and liberation.

The meaning is that one should extract the letters of this vidyā by making those beginning with the letter *ḍa* and ending with *ny* begin instead with *ha* and end with *ḍa*. Thus, the extraction proceeds in the sequence: *hasakalare ḍa aiṃ*, and so forth.
The eternal goddess Śrī Bhairavī is the remover of enemies and the destroyer of misfortune;
one should perform all rites, such as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship, as previously described.
Leaving aside the western lion-throne, he speaks of the northern lion-throne in the Jñānārṇava:
O beloved Sureśvarī, the first is the Vāgbhava [syllable] preceded by *ha*;
the second seed-syllable extracted is the Bhū-bīja, which is Bhuvaneśānī.
O Maheśānī, Śiva and Candra, Bhuvaneśī and Bhairavī;

Vāgbhava is the syllable *aiṃ*; *ha* and *sa* [form] *hasau*. Therefore, *hasa aiṃ*. At the end of *hasaka*, that is, at the end of the letter *hasaka*, is the seed-syllable of the Earth (*bhūbīja*), the letter *la*; [then] Bhuvaneśānī is *krīṃ*. By that [is formed the mantra].

*Hasakala hrīṃ śivacandrau hakāra-sakārau, aukāra-visargau*. By that [is meant] *hasa auḥ*. Now, if it is asked how the vowel *au* and the *visarga* are obtained here, [the answer is] from another tantra: "from *surasāt*."

As it is stated in the Vārāhītantra: "The three *haṃsa*s, joined with the letters *ha*, *sa*, and *ka*, and divided by the vowels of the first half of the row; in the middle, joined with Viriñci, Indra, Hara, and Agni; the first two [are] followed by *du* and the *visarga*—thus the *haṃsa* is the letter *ha*. Those three, joined with the letter *sa*..."
The letter *ka* is neuter because it is not counted among the names; the letter *i* is its half; the letter *au* is the *paṅkti* vowel;
*viriñci* is the letter *ka*; *indra* is the letter *la*; *hara* is the letter *ha*; and *agni* is the letter *ra*—this is obtained through a single syntactical connection.

Thus it has been stated by Devanātha and others that "Bhuvaneśī" is an epithet for Bhairavī; however, in reality, because there are different mantras according to the differences in the tantras, a single unified syntactical structure (*aikavākyatā*) is not logically consistent.
In the Jñānārṇava.
Because there is no indicator for the sequence of vowels (*paṅktisvara*), it is as follows: Śiva (H), Candra (S), and Bhuvaneśī (HRĪM) are the qualifiers;

since the term *bhuvaneśī* is required by the sense of the passage (*arthāpatti*), the final seed-syllable is *hasahrīṃ*. Likewise, O Goddess, with the middle seed-syllable, one should distinguish it by means of the six long vowels.
Having duly applied the six limbs [of the ritual], one should meditate upon the four-armed Goddess,
who resembles the hibiscus flower and saffron, and is like the blossom of the pomegranate tree.
She has a crescent moon in her matted locks, three eyes, and a red garment;
she is auspiciously adorned with various ornaments and possesses full, elevated, and firm breasts.
O Auspicious One, one should meditate upon the auspicious Goddess as holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
having thus meditated, one should worship the Goddess and perform the extraction of the yantra as before.
O Supreme Goddess, O Bhairavī Devī, who possesses consciousness like a mantra;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should worship Rati and the others within the triangle.
O beautiful one, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are to be worshipped right there;
by that, this vidyā is attained, and he shall become a king of wealth.
Likewise, one should utter Tāram (Om), Bhuvaneśānī, the Śrībīja (Śrīm), and Kāmarājaka; then, at the end of "Hṛt," one should speak the syllables of "Bhagavati" followed by the word "Māheśvari."
The twenty-syllable mantra beginning with "annapūrṇe" and ending with "agnijāyā" should be known;
there is no vidyā on earth equal to this which bestows such accomplishment.
Therefore, [the mantra is]: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ bhagavati māheśvari maheśvari annapūrṇe namaḥ svāhā*. Likewise, 75b).
O Bhuvaneśvarī, another distinction of Bhairavī is now being stated:
O Goddess of gods, she herself is then Sahādyā, and she is the Mistress of the Sakala.

O Pārvatī, all [practices] such as meditation and worship belong to her alone; she is the bestower of all prosperity. If she is present in the hand, she becomes the Mistress of the Hand (Hastakarī). "Bhuvaneśvarī" is an invocation. For this very reason, it is stated in the Svarasamuccaya: "The Bhairavī who is joyful, the Kula-pūrvā, [is taught] by the teachers."
If it were Kula, that very [Kula] would be the one that grants swift fruit. Akula is the letter *ha*, and Kula is the letter *sa*.
Likewise, O Pārvatī, she who begins with *ha* and *sa* is Bhairavī.
This is the beginning and end of this very Vidyā; such is she.

O Supreme Mistress, she is named Sakalasiddhidā (Bestower of All Siddhis) and is like Bhairavī, the Bestower of Prosperity, through meditation and worship. Regarding her three seed-syllables (*bījas*), when the first seed-syllable is at the beginning and the end, or when the Vāgbhava syllable is devoid of the letter *ra* at the end, she is known as Sakalasiddhidā. [This occurs] in the first *kūṭa* of the Bhairavī mantra.
Because of the presence of the letter *ra*.
Now, in the *Sāradātilaka*:

Having received initiation and mastered the mantra, one who has conquered the senses should offer flowers born from the Brahma-tree into the fire for a hundred thousand times, as many as the thousands of suns.
The *Prapañcasāra* states that there are twelve *tattvas*, or even half a *lakṣa* of *tattvas*.

Following that, one should perform a *homa* with *taruja* (wood-derived) materials smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), and on the day of Śiva, one should offer oblations; likewise, in this path, for the sake of attaining the imperishable state, one should perform [the rite] nine *lakṣas* of times.

76a) Regarding the phrase "then one should characterize," various types [of definitions] are heard in various scriptural statements. Among those, there is the statement by Devanātha that "the reality (*tattva*) is the characteristic. That is not so, because statements that establish [reality] as either deficient or excessive would be meaningless.
Regarding the word *patera*: we, however, maintain that the *puraścaraṇa* is indeed one hundred thousand recitations as stated in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*.
Statements that provide a higher number are for the sake of greater fruit; for this very reason, there is the attainment of the "imperishable state" (*akṣayapada*) and so forth.
This is because, as the venerable Bhairavī says, "it is so," and thus the same rule applies everywhere—this is the intended meaning.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Mantras of Bhairavī and Tripurabālikā," within the *Gamasāranirṇaya* composed by Śrī Ramāramaṇa Devaśarman.
In this context, although it is stated that the exposition of the *siddhividya* follows immediately after the exposition of the *mahāvidyā*.

Nevertheless, since the various Vidyās are interwoven with the practices of both [Kaula and Śākta] traditions, it is appropriate to describe them within the context of both. Therefore, first the mantras of Bhuvaneśvarī are written here according to the *Sāradā-tilaka*, as follows:
Now I shall describe Madhu-bhuvaneśvarī, the sustainer of the world,
by knowing whom even Brahmā and the other gods attained exalted prosperity.
Nakulīśa is mounted upon fire and possesses the left eye and the half-moon.
Nakulīśa is the syllable *ha*; fire is the syllable *ra*; the left eye is the long vowel *ī*. Thus, [the seed-syllable is] *hrīṃ*. Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*).
One should worship Bhuvaneśī, who wears a crown with the radiance of the rising moon, whose breasts are lofty, who is endowed with three eyes, whose face is smiling,
and who holds in her hands the gestures of granting boons, the goad, the noose, and the protection mudrā.
One should perform the six limbs in sequence using the seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels:
*hrāṃ* for the heart, *namaḥ*, and so forth in order. Likewise, one should perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
Then the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra thirty-two hundred thousand times according to the prescribed measure.
In this case as well, there is a curse.

As is seen in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "In former times, this Mahāvidyā Bhuvaneśī was propitiated by the King of the Gods; and this Vidyā, though nameless and devoid of seed-syllables (*bīja*), was extracted in the past by means of the *Vāgbhava* [syllable]," and so forth. For this very reason:
The meaning is that there is no curse regarding the Vāgbhava and the others. Likewise,
the practitioner of mantra should extract the mantra consisting of the three seeds— Vāgbhava, Śambhu-vanitā, and Ramā— which is the means for accomplishing the fruits of the three aims of life.
Vāgbhava is the syllable *aiṃ*; Śambhuvanitā is *hrīṃ*; and Ramā is *śrīṃ*. Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*).
I meditate upon her who has a body crimson as vermilion, three eyes, and a crown-jewel shimmering like a star; she rests upon the serpent Śeṣa, her face is smiling, and her breasts are full;
she is gentle, holding in her two hands a wine-cup filled with jewels and a red lotus.
One should meditate upon the supreme Mother, whose feet rest upon a pedestal of peacock feathers.
The preliminary rite.

The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; he should then perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with ten parts of milk-rice soaked in honey, while remaining composed and worshipping upon the ritual seat (pīṭha).

Likewise, this three-syllabled vidyā becomes encapsulated by the seed-syllable of speech (vāgbīja) according to my [tradition]. The seed-syllable of speech is the syllable *saiṃ*; the meaning is that the *māyā*-seed-syllable is thus encapsulated by it.

Māyā Hrīṃ: [I bow to] the eternal Śyāmāṅgī, who bears on her head a crescent moon, and who holds in her own hands the knowledge-gesture, a red lotus, a jewel-adorned vessel, and the supreme protection from fear.
I salute the consort of Hara, worshipped by the gods, who rests upon a red lotus, whose three eyes are radiant, and who bows with breasts shimmering with pearls.
One should fashion it with the middle [finger] joined to the long [finger], using the cavity of the mouth.
"AIṂ HRĀṂ AIṂ, obeisance to the heart"—thus in sequence. Now, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and then perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number.
Likewise, [the mantra consists of] Ananta joined with the Bindu, Māyā, Brahmā, Agni, and Tāra.

The three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa* (the noose) bestows the fruit of universal subjugation. *Ananta* is the letter *ā*; *māyā* is *hrīṃ*; *brahmā* is the letter *ka*; *agnī* is the letter *ra*; and *tāra* is the syllable *oṃ*. Thus, it becomes *krāṃ*. Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*).

I worship that primordial Bhuvaneśvarī, who holds a goad, a hook, a noose, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands; who is seated upon a lotus throne; and who possesses three eyes, resembling ten million rising suns.

Now, if it is argued that by the words "then Ananta joined with Bindu" and so forth, there is a mantra consisting of three syllables, and that if this very [mantra] begins with Pāśa, it ought to become four syllables—[we reply: here the word *ādi* (beginning/first) has the sense of a constituent part (*avayava*). Therefore, the mantra beginning with Pāśa—which consists of Ananta, Bindu, Brahmā, Agni, and Tāra—is the first constituent part of the three-syllabled [mantra].
The meaning is "noose."
Likewise is the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).

Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), having conquered the senses, and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkās upon his body according to the path of withdrawal and emanation, he should recite the mantra one million times.
Then one should perform the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) for the sake of attaining the state of the deity.

By that means, having performed the morning rites, the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), bathing, and so forth, as well as the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other preliminaries according to the sequence prescribed in the *Sundarī-mantra*, one should perform the *mātṛkā* [placement] in both direct and reverse order; thereafter, [one should perform the placement of] the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the rest.

Having performed the *kanyāsa* (the placement of the fingers), one should perform the *mantranyāsa* (the ritual placement of the mantra); for, according to the maxim that "since there is no specific mention [of a different rule], what is determined in one place [applies] everywhere," it follows that this is so.
Likewise, the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the mantra shall be Śakti, the meter (*chandas*) shall be Gāyatrī, and the deity (*devatā*) of the mantra shall be Manu.
The Goddess Bhuvaneśvarī was thus described by Svarasaṃha, the Lord of Gods.
Having thus assigned the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and *devatā* to the head, face, and heart, one should perform the mantra-assignment (*mantra-nyāsa*).
For example:
one should place *Hṛllekhā* on the head and *Gaganā* in the lotus of the heart.
One should perform protection with Karālikā at the secret place and with Mahāśuṣmā on the two feet.

With that [mantra], one should place [the seed-syllables] in sequence on the head, beginning with "Hṛllekhāyai namaḥ" and so forth. Likewise, one should place Brahmā together with Gāyatrī on the forehead;
one should place Viṣṇu together with Sāvitrī on the right temple.
One should place Maheśvara on the left cheek, conjoined with Vāgīśvarī;
furthermore, one should place Dhanapati, the Lord of Wealth, at the tip of the left ear.

Having placed [the seed-syllables] in the mouth, one should place Gaṇeśa on the back; one should place them all around, and deposit them in the two left ears, the two cheeks, and the space between the temples.
One should place a lotus in the mouth, and then one should place these [other syllables] upon the two outstretched arms,
at the base of the throat, on the pair of breasts, on the left shoulder, and in the lotus of the heart.
The preceptor [should place the seed-syllables] on the left side, on both sides, at the region of the navel,
on the forehead, on the sides of the abdomen, on the other side of the abdomen, and in the heart.
Then, one should install the [deities] beginning with Brāhmī, who possess the characteristics described according to the ritual rule;
having installed the pervasive [deity] Malena, the embodied one should meditate upon the Goddess.

By this [method], one should meditate on her in the form previously described; then, having performed mental service (mānasopacāra), worship, and the offering of the special arghya water, one should place the yantra before oneself.

Having performed the invocation (āvāhana) with the appropriate mudrās and so forth, one should offer the water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings—such is the traditional practice. As for the drawing of the yantra, it is as follows:
Outside, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with sixteen petals surrounding it;
in the center, one should write a most beautiful triangle within the pericarp.
Then one should worship the pedestal (pīṭha) endowed with the nine powers (nava-śakti):
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā;
Having prepared the seat enriched with the seed-syllables— Vidyā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, Maṅgalā, and the nine [others]— one should fashion the form by means of the root-mantra.
"Bījādya" means beginning with the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ). Likewise, one should worship the Goddess within that [maṇḍala], having invoked Her along with the attendants in sequence:
in the east, center, south, north, and west, according to the proper order.
Having worshipped Hṛllekhā and the others, who possess most wonderful radiance,
who hold a boon-granting gesture, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness, and who are adorned with immense ornaments;
One should worship the deities of the limbs in the previously mentioned locations;
and in the northeast corner, one should worship Gāyatrī together with Brahmā.
One should worship Sāvitrī together with Viṣṇu in the southeast corner,
and one should worship Sarasvatī together with Rudra in the northwest corner.
In the southeast corner, one should worship Mahālakṣmī;
and in the west, one should worship Rati, who is seated on the lap of Dhanada and embraced by Kāmadeva.
In the northeast, one should properly worship Vighnarāja together with his beloved;
thereafter, Digaṃvarī, who carries one across the ocean of worldly existence, should be worshipped.
The two treasures (Nidhis) are to be worshipped in the pericarp, and then on the two sides of the hexagon:
Anaṅgakusumā and likewise Anaṅgamadanā.
Then Anaṅgadhāriṇī, then Manaṅgā, then Madanāturā;
after that, the one named Bhuvanapālā, and then Gaganavegā.
Śaśirekhā, Galarekhā, and Pūjyatā—these are indeed the eight Śaktis;
then, upon the sixteen petals, [there are] Karālī and Vikalpyumā.
Sarasvatī, Śrī, Ṛddhi, Doṣā, Lakṣmī, Satyā, Smṛti,
Dhṛti, Śraddhā, Medhā, Mati, and Kānti are the sixteen primordial Śaktis.
Outside the lotus, the attendant Śaktis are to be worshipped:
first Anaṅgarūpā, then Anaṅgamadanā, and likewise [Anaṅgamadanāturā].
Then, afflicted by passion in this world, she is the impetuous protectress of the universe;
she is the one who cools all things, whose face is the bodiless god of love, and whose girdle is the bodiless god himself.
Holding in his lotus-like hands a water-pot, a palm-leaf fan, betel, a radiant umbrella,
auspicious chowries, and flowers.
Having thus worshipped the Goddess of the Gods, what may the practitioner not accomplish?

Having worshipped in the aforementioned places, having offered libations three times with the root mantra, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), and having worshipped according to one's means, one should recite the mantra, offer the recitation, and taking up the remains of the offering (nirmālya) with the *saṃhāra* mudrā—
Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Nirmālyavāsinī in the northeastern quarter," one should perform the dismissal; this is the summary.
Now, the Yantras of Lakṣmī [are described] in the Śāradātilaka.
Now I shall proclaim the mantras of Śrī, which bestow the fruits of prosperity and good fortune;
by whose mere sidelong glance even the three worlds are obtained.
The syllable *va* joined with fire (*ra*), conjoined with the moon of the left eye (*i*),
is declared to be the seed-syllable of Śrī, like another wish-fulfilling gem.
The letter *śa* is "vomited" (*vānta*); the fire (*vahni*) is *ra*, and the left eye (*vāmanetra*) is *i*. By that [is formed] *śrīṃ*.
Now, meditation.
Resembling molten gold in luster, with four arms resembling Mount Kailāsa, she bestows prosperity upon all by pouring from golden jars filled with nectar held aloft;
she bears the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her hands, and wears a crown blazing with light.
I bow to her who stands upon a lotus, her silken garment slipping from her rounded hips like a silken cloth.
One should perform the six limb-protections (aṅga) in sequence using the six long seed-syllables.
Having been initiated and having conquered the senses, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Likewise,
Vāgbhava, Vanitā, Viṣṇu, and Māyā-Makaraketana constitute a mantra consisting of four seed-syllables, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
One who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; at the end, one should also perform oblations.
Vāgbhava is the syllable *aiṃ*; Viṣṇu’s consort is *śrīṃ*; Māyā is *hrīṃ*; and Makaraketana is *klīṃ*.
Now, meditation.

May Hara grant the desired [boon] to his beloved, he who is perpetually being sprinkled by four lofty arms— white as snow— with water from jewel-filled jars held at their tips; and who, with the tips of his [other] hands, displays the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), along with a pair of lotuses, possessing a splendor like that of a ruby.
I salute the Parijata creeper, who has a lotus as her seat.
The seer is Bhṛgu, the meter is Nivṛt (or Nivṛt, according to another reading), and the deity is declared to be Śrī.
One should perform the six limbs in sequence by joining the six long vowels with the middle [syllable].
"Śrāṃ, salutation to the heart," and so forth in sequence.
Likewise, one should here properly worship the pedestal (pīṭha) endowed with the nine powers:
Vibhūti, Unnati, Kānti, Sṛṣṭi, Kīrti, and Sannati.
Vyutthiti, utkṛṣṭi, and ṛddhi are proclaimed as the nine powers;
having invoked the Goddess there together with her retinue, one should worship her.
Having offered a seat enriched with seed-syllables (bīja), one should fashion the form [of the deity] by means of the root-mantra (mūla).

Although the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth are not explicitly mentioned at the beginning of this tantra, they should nevertheless be inferred because they have been extracted from the general chapter (sāmānyapaṭala). Likewise, as before, one should perform the morning duties, bathing, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and the offering of water (argha).

Having performed the placement (*sthāpana*), purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the assignment of letters (*lipinyāsa*), and so forth, one should perform the special assignment (*viśeṣanyāsa*) and the preceding rites; however, everything is not written here for fear of excessive prolixity. This is because they are necessary. Likewise, having offered the mental oblation enriched with seed-syllables (*bīja*) and having visualized the form as described, one should give [the offering] and worship.
By the word "the Goddess," even without [explicit] ritual service (*upacāra*), the offering vessels (*pādyādi*) and so forth should be inferred as objects of worship.
By the phrase "having invoked" (*āvāhya*) and so on, the mudrās for invocation and the rest are to be connected. Thus, one should worship as before;
with the mantra, one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) as previously described. Likewise, one should worship Viśvandhana.

Then, regarding the directional bindings (*digbandhana*) upon the eight and fourteen petals— due to the eightfold number of the enclosures— he states the specific details as follows: Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
The god, who has the luster of gold, yellow, and the great blue sapphire,
is clad in yellow garments and likewise holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
Kamala, salita, rūpa, guggulu, and kuraṇḍaka. || 4 ||
Likewise, one should worship Śaṅkhanidhi and Devī according to the sequence starting from the right;
on the tips of the petals, one should worship Varākī and the others all around.
Valākīnī, Malā, Kamalā, and Na-mālikā; Vibhīṣikā, Mālikā, Śaṃkarī, and Sumālikā.
One should worship the Lokeshas, who possess the radiance of pearl necklaces and hold the two [attributes] upon lotuses;
outside of them, one should worship the weapons, beginning with the vajra.

Having worshipped in this manner with the root mantra, having worshipped three times with the *saṅketamudrā*, having performed *prāṇāyāma* and recited the mantra as much as possible, one should offer the recitation with the verse beginning "guhyātiguhyam" and so forth.
Then, taking up the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) with the *tulānalasaṃhāramudrā*, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*). This is the summary.
Thus, the supreme practitioner who constantly worships the Goddess according to the prescribed rite shall attain abundance of wealth and grain, and shall obtain irreproachable prosperity.
Standing in water up to the chest, the practitioner of mantra,
self-restrained, should recite this mantra three hundred thousand times while meditating on the Goddess within the solar disc.
That knower of mantras, having taken up residence at the very root of the temple of Viṣṇu, shall become a stable abode for Ramā in a short period of time.
The practitioner of mantra should recite it three hundred thousand times and will obtain the desired wealth;
by this very [number], the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of exactly three hundred thousand—this is the summary.
Now follows the mantra for the food-filled vessel, as stated in the Śāradātilaka:
One should utter "Māyā" (Hrīṃ), then "Bhagavati," followed by "Māheśvari";
then "Annapūrṇe" and "Vahnijāyā" (Svāhā). This mantra consists of seventeen syllables.
Māyā (Hrīṃ), Hṛn (Namaḥ), and Vahnijāyā (Svāhā).

Then, having performed the morning duties in the previously mentioned order—namely, the bath, the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), the general offering (*sāmānyārgha*), the ritual installation (*sthāpana*), the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the deposition of the alphabet (*mātṛkā-nyāsa*), and so forth—one should perform the deposition of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [limbs]. The seer is Brahmā, the meter is *triṣṭubh*, and the deity is Annapūrṇā; thus [one should assign them] to the head and the face.

One should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) using the root mantra of Hṛtsunda. As it has been said: "Having performed the assignments for the limbs with the root mantra, one should then meditate upon the Goddess—red in color, wearing variegated garments, with a crescent moon as her crest-jewel, and intent on the bestowing of food."
I worship the Blessed Lady, the destroyer of the suffering of worldly existence, who is bowed by her burden and who rejoices upon seeing the entire ocean dancing with that very burden.

Having meditated thus, having invoked [the deity] with the root mantra, and having worshipped her with water for the feet and other offerings, one should offer obeisance at the end of the root mantra with the words: "Obeisance to Annapūrṇā together with her retinue.
In the same way, having offered libations three times with the thought, "I satisfy Annapūrṇā together with her retinue," and having recited the mantra as much as one is able,

one should offer the recitation with the verse beginning "O most secret of secrets," and after praising and bowing, take up the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and dismiss [the deity]; this is the summary.
Likewise, regarding the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa): one should recite the mantra according to the rules eight thousand times. 16.
Immediately thereafter, one should offer oblations of food mixed with clarified butter;
subsequently, the practitioner of mantra should daily recite the mantra one hundred and eight times at dawn.
The abundance of food for this [mantra] shall be even greater than that of Śrī;
therefore, its preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) consists of sixteen thousand [recitations], such is the general rule.
Now, the hurried mantra is in the *Śāradā-tiraka*.
*Tāra*, *māyā*, *carma*, the seed-syllable *mṛd*, and *īśakhara* (the vowel *ī*) combined;
the Lord with teeth upon a tortoise, the letter *kṣa*, the feminine suffix, and a long garment.
The twelve-syllable mantra is: *saṃvarta* (the syllable *sa*), *bhagavān* (*bha*), *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), *phaṭ*, *ntā*.
*Tāra* is the syllable *oṃ*; *māyā* is *hrīṃ*; the seed of the skin (*carmabīja*) is *hūṃ*; *ṛddhi* is the letter *kha*; *īśasvara* is the vowel *e*; *kūrma* is the letter *ca*;
*danta* is the letter *cha*; *bhaga* is the vowel *e*; and *kṣa* is the form of *tī*.
The mantra is:

*oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ khecacchakṣastrī hūṃ kṣa hrīṃ phaṭ*. Then, according to the prescribed method, one should perform the preliminary rites (*pūrvakṛtya*), including bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), the offering of water (*argha*), and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
