Having performed the *prāṇāyāma*, the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, and so forth, one should perform the *ṛṣi-nyāsa* and other assignments (*nyāsa*). Thus, the sage is declared to be Arjuna, the meter is proclaimed to be Virāṭ,
and the deity is said to be Tvaritā, who bestows the fruits of the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*).

81a) Furthermore, having remembered that for this mantra the seer (ṛṣi) is Arjuna, the meter (chandas) is Virāṭ, the deity (devatā) is Tvaritā, and the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), Śiva, having placed [the mantra] upon his face and heart, should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (mantra-nyāsa).

Just as one who is free from illusion, the practitioner should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) by assigning the letters to the crown of the head, the forehead, the throat, the heart, the navel,
the secret place, the two thighs, the knees, the shanks, and the feet,
and thus encompass the entire body.

Having thus excluded the *māyā* seed-syllable from the root mantra, one should place it starting from the crown of the head; the meaning is that one should then perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the entire mantra. Likewise, [one should do so] with the seven syllables beginning with *kūrma*, excluding each preceding one in turn.
The most excellent practitioner should arrange the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of two [syllables] at a time.

Likewise, he should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) using the seven syllables beginning with *kū* and *kā*, omitting each preceding one; thus, for each pair, there are two movements.

The meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) after reciting [the mantras]. Thus, one should place them in sequence as follows: *ca-ccha* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *cha-kṣa* to the head, *svāhā*; *kṣaṃ-strī* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*, and so forth. Then, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the root mantra, one should meditate: [She is] dark-complexioned, adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, wearing a half-silk cloth (*ardhapaṭṭāṃśuka*).

"I worship the three-eyed Goddess, who wears a garland of *guñjā* berries shimmering upon her breast, who bears eight serpents, whose earrings, armlets, girdle, and anklets have been transformed into a multitude of *gaṇas*, and whose hands are raised in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. Having thus meditated and worshipped her with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*), one should perform the ritual installation of the special water-offering (*viśeṣārgha*).
Having drawn the pedestal (pīṭha) in front, one should worship it;
81b) just as one would write the syllable Māyā in the center of a lotus endowed with ten petals, containing within it the desired object of accomplishment (sādhya).
The *Tvaritā* yantra, which consists of the syllables beginning with *tā* situated upon ten petals, encircled by a hexagon and resting upon the earth-element (*vasudhā*),
neutralizes black magic, malice, and the like, removes the fear of wild beasts and thieves,
and especially bestows victory when worn.
With that [mantra], one should worship the pedestal—a six-cornered, ten-petalled lotus—using the pedestal mantra. The mantra is as follows:
*samvartaka* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*), followed by *sakalaṃ viyat*, then addressing [the deity] as "O you whose body is diamond" (*vajradeha*), and finally the two syllables *hiṅgulu*.
The pair "garja" should be separated by the moon (i), and the end of the armor (va) should be long with a bindu.
The heart-mantra for Pañcāmānā is proclaimed as the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra).
One should offer the seat with this [mantra] and fashion the image (mūrti) with the root-mantra.

*Saṃvarta* is the letter *kṣa*; *kavaca* is *hūṃ*. *Vi* is the letter *ha*. What has come into being? Everything (*sakala*) existing together with a portion (*kalā*), namely *hūṃ*. Therefore: *kṣaṃ hūṃ haṃ vajradeha kuru kuru hiṅgulu hiṅgulu garja garja haṃ hūṃ kṣaṃ pañcānanāya*.

*Namaḥ* is the syllable *viyat* (the letter *ha*). *Varma* is *hūṃ*. *Aḥ* is the letter *kṣa*. A "long dot" (*dīrghabindu*) refers to both a long vowel and a dot; the "long" is the vowel *ā*, and the "dot" is the *anusvāra*. Alternatively, it means joined with a long vowel, a dot, and a *visarga*. Having thus worshipped the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with this *pīṭha-mantra*:
Having worshipped with the root mantra in due order, likewise [worship] upon the filaments with *praṇādā* (and) *hrāṃ*,
*hrīṃ*, *hrūṃ*, *hraim*.
As it has been said:
"One should worship these [goddesses] among the deities, preceded by the seed-syllable of Śrī and adorned with their own ornaments.
Hūṃkārī, Khecarī, Caṇḍā, Chedinī, Kṣepaṇī, Strī,
Hūṃkārī, Kṣemakārī, Lokeśā, and Varabhūṣaṇā.
One should worship in that same sequence with "Oṃ Śrīṃ Hūṃ Kāryai Namaḥ" and so forth;
likewise, one should worship Phaṭkārī outside in front, holding a bow and arrows.
On both sides of the door, one should worship Jayā and Vijayā, who hold golden lotuses in their hands; after that, [one should offer] the word "Oṃ" and the phrase "Kaṃ kalāya."
At the end of the word "vakṣayugma," one should say "tvaritāṅga sthiro bhava";
with this mantra ending in the armor (varma) and weapon (astra) syllables, one should worship that servant outside.
Nor [did she see] Kṛṣṇa carrying molasses, with his hair as black and excellent as that of Kṛṣṇa.

And so: one should worship with the mantra, "O servant, protect, protect quickly with your limbs; be firm, hūṃ phaṭ! Homage to the servant (kiṃkara)! Then, having gratified the root [mantra], performed the recitation as much as possible, and offered the recitation with the verse beginning "The secret of secrets," one should praise and bow, and [remove] the floral remains (nirmālya) with the withdrawal mudrā (saṃhāramudrā).
Having taken [it], one should release it.
Now, the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).

Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, the knower of mantras who has conquered his senses should perform a fire sacrifice with ten parts of the best fuel-sticks smeared with the three sweets.
Thus, once a practitioner of mantras has attained success, he is honored by women, men, and kings—
just as the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) is honored by the gods before he had conquered Lakṣmī.
Such is the summary. Now follows the *trikūṭā* mantra.

The two mantras consisting of the three seed-syllables are proclaimed as *Śrī*, *Māyā*, and *Madana*: *Śrīṃ*, *Hrīṃ*, and *Klīṃ*. Then, having completed the morning rites and so forth up to the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* according to the previously mentioned method, one should conclude with the armor (*varma*) and perform the *ṛṣyādi-nyāsa*.
Just as the seer is Saṃvāhana, the metre Gāyatrī, and the deity Manāḥ;
so too, by means of those three-seeded syllables known as the Tripuṭā, the six limbs [are assigned] in successive order.
Having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) by assigning the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, deity, and limbs to the head, face, and heart, one should meditate as follows:

*śrīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *hrīṃ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *śrīṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *hūṃ*; *hrīṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *klīṃ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. Having thus performed the six-limbed assignment, one should meditate.
In the delightful Pārijāta grove, within a pavilion with jeweled floors,
upon a gentle gem-encrusted throne, there was a lotus adorned with six angles.
One should visualize a goddess seated beneath the Kalpavṛkṣa tree,
holding a bow, a noose, a lotus, a rosary, a goad, and a flower-bow.

Bearing lotuses marked with the syllable *kṣāṃ* and adorned with jewels and pearls, she has three eyes; she possesses the luster of a golden lotus, is bent by the weight of her breasts, and her body today shines with jeweled anklets, a golden girdle, and necklaces— she who is the primordial manifestation of the power of devotion.
Surrounded by female messengers burdened by the weight of their breasts, who carried chowries, mirrors, betel-boxes, and other such items.
Beholding the practitioner with a gaze that rains down the nectar of compassion,
and having meditated thus, one should worship with mental offerings; then,
having performed the ritual installation (*sthāpana*) and placed the pedestal (*pīṭha*) before oneself, one should worship it.

Having established [the deity] there, having invoked [it], having displayed the mudrās, and having worshipped with flowers and other offerings, one should worship in the corners starting from the southeast (agni). As it has been said:
Lakṣmī, with a golden luster, slender, and possessing the splendor of a hundred moons, was born at the beginning of the Dvāpara Yuga.
[One should meditate on the Lord] holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, resembling gold, within the heart.
[He beheld] Śiva, who holds the deer and the ṭaṅka-axe, who bestows desired boons, and who is golden-hued. || 4 ||
Holding a blue lotus in her hand, gentle, and resembling the color of gold. || 5 ||

The meaning is that one should worship Lakṣmī and the others, ending with Smara, within the six corners— Smara being the one who holds a noose, a goad, and a bow of flowers, and whose essence is death.
As before, one should worship the pair of treasures on both sides;
having worshipped the outer limbs, the Mothers are to be worshipped upon the petals.
The meaning is that one should worship the Mothers, beginning with Brahmāṇī, who are the consorts of the world-protectors (lokeśas) and possess gentle forms.

Having thus worshipped Indra and the other guardians of the quarters, having gratified them with the root mantra, having worshipped them with flowers and other offerings, and having performed recitation (japa) according to one's capacity, one should offer the recitation with the verse beginning "O secret of secrets... while employing the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
"Having taken up the remains of the offering (nirmālya), one should dismiss [the deity]. Thus,
he who daily worships the Goddess in this manner, endowed with devotion,
shall attain divine poetic skill and achieve the wealth of his heart's desire.
Having obtained incomparable good fortune, one shall sport upon the earth for a very long time.
Now, the *puraścaraṇa*.
One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times,
and likewise offer oblations with hibiscus flowers ten thousand times, and satisfy one's own guru.
This is the summary.
Now follows the mantra of Mahiṣamardinī, as found in the Śāradātilaka.
Bhāntaṃ, viyet, sa, nayana, śveta, and the pair of ṭha-s in mardini—
this is declared to be the eight-syllabled Vidyā known as Mahiṣamardinī.
The letter *ma* is radiant; *ha* is the sky; *i* is the eye; *ṣa* is white; the two [syllables] are *svāhā*.
Then follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, according to the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
Nārada is declared its seer, and Gāyatrī is said to be its metre;
this deity is Mahiṣaghnī, whose primordial seed-syllable is both supreme and non-supreme.
Having thus performed the morning rites and so forth, as previously described, up to the end of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, one should perform the special nyāsa.
As it has been said:
"O Slayer of Mahiṣa, *hūṃ phaṭ* is proclaimed as the heart."
"Mahiṣa śatro vi hūṃ phaṭ" is proclaimed as the head limb.
"Mahiṣaṃ bhīṣaya dvandvaṃ hūṃ phaṭ"—this is the mantra for the crest (śikhā) ending with *ḍantaḥ*.
"Mahiṣaṃ hana" at the end of the pair, O Goddess, followed by *hūṃ phaṭ*, is the armor (tanucchada).
At the end of "mahiṣāntesūdini," the mantra ending in "hūṃ phaṭ" is uttered.
Likewise, in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi:
At the end of the seed-syllable of the three worlds, followed by the vocative case, there are two syllables representing emanation and withdrawal; this is the Vidyā Mahiṣamardinī.
The most secret great mantra (mahāvidyā) that ordains creation and maintenance;
the syllable *hrīṃ*, which is the seed of the three worlds; the address "O crusher of Mahiṣa"; the two syllables of emission and withdrawal (*sṛṣṭi-saṃhāra*); and *svāhā*. Likewise:
This "Unfailing" accomplishment, once revealed, must not be imparted to anyone;
however, if it is told to one who is pure and possesses devotion to the Guru, it shall be successful.
Then the eight-syllable mantra should be given; it is neither a seed-syllable nor a means of accomplishment. The *hṛllekhā*, the common science of vital breaths, is within the sphere of attainment.
This goddess, who previously resided [there], is the destroyer of the teacher’s siddhi.

She is called *hrīṃ* by means of the word that is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the three worlds. That very [syllable] has been made manifest as the common *prāṇavidyā*, beginning with *hṛllekhā*; *hṛllekhā* is *hrīṃ*. Therefore, there is no [other] mantra for this.

Having recollected: "The Seer is [the sage], the Gāyatrī is the metre, Mahiṣamardinī is the deity; the application is for the attainment of desired success," and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the head, face, and heart, [one recites]: "O slayer of Mahiṣa, *hūṃ phaṭ*, obeisance to the heart" (84a).

Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) with the mantra: "O buffalo, of the enemy, vi hūṃ phaṭ svāhā to the head; terrify, terrify the buffalo, hūṃ phaṭ vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); slay, slay the buffalo, hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ to the armor (*kavaca*); O buffalo, bhūdini hūṃ phaṭ namas to the weapon (*astra*)," one should then place these [mantras] on the thumbs and other fingers using the root mantra. Then, by means of the root mantra...
Having performed the pervasive ritual (vyāpaka), one should meditate upon the Goddess: "I bow to her who resembles the brilliance of a garuḍa-stone, adorned with a jeweled crown and earrings,
possessing an eye on her forehead, seated upon the severed head of Mahiṣa,
and holding in her hands a discus, a conch, a sword, a shield, a noose, a bow, a trident, and also a threatening finger."
With his own arms, he [upheld] the moon and the remainder of the mountain.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the installation of the special *argha* water, and having prepared a pedestal before him, one should invoke [the deity] there, display the respective mudrās, worship with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings,
and then perform the worship of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the previously mentioned six-limbed mantra. As it has been said:
Having worshipped the limbs upon the petals, one should worship her named Durgā of excellent complexion,
the third as Āryā, and the fourth as Kanakaprabhā.
The practitioner of mantra should worship the maiden Svarūpā, who is the fifth named Kṛttikā and the sixth who bestows fearlessness, using the long vowels in their proper sequence.

With long vowels, such as Āṃ, Īṃ, Ūṃ, Aiṃ, Auṃ, Aḥ, and so forth; one should worship on the eight petals in sequence with "Āṃ, obeisance to Durgā," and so on. Likewise, one should worship the weapons—the discus, the conch, and the shield—in front [of the deity].
The arrow, the bow, the trident, and the threatening gesture, in sequence starting from the first.
The meaning is "with the initial long vowels. Therefore, one should worship in sequence with "Āṃ, obeisance to Cakra," and so forth.
Likewise, the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped thereafter, and their weapons immediately after that.

Having thus worshipped in sequence and having worshipped again with perfumes and other offerings, having gratified [the deity] with the root mantra, and having recited it as much as one is able, one should conclude the recitation with the verse beginning "The most secret of secrets," and then, having offered praise and prostrated like a staff, [one should perform the concluding rites].
Having prostrated and taken the remains of the offering with the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should dismiss [the deity].

Having performed the recitation (*japa*) and the mantra, and having offered oblations together with auspicious *antailas*, one should worship Mahiṣamardinī on the previously mentioned seat; such is the detailed procedure.
O Goddess, while he was intent on reflection, [he saw] his bud-like [organ].
Tell me before me that life-force which is free from defect;
he is the leader of the hosts at the end of the multitude of obstacles to the Vedas.

The syllable *ai*. Therefore: *oṃ oṃ duṃdu*... *namaḥ*. ...should be joined. That goddess is not to be joined, yet she is the bestower of enjoyment (*bhogadā*). By this, having abandoned the seed-syllable *ādudum* at the beginning of this mantra, she shall grant the abode...

Having stated that it is preceded by the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbīja*) is mentioned first as the form of the seed-syllable of emanation (*sṛṣṭibīja*). As for the previously mentioned *aiṃ*, the seed-syllable of emanation, and *hrīṃ*, the seed-syllable of desire, [this is] in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*.
Or she is called Ugradurgā; that supreme one is borne by a lion.
At the end of the seed-syllable of the three worlds, she is the crusher of the Kula.
Better is a beloved woman endowed with fire and joined with ten thousand faces,
who bestows great curses everywhere upon those who know the family scriptures.
Therefore, with every effort, this nine-syllabled mantra should be known;

it is the seed of the three worlds, "hrīṃ. If the eight-syllabled mantra of Ugrā Durgā follows at its end, then it must by all means be kept secret. Likewise, having completed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with the *mātṛkā* according to the previously mentioned sequence, [one should proceed].
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and so forth. As it has been stated:
"Nārada is declared to be its sage, the Gāyatrī is said to be its meter, and the Vidyā known as Ugradurgā is Mahiṣamardinī."

And so, having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣi, Chandas, Devatā, and so forth upon the head, face, and heart, and having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root mantra, one should meditate upon the Goddess.
Terrible, dark as a durva blade, most fearsome, four-armed,
holding a conch, a discus, a bow, and arrows, she was looking upward with great intensity.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess seated on the lion-throne, the bestower of knowledge and sovereignty,
and having worshipped her with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the special *arghya* water and place the pedestal before her, as follows:
In the eight-petaled Yantra, which is endowed with the Anuṣṭubh meter and the Mātṛkā alphabet,
one should write the seed-syllable (bīja) in the center of the petals joined with the eight syllables.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess in the center, within the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) at the heart of the diagram.

By that [means], one should extract the yantra as being joined with two seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the center and joined with eight syllables on the petals; this is the meaning. Having established the Goddess there with the root-mantra (*mūla*), having invoked her, and having displayed the respective mudrās, [one should worship her] with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings.
Having performed worship with the six-limbed mantra ending in "namaḥ," and having fully worshipped the six limbs, one should worship upon the petals.
As follows:
Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Śūkṣmā, Viśuddhā, and again Nalinī.
Suprabhā, Vijayā, and Sarvasiddhidā are the nine Śaktis.

The meaning is that they are to be worshipped. Likewise, one should conquer the Lion Throne with seed-syllables (*bīja*) lacking vowels, being short, and neuter. Having worshipped there with "ĀṂ ĪṂ DUṂ EṂ AUṂ AḤ, obeisance to the Lion Throne," and having worshipped the Goddess therein, one should worship the weapons (*astra*). As it has been said:
The first repetition [of the mantra] is for the limbs and so forth; the second is with the powers (śaktis);
the third shall be the repetition of the weapons (astras); and the fourth is with the world-protectors (lokapālas).

The transformation and those weapons have been fully explained to you. By this, it attains a fivefold nature through the limbs (aṅgas) and so forth, and through the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅgas) and so forth; the second [fivefold nature] is again by means of the powers (śaktis). This is the meaning. As follows:
Jayā, Vijayā, Kīrti, Prīti, followed by Prabhā,
Śraddhā, Medhā, and Dhṛti are proclaimed, each endowed with the first letter of its own name.
The meaning is that one should worship in sequence with "Salutation to Jayā" and so forth;

likewise, one should worship the conch, discus, mace, lotus, noose, goad, arrows, and bow. Similarly, one should worship the world-protectors beginning with Indra, as well as the deities of the weapons beginning with the thunderbolt (vajra). By this—

Having performed the fivefold *māyā* [rite], one should then satisfy [the deity] with the root mantra, worship them with perfumes and other offerings, recite the mantra according to one's capacity, and conclude the recitation with the verse beginning "guhyātiguhyam. Then, having offered praise and prostration, one should take the *nirmālya* (remains of the offering) with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and dismiss [the deity]. Thus it is said.
O Maheśvarī, out of affection for you, I have revealed this entire secret;
this supreme vidyā, which bestows victory everywhere, must not be given away.
The Goddess who bestows mastery over speech, the Goddess who grants great liberation,
and the Goddess who bestows the eight supernatural powers— what is the use of further elaborate talk?
86a) It must not be given to anyone whatsoever; it must not be given under any circumstances.
For by whomsoever this vidyā, which effects the destruction of evil, is bestowed upon whomever...
With a vajra weapon hurled, I shall take away his life.
Now, the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
Having meditated thus, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and then perform a fire offering (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that amount;
such is the summary.
Now, the mantra of Navadurgā, as given in the Śāradātilaka:
"Arise!"—addressing her thus, O woman, there would then be a step;
that grandfather, whose eye is the moon, might sleep, and yet there would be fear for me.
Having recited what has been presented, one should then tell me, O Blessed One, whether that which follows is possible or impossible.

The mantra consists of thirty-seven syllables, beginning with the word *śamayāgni-vadhūḥ*. The letter *ka* is the Grandfather (Brahmā); the letter *ī* is the Eye; and the *bindu* is the *anusvāra*. Thus: "Arise, O Woman! Why do you sleep?
A danger has approached me. Whether it be possible or impossible, O Blessed One, pacify that for me!"
Svāhā! Then, having completed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, one should perform the Nyāsa of the Ṛṣis and so forth. As it has been said:
The seer is Āraṇyaka; the meter is Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is Vanadurgā, who liberates one from all difficulties.
Having thus assigned the seers (ṛṣis), meters (chandas), and deities (devatās) to the head, face, and heart, one should assign the syllables of the mantra to these limbs. As it has been said:
[The vital points] are located at the eight joints of the feet, in the anus, the genitals, and the *ādhāra*;
on the petals [of the heart-lotus], on the sides, in the hearts, in the throats, and again at the eight joints of the arms.

One should place the syllables of the mantra upon the mouth, nose, cheeks, eyes, ears, the space between the eyebrows, and the crown of the head, for the sake of purification through identification with the deity.
With that [syllable], one should place "uṃ" and "maḥ" and so forth in sequence upon the feet and other limbs.
Likewise:

The formation of the limbs [of the mantra] should be made by assigning six, four, eight, eight, and six syllables of the mantra respectively, joined with the [five] seed-syllables (jāti) in due order.

With those six syllables of the mantra, one should place the *vidyā* and so forth in sequence upon the heart and other limbs, starting from the thumb. Then, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, one should meditate [on the goddess] seated in the center of a golden lotus, three-eyed, resembling lightning, holding a discus, a conch, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and bearing a digit of the moon.

One should meditate upon the moon-faced goddess dwelling on the Vindhya mountains, who wears necklaces, armlets, and large earrings, who is praised by Indra and the other gods, and who has a lion standing at her side. Having thus worshipped with the various offerings consisting of meditative visualizations, and having performed the ritual installation of the *argha* water, one [proceeds] to the nine-cornered [mandala].
Having placed before oneself the eight-petaled yantra beginning with the syllable *bhūḥ* and endowed with its proper characteristics, and having meditated upon her in the form previously described,

one should establish her within the yantra, invoke her, worship her with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, honor her with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and then worship her upon the petals.
Āryādurgā, she named Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, and then Ambikā;
Kṣamā, and another named Agarbhā—these are the six Śaktis at the end of Kṣama.
With that [mantra], one should worship in sequence with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Noble One" and so forth;
the tantras are on the middle petals, and the discus, conch, sword, and shield [are on the others].
One should worship the arrow, the staff, the trident, and so forth, ending with the skull;
then the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī on the tips of the petals, and after that, the world-protectors (lokapālas).

Therefore, one should worship these weapons in the aforementioned locations. Then, having gratified them with the root mantra, and having recited it, praised, and bowed, one should dismiss them. One should worship the Goddess in this manner during the application of perfected mantras. Such is the detailed explanation.
Now follows the mantra of Caṇḍikā.
Now I shall declare the mantra of Caṇḍī, the auspicious one who is the abode of all auspiciousness:
the letter following *va* (pha), mounted upon fire (*ra*), and adorned with the fourth vowel (*ī*).
Joined with the *anusvāra* and encapsulated by the *māyābīja*:
the letter *śa* (the "emitted" sound), fire (*ra*), the fourth vowel (*ī*), and *māyā* (*hrīṃ*). Thus, [the mantra is] *hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ*.
Then, having completed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, one should perform the *ṛṣyādi-nyāsa*.

The seer (ṛṣi) is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Śiva. One should recite the mantra for six hundred thousand times (ṛtulakṣa), perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) for half of that,
perform the fire sacrifice (homa) for half of that, and perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for half of that.
Having offered a *bali* with half of that amount, one should worship with five hundred;
this refers to the *yantra*.
Within a hexagon, one should draw a complete lotus endowed with the three qualities;
this is declared to be the Yantra, an abode of the earth with eight doors, enriched with seed-syllables.
"Endowed with three qualities" means it is joined with lines; "having eight doors" means having eight entrances. Having thus placed this yantra before him, he should meditate upon it as follows:
"Like a magnificent great island situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar."
Adorned with flowers and antelopes, it was graced by the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
It was adorned with banners and flags, and beautified by white chowries;
in its center was a golden couch endowed with various jewels.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess seated atop a full golden pitcher, completely surrounded on all sides by golden jars filled with water.
Seated upon five lion-thrones, possessing the luster of molten Jāmbūnada gold,
resembling an Aṭasī flower, and as ruddy as the rays of the rising sun.
The goddess holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, her remaining portion formed by the crescent moon;
her face is bright with a gentle smile, and her sprout-like lower lip is the color of the bandhūka flower.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess within the center of the yantra with mantras.
Having meditated in this way and worshipped her with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) and other rites, [the ritual] is complete.
Now follows the mantra of Mahāmāyā.
The first seed-syllable is Vāgbhava; the second is Kāmabīja;
[the third is]...; again, Vāgbhava is declared.
Then follows the seed-syllable of Lajjā, after which the seed-syllable of Padmā;
then Varma, Agni, and Priyā—this is the great mantra of Mahāmāyā.
Vāgbhava: Aiṃ; Kāmabīja: Klīṃ; Śaktibīja: Sauḥ; Vāgbhava: Aiṃ; Lajjābīja: Hrīṃ;
Padmābīja: Śrīṃ; Varma: Hūṃ; Agnipriyā: Svāhā.

Therefore, with "aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ svāhā," and likewise having completed the morning duties, the twilight rituals, and all actions up to the end of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa according to the previously stated sequence, one should perform the mantra-nyāsa.
Likewise, with the six-limbed mantra.
One should place [the mantras] starting from the thumb and ending at the palm of the hand upon the heart and other centers. Thus,
Brahmā is declared as the Seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī meter is proclaimed,
and the deity is declared to be Mahāmāyā, who is well-guarded in secret.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, one should meditate as follows:

One should meditate upon her who is clothed in the directions, whose face is smiling, whose splendor possesses the brilliance of ten million suns, who stands upon a lotus, who holds a lotus while granting boons, and who bestows desired objects and liberation with her right hand;
she is surrounded by those seeking primordial liberation, wears a garland of severed heads around her neck, and is radiant.
She whose breasts were slightly budding, who was the supreme Śivā, and who stood between the two excellent arms of Hari.
Having meditated thus, worshipped with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*), performed the installation of the special water-offering (*viśeṣārgha*),

and placed the *yantra* before him, one should invoke [the deity] there, worship with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, offer the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, praise and prostrate, take up the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) with the *saṃhāramudrā*, and dismiss [the deity]. This is the summary.
Likewise,
having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should place the word "Mahāmāyā" at the end.
The great mantra of Mahāmāyā is "ṅenta magni priyānto yaṃ."
The seed-syllable of Māyā is *hrīṃ*; the wife of Agni is *svāhā*. [This is] the meditation (*dhyāna*).
I bow to her whose body is crimson as vermilion, who has three eyes, and whose crest-jewel of rubies shines with a central gem; she whose face is smiling, whose breasts are full, and who,
gentle and adorned with jewels, holds in her two hands a ruby filled with gems and a red lotus.
One should meditate upon the supreme Ambikā, whose left foot rests upon a water-jar.
The mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and then perform a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that amount;
thereafter, he should worship the previously mentioned pedestal and perform the ritual of worship as before.
Likewise,
[the names] ending in *ha* and *anta*, preceded by *ma* and *na*, as well as those ending in *ṇa*; beginning with the eleventh *ka* and so forth, ending in *kha*, and preceded by *viṣṇu*.
One should write the mantra with these eight syllables, resembling a red lotus;
having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, it is to be recited, with Nārada as the sage (*muni*).

The meter is to be known as Anuṣṭubh, and Mahāmāyā is the deity. The letter *sa* at the end of *ha*; that same [letter] with *ṣa* at the end; *śa* preceding that; *ya* at the end of *ma*; *pa* at the end of *ma*; *ta* at the end of *ṇa*; *ṣṭa* eleven times; *ca*, the sixth letter starting from *ka*; and the end of *kha*.

The letter *ka* represents Viṣṇu, and the letter *ra* [represents Śiva]; by reversing this order, one obtains *a-ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa-ya-śa*. The meaning is that one should recite this mantra after first placing the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning. Now, if it is asked how the extraction [of the mantra] is obtained in reverse order, it is understood from the phrase "preceded by Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇupuraḥsara*); otherwise, there could not even be such a thing as being "preceded."
The practitioner should first recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times.
Now, as for meditative absorption (dhyāna).
There, one should visualize the Golden Island situated within the ocean of sugarcane juice;
in its center is a couch located within a pavilion of jewels.
Always sprinkled with the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā and other auspicious substances,
that red lotus upon the couch is always praised as bringing prosperity.
One should contemplate the pericarp as golden in color, marked with a golden garland, having seven underworlds as its stalk, and reaching up to the world of Brahmā.
There, one should meditate upon Mahāmāyā, who is seated, undistracted,
resembling a white lotus, and adorned with matted locks of hair.
She wore a radiant garland and earrings set with shimmering gold,
and she bore an excellent crown adorned with gold and jewels.
Her skull was as brilliant as the copper-colored twilight, and her eyes were flickering.
With teeth like the seeds of a pomegranate free from impurity, radiant with the qualities of a diamond,
possessing a neck like a conch shell, large eyes, and a splendor equal to ten million suns;
four-armed, unclothed, and with full, elevated breasts.
Beyond the right [hand], she holds a sword and a lotus, while with her two left hands she displays the gestures of fearlessness and the boon-granting mudrā.
She whose navel was deep, whose feet were well-proportioned, whose waist was slender, who was captivating,
whose thighs were beautiful, and whose private parts were well-concealed.
She was resplendent with a firm posture through her resolve for the *vardhamāna-paryaṅka* [posture], and she remained standing, leaning gracefully against a jeweled pillar with her body.
She repeatedly uttered the words, "What do you desire?",
while gazing at the five-faced one standing before her, her own vehicle.
A pearl necklace, a golden jewel-harmer, and so forth with kanaka and other materials.
She was endowed with all the ornaments and possessed a face like that of Uḷvāṇā; she resembled ten million suns and was possessed of every auspicious mark.
Having meditated upon Ambikā in such a manner and contemplating "I am she indeed," one should then perform the *aṅganyāsa* and *karanyāsa* in due order.
By means of these mantras, accompanied by vowels, consonants, and *sāmans* arranged in sequence,
and preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, they are endowed with the *praṇava* and are red in color and captivating.
One should perform the encircling with the mantra from the thumb to the little finger with the syllable *phaṭ*;
then, one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) upon both palms.

With that [mantra], one should perform the placement in sequence, starting with "Oṃ Āṃ Phaṭ, obeisance to the heart" on the two thumbs; "haṭā" means with the *phaṭ* syllable situated at the end. Likewise, one should place [the mantras] in order upon the heart, head, crest-lock (*śikhā*), armor (*kavaca*), and eyes.

One should likewise place those very same phonemes in the heart and other locations; then, one should place the syllables of the root mantra on the crown, the back, and the belly, as well as on the anus,
the genitals, the feet, the shanks, and the hips.
One should place eight syllables while likewise recollecting the syllable *oṃ*.
Having placed each syllable of the root mantra preceded by the *praṇava* at the *mūlādhāra*, one should install them in the *cakras* and other locations. Likewise,
one should worship the Supreme Goddess Kāmākhyā in her fivefold form.
And that man shall remain in my world for millions of billions of eons.
Having remained [in this state], the goddess, through grace, shall attain supreme nirvāṇa;
all else is as before—this is the summary.
Now follows the mantra of Vārāhī.
Likewise Vārāhī, and likewise ending in -ṅī, as taught in the Māyājāla and other tantras up to the limit of the dual [form].
The term "vārāhī" ends in the feminine suffix ṅīp; the meaning is that it is in the dative case.

*Māyā* (the seed-syllable *Hrīṃ*), *Bhuvaneśvarī*, *Hrīṃ*, two *Ṭha*s, and *Svāhā*. Thus, the mantra is *Hrīṃ Vārāhyai Svāhā*. Furthermore, having completed the morning rites up to the *Mātṛkā-nyāsa*, one should perform the *Ṛṣi-nyāsa* and so forth; for it is said that the Seer (*Ṛṣi*) is Nārāyaṇa, the metre (*Chandas*) is Triṣṭubh, and the Deity (*Devatā*) is declared to be Vārāhī.

And here one should employ it for all purposes. Then, having performed the pervasive [placement] with the root mantra and having placed the yantra before oneself, one should meditate upon it. As it has been said:
Having drawn a triangle wheel, followed by an eight-petaled one,
and then the abode of the Earth, one should subsequently arrange the vajras along with the gates in due order.
One should meditate upon her, possessing the luster of molten gold and adorned with various ornaments,
holding a noose and a goad in her right hands, as well as the gesture of emanation, stability, and the boon.

Having meditated thus upon her who wears a jewel-crown and who is the destroyer of the sins of the three worlds, and having worshipped her with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the *argha* vessel, invoke her into the *cakra*, display the respective mudrās,
worship her with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, perform libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the root mantra, carry out the recitation (*japa*), and then offer it.
"One should dismiss [the deity]"—likewise, the triple-tattva (tritatva) between the two *tāras* becomes *vārāhī*, the supreme.
The triple-tattva is *hūṃ*, the *tāra* is *oṃ*; by means of that, *oṃ hūṃ oṃ*. The meditation and so forth are as before.
Now, the Mālamukhī mantra from the Rudrajāmala.
One should recite "Vahni-hīna-indra-yuk-māyā-vagalāmukhi-sarva-yuk," followed by "duṣṭānāṃ vācaṃ" and then "mukhaṃ stambhaya."
One should say "Kīlaya jihvām" (nail the tongue), then "Vināśaya buddhim" (destroy the intellect), and then utter the word "Padam.
Then follows the seed-syllable, then the *tāra* (OM), ending with the fire-conqueror (*vajra*).

The thirty-four-syllable Vagalāmukhī mantra begins with *tārā* (Oṃ). What is *māyā*? It is *hrīṃ*. Deprived of fire (*ra*) and joined with the sense-organ (*i*), it is joined with the letter *la*; thus, *hlīṃ*. Then *tārā* is *oṃ*.
The wife of Fire is *svāhā*. With that [mantra]: *oṃ hlīṃ oṃ hlīṃ vagalāmukhi sarvaduṣṭānāṃ vācaṃ mukhaṃ stambhaya jihvāṃ kīlaya buddhiṃ vināśaya hlīṃ oṃ svāhā*.
And so, having performed the morning rites and other duties up to the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, one should perform the *ṛṣyādi-nyāsa* for this mantra as follows:

"Nārada is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Paṅkti is the meter (*chandas*), the venerable Vagalāmukhī is the deity (*devatā*), *hlīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). This is the application (*viniyoga*) in recitation for the purpose of paralyzing the mouths of all enemies. Having thus recollected this, [one should proceed].

Having performed the placement [of mantras] on the head, face, and heart with the seed-syllables possessing the six long vowels, and having performed the ritual assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should meditate:

"I bow to the Goddess, who is seated upon a lion-throne on the altar in the center of a jeweled pavilion in the midst of the ocean of nectar; she is of a deep yellow complexion, her body adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, and garlands."
The enemy’s tongue was seized by Dhṛtakuṇḍala.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the *argha* vessel; then, having invoked the deity into the *yantra*, worshipped with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, performed the recitation (*japa*), and offered the recitation, one should dismiss [the deity].
This is the summary in the *Nigamasāranirṇaya* composed by the venerable Ramāramaṇa Devaśarman.
Thus concludes this third chapter, accompanied by the intermediate rites.
Now, following the description of the intermediate sciences (*avāntaravidyā*), the perfected sciences (*siddhavidyā*) are described.
Among these, those that can be accomplished with little effort are to be described first; thus, at the outset:
Therein is the mantra of Mātaṅgī.
90b) Listen to the mantra, O Great Goddess; I shall explain it to you exactly as it is:
one should utter the word "ucchiṣṭa" and likewise "cāṇḍālinī."
Then one should proclaim the goddess Sumukhī;
immediately after that, Mahāpiśācinī; and after that, the seed-syllable of Māyā.
Then, O Great Goddess, there are three instances of the letter *ṭha* joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, followed by the *visarga*; this bestows the fruit of all siddhis.
*Māyā* is *hrīṃ*. By that [is meant] *ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī sumukhī devī mahāpiśācinī hrīṃ ṭhaṃḥ ṭhaṃḥ ṭhaṃḥ*. Likewise, or else, one should utter the words *ucchiṣṭacāṇḍāli mātaṅgi*.
Then, within the heart of all the deceivers, she is the beloved fire.
With nineteen syllables, it shall grant all desired objects.
[The mantra is: *Hṛn-namaḥ-vahni-vallabhā-svāhā* (Heart: *namaḥ*, beloved of fire: *svāhā*). By that, [the mantra] is: *ucchiṣṭe cāmuṇḍe vali-mātaṅgi sarvavaśaṅkari namaḥ svāhā*. Likewise:
Now, O Beloved, I shall fully proclaim the most secret Goddess Mātaṅgī,
who is preceded by Ucchiṣṭa and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
[They seek] that which is the counteragent to everything, free from all defects,
and by means of which the Goddess, when unrecognized, causes calamities to become inexhaustible.
O Goddess, one should recite this vidyā, which is based upon the supreme limb; it consists of the stationary, the moving, the artificial, and that which is born of the body.
This knowledge is a great knowledge that removes all sins;
it bestows heaven, bestows liberation, and likewise bestows fortune.
This vidyā, when recited even once, removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
one should never remember the Goddess while remaining in a state of impurity from food remnants.
Then, O Goddess, she would become tranquil even without [the ritual] being performed;
the unfortunate would become fortunate, and the suffering would become happy.
Even a barren woman obtains a son who lives for a hundred years;
O goddess of beautiful countenance, listen as I describe the ritual procedure for this.
91a) O Goddess, immediately after eating, even without having performed the *mudrā*,
the practitioner should first offer the *bali* with the root mantra.
Then, having meditated upon that goddess, one should recite the mantra; thus the desired success will be attained.
There is no need for a lunar day (tithi), nor a constellation (nakṣatra), nor the [limbs of the mantra], nor even the ritual placement (nyāsa).
There is no fault regarding women, no enmity, no impurity, nor even restrictive observances;
he in whom this mantra resides is not overcome by obstacles.
And so, having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with the *mātṛkā*, and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra,
one should meditate.
Seated upon a corpse, draped in red garments,
adorned with red ornaments, and embellished with a necklace of gunja berries.
And she is a sixteen-year-old maiden with full and elevated breasts,
holding a skull-cup and a chisel in her hands, whose essential nature is the supreme light.
The best of mantra-knowers should meditate upon her through the yoga of the left and the right.

Having meditated thus, having worshipped with mental recitations, having prepared the *argha* water and placed it upon the *yantra*, having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) and displayed the various mudrās such as *āvāhana* and so forth, having worshipped with *pādya* and other offerings, and having gratified [the deity] with the root mantra;

"Having performed the recitation (*japa*), having offered it, having praised [the deity], and having bowed, one should dismiss [the deity]. Likewise, having offered the bali-oblation with the remnants of food (*ucchiṣṭa*), one should perform the recitation with the mind fixed upon that.
One who desires success must not perform the recitation while still possessing the remnants of food; for if one performs the recitation while possessed of remnants, [obstacles] arise."
All accomplishments [are attained].
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall proclaim that which bestows fruit:
the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa), for the sake of accomplishing all desires.
Having meditated upon the Goddess, one should perform the fire sacrifice with rice grains mixed with curd and ghee;
by performing a thousand oblations, one shall bring even a king under one's control.
One should perform the oblation for the Goddess with the flesh of a cat;
thus one attains the supreme knowledge that brings weapons and scriptures under one's control.
And with bilva leaves smeared with honey, offered continuously for one month;
Even a barren woman shall obtain an excellent son who lives for a long time,
provided that someone rises early in the morning and performs the fire-oblation (homa) day after day.
O Śivā, with a japā flower and clarified butter, one should perform more than a hundred recitations of the mantra.
Now, immediately following the intermediate sciences, the science of supernatural powers (*siddhividya*), which consists of the nature of consciousness, is described.
In that regard, first, [the objects] to be determined are those accomplished with little effort, and so forth.
Listen to the mantra, O Great Goddess; I shall tell it to you exactly as it is:
one should utter the word "ucchiṣṭa" and likewise "cāṇḍālinī."

Then [the mantra] "sumukhī" for the Goddess... [then] the three *ṭha* syllables joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, followed by the *visarga*, O Great Goddess; this bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
Māyā Hrīṃ! By that [mantra], O Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī, the fair-faced goddess Mahāpiśācinī, Hrīṃ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ! Likewise.
Alternatively, one may utter the words *cchiṣṭa*, *cāṇḍāli*, *mātaṅgi*;
then [the goddess] Sarvavaśaṅkarī, the beloved of the Fire who causes transformation at the end of time, [is attained].
With nineteen syllables, it shall grant all desired objects.
*Hṛt* (heart) is *namaḥ*. *Vahni-vallabhā* (the beloved of fire) is *svāhā*. With that [mantra]: *Acchiṣṭa-cāṇḍāli mātaṅgi sarvavaśaṅkari namaḥ svāhā*. Likewise:
Now, therefore, O beloved, I shall fully declare the most secret goddess Mātaṅgī,
who is preceded by Ucchiṣṭa and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
The Goddess who closes all doors of misfortune and is free from all defects—
by knowing this Goddess, people desire the destruction of their calamities.
O Goddess,
recite this vidyā, which is based upon the supreme limb, [consisting of] the stable, the moving, the artificial, and likewise that which is born of the body.
This knowledge is a great knowledge that removes all sins;
it bestows heaven, liberation, as well as sovereignty and good fortune.
This vidyā, when recited but once, removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
having always maintained a pure mouth, one should never fail to remember the Goddess.
Then, O Goddess, one becomes pure even without having performed an ablution;
an unfortunate woman certainly becomes fortunate, and a sorrowful woman becomes happy.
"Even a barren woman obtains a son who lives for a hundred years;
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, listen as I describe the ritual procedure for this."
O Goddess, immediately after eating, even if one has not performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana),
the practitioner should first offer the *bali* with the root mantra.
Then, having meditated upon that Goddess, one should recite the mantra for the attainment of desired success;
there is no requirement for a lunar day, nor a constellation, nor even the ritual placement of limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Neither foreign land, nor enmity, nor impurity, nor even restrictive observances affect him in whom this mantra abides; he is not overcome by obstacles.
And so, having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with the *mātṛkā*, and having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) by means of the root mantra,
one should meditate.
Seated upon a corpse, clad in garments of red cloth,
adorned with red ornaments, and decorated with garlands of guñjā berries.
And she is a sixteen-year-old maiden with full and elevated breasts,
holding a skull-cup and a chopper in her hands, whose essential nature is the supreme light.
The most excellent knower of mantras should meditate upon her through the yoga of the left and the right;
having thus worshipped with mental offerings and having established the *argha* water in the yantra.

Having established [the deity] and invoked it, having displayed the mudrās such as the vehicle (vāhana) and others, having worshipped with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings, having gratified [the deity] with the root mantra, and having performed the recitation (japa), one should offer it and then dismiss [the deity] with "svāvisarjaya."
Likewise, having offered the bali-oblation with the remains [of food], one should perform the recitation with the mind fixed upon that;
for one desiring success, this recitation must never be performed with the remains of food.
All perfections arise for one who recites [the mantra] while remaining in a state of ritual impurity (ucchiṣṭa).
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall explain that which bestows fruit.
For the accomplishment of all desires and aims, one should perform both the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa);
having meditated upon the Goddess, one should carry out the oblation with curd, white mustard seeds, and rice grains.
By performing one thousand oblations, one may bring a king under one's control;
with the flesh of a cat, one should perform an oblation for the Goddess.
One attains supreme knowledge, mastered through both weapons and scriptures,
by offering bilva leaves smeared with honey continuously for one month.
Even a barren woman obtains a son who is long-lived and most excellent;
having risen at dawn, she should perform the fire-oblation day after day.
O Śivā, one should perform one hundred and eight recitations while using a hibiscus flower as an offering,
whether in a thicket, a cremation ground, an empty house, or at a crossroads.
By the offering of the *vali*, the Goddess certainly becomes manifest;
by making the remains of the offering her ornament, one will certainly become purified.
Although the *puraścaraṇa* has not been explicitly written down here, nevertheless, the recitation (*jāpa*) consists of eight thousand [verses]. This has been stated as follows:
For those mantras for which no specific number has been stated by the wise regarding recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa),
the number for both recitation and oblation shall be eight thousand.
This is the summary because of such a statement. Now, the severed mantras, according to the Bhairavatantra:
Lakṣmī, Lajjā, and likewise Māyā; then the twelfth *mātrā*.
(93a) The two Vajravairocanīs, with the two *māyās*, followed by *phaṭ* and joined with *svāhā*.
Lakṣmī is Śrīṃ; Lajjā is Hrīṃ; Māyā is Hūṃ; Dvādaśakī is Aiṃ. And likewise: Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ Aiṃ Vajravairocanīye Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā—this is the mantra. Likewise:
The seed-syllable of Lakṣmī is at the beginning of her [mantra], and thus Śrī is present on all sides;
by means of the first seed-syllable of Lajjā, women come under one's control.
With the first seed-syllable of Māyā, there is the destruction of the great sins;
with the first syllable consisting of twelve morae, it becomes the bestower of great liberation.
Therefore, by the offering of any one of these seed-syllables at the beginning of the previously mentioned mantra and so forth, it becomes a specific mantra. Likewise:
The best of mantra-knowers should proclaim the beginningless seed-syllable of the mantra;
for Vajravairocanī, it is the Māyā-seed-syllable, and that follows thereafter.
The mantra joined with *phaṭ* and *svāhā*, O great serpent among mantras, bestows all accomplishments; it is meritorious and grants the happiness of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The beginningless seed-syllable is: Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Likewise:
One should extract the three bodies of Śakti from the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja) and the Tāra-mantra;
at the end of "Vajra Vairocanī," there shall be the Blessed One Māruta.
The *kūrca* mantra ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā) is proclaimed as the Three Powers (*triśakti*).

The seed-syllable of Power (*śaktibīja*) with three bodies is *hrīṃ*; with three bodies it is *hūṃ*; Speech is *aiṃ*; the Savior (*tāra*) is *oṃ*. The Wind is the letter *pa*; Bhaga is the letter *e*; the Weapon (*astra*) is *phaṭ*; and *dviṭha* is *svāhā*. Thus: *hrīṃ hūṃ aiṃ oṃ*.
Vajravairocanīye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Thus is the fifteen-syllable [mantra].
It is likewise in another tantra.
Then *ramā*, *kūrca*, as well as *lajjā*, *vāgbhava*, and the word "vajra";
then *rocanīye*, *parā* in the dual, and thereafter the mantra beloved by Agni.
This is declared to be the sixteenth [vowel]; it is designated as the triple power (triśakti):
Ramā is Śrīṃ, Kūrca is Hūṃ, Lajjā is Hrīṃ, Vāgbhava is Aiṃ, and the supreme pair is Hrīṃ.
Hrīṃ! Astra phaṭ! Agnivallabhā svāhā! By that [mantra]: Śrīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ aiṃ Vajravairocanīye hrīṃ hrīṃ astraṃ phaṭ svāhā. Likewise.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for the Goddess in brief,
as follows:

Having performed the ritual procedures beginning with the morning duties and ending with the *mātṛkā*, one should perform the conjunction (*vyāsaṃkaraṇa*) of the flowers and other offerings. As it has been said:

O fair-faced one, Bhairava is its seer (*ṛṣi*), [the metre is] Saṃrāṭ, and Chinnamastā is its deity; its seed-syllable (*bīja*) shall be the two Māyās. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and having made the pervasive application (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, one should place the yantra before oneself.
Thus it has been said:
Now I shall describe the internal sacrifice; comprehend it exactly as it is.
Drawing in the breath through the left [nostril], one should firmly contract the throat slightly;
then, exhaling through the path of the sun (the right nostril), one should place the tongue against the palate.
Having joined the empowered [deity] to the state of Śiva for a moment with the hands slightly contracted,
and having performed the rite of the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), one should perform the external worship.
Likewise.
One should utter the first mantra, its head marked with a bindu, which extends through the sword and wheel; joined with "svāhā," it is the youngest [mantra].
And then, O Goddess, one should utter the vowel *ī*, which possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons;
thereafter, "Sukhaḍgāya" should be spoken, and immediately after that, "Śirase."
Then, O Goddess, one should utter [the mantra] joined with "svāhā," with the fingers forming the purifying mudrā; and then the letter "ū," its head marked with a bindu.
Then one should join "Śrīvajrāya," and after that, "Śikhāyai";
ending with "Svāhā," one should subsequently place this upon the middle finger.
O Goddess, immediately thereafter, one should place the twelve-syllable *mātrā*;
subsequently, one should place the mantra ending in *svāhā* upon the index finger (*tarjanī*).
Then, O Goddess, [place] the letter *a* with its head marked by a bindu,
joined with three eyes, upon the two thumbs of both hands.
The syllable *A* ending in the *visarga*, joined with *surakṣayāya*,
and then joined with *asurakṣayāya*, followed by the word *mantrāya*.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) on both hands joined with the *phaṭ*-syllable;
having performed the placement on the heart and other centers, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra.
With the mantra "tena āṃ khaḍgāya hṛdayāya svāhā," one should perform the placement [of the mudrās] in sequence, beginning with the two little fingers, and so forth.
Likewise.
Now I shall describe its mandala; listen attentively as it truly is.
One should first make the eastern petal auspicious, and the southeastern one red in color.
To the south of that, one should make a black mandala; then a yellow one; then a white and red one, even more extensive than the former; and then a yellow one—this is the mandala of Caṇḍaroṣaṇa.
The lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas are red, white, and black respectively;
likewise, there is a pair of māyās, accompanied by the syllable "phaṭ" of equal measure.
One should construct the outer and inner wheel provided with three gates;
first red, then yellow, white, and yellow again, in that sequence.
It is provided with four gates and presided over by the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas).
By this [description of] the lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas, the triangle is formed.
Furthermore, the measurement of the petals and so forth should be made sharp at the beginning of the [mantra] "dalaṃ pūrvaṃ" and so on;
this is to be understood also in the case of the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*). Likewise:
Karāla and Vikarāla are at the eastern gate; Atikāla and Mahākāla are likewise at the western and inner [gates] on the south.
And on the fourth [day], one should perform their worship with "namas" at the end;
by that means, one should worship in sequence starting with "kalāyai namaḥ," and so forth. Likewise:
A man who knows the mantras should then worship the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), the Tortoise (Kūrma), the King of Serpents (Nāgarāja), the lotus stalk (Padmanāla), and the lotus (Padma).
Having worshipped Maṇḍala, Caṇḍaraśmi, Rajas, Sattva, Tamas, as well as Rati and Kāma, one should perform the worship of Śakti.

With that [mantra], one should worship in sequence, beginning with "Obeisance to the Support-Power" (ādhāra-śakti) and so forth. This mantra consists of the specific name preceded by the Praṇava (Om) and ending with "namas. Thereafter, one should meditate upon the Goddess.
Then one should meditate upon a pure, fully blossomed, white lotus;
and in the center of that lotus calyx is the mandala of the fiercely radiant one.
Resembling the flower of the javā, similar to the fresh bandhūka,
it possesses the lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas, and resembles the circle of the womb.
And in the center, one should always visualize the Goddess, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
and that Goddess holding her own head in her hand.
With its mouth wide open and its fierce tongue lolling out,
it was drinking the stream of water rising from its own neck.
With her hair disheveled and her own cries, adorned with various ornaments,
naked, most terrible, and standing in the pratyālīḍha posture.
What ministers would meditate upon her who stands above the objects of pleasure and desire? Likewise:
And one should meditate on Rati and Avābhavā, who are engaged in inverted sexual union;
they are joined with Varṇinī and Ḍākinī on their left and right sides respectively.
One should meditate on Ḍākinī as a maiden on the left, and likewise on Varṇinī on the right;
Varṇinī is red, gentle, with loose hair and naked.
The goddess holds a skull-cup and a flaying knife in her left and right hands respectively,
and she drinks the stream of blood gushing from the neck.
On the right side is the goddess Ḍākinī, who wears a garland of bones, has a snake as her sacred thread, and resembles the fire at the end of an aeon.
Her eyes possess the brilliance of a flash of lightning, her row of teeth is like a flight of cranes,
her face is made terrifying by her fangs, and her breasts are full and elevated.
The great goddess, most terrible, with disheveled hair and naked,
her great tongue lolling out, adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Her hands, joined in the left and right, hold a skull-cup as a weapon;
the Goddess is intent on drinking the stream of blood gushing from the neck.
The best of practitioners should meditate upon the goddess, who is terrifying with her skull held in her hand, and who is attended by these two [messengers].
And so it is said:
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall explain [it] in due order:
within one's own navel is a pure lotus, adorned with a solar disc.
One should meditate upon that Great Goddess, the presiding deity, who is joined with the vulva and mouth and endowed with the three qualities, situated in the midst of the radiant light.
The intellect is established in the form of a blazing bud,
joined with a sword held in her hand, and seated upon a red lotus throne.
United with yogic sleep, with her eyes fixed upon her heart—
this is the meditation on the partless (niṣkala), as well as that which abides as the exceedingly manifold (sakala).

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the installation of the *argha* vessel, and having brought the Goddess from one's own heart, one should establish her within the yantra through the right nostril and invoke her with this [mantra], beginning as follows: "O bestower of all perfections," the most excellent practitioner should first utter.
Then one should speak the word *varṇinīye*, and then *sarvasiddhiprade*.
Then the name of the ḍākinī should be uttered, followed by the word "Devi";
then "ehy ehi" (come, come) should be spoken, and immediately after that, "iha" (here).
Then one should utter "Stay! Stay! followed by the two illusory syllables (māyāyugma), and thereafter, conjoined with the six syllables, the word "svāhā."
Thus is the invocation described, together with the ritual of installation. [The mantra is:

*Māyā* (Hrīḥ), *Hūṃ*, the address by name of the Goddess, followed by: "O bestower of all accomplishments, O Varṇinī, O bestower of all accomplishments, O Ḍākinī, O Chinnamastā! Come, come! Stay, stay! Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Thus.

Having invoked [the deity] with the mantra and displayed the mudrās such as āvāhana and others, and having shown the yonimudrā and so forth, one should offer water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (argha), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and other items in their proper places using the root mantra; then one should present an offering of meat and rice (māṃsabhaktavali). One should recite the following vali-mantra:

First, the Praṇava [should be recited], followed by [the mantra] "Obeisance to the one endowed with the bestower of all accomplishments," and then "Obeisance to the one who bestows all accomplishments" should be spoken.
Then the name of the ḍākinī should be uttered, followed by the name of the goddess;
then "Come! Come! should be said, and after that, "This bali [offering]."
"Grasp, grasp! Then say: 'Grant me my success thereafter!
Then say: 'Give, give! O Māyā! Then phaṭ svāhā!'—this is joined with the hands."
The *valimantra* has been fully explained; it is worshipped, O Goddess of the Gods.
With that [mantra]: *Oṃ sarvasiddhiprade varṇinīye sarvasiddhiprade ḍākinīye chinnamaste ehyehi imaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa mama siddhiṃ dehi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus is the *bali*.
The mantra.

Having offered the bali-oblation in this manner, having satiated [the deity] three times with the root mantra, and having performed the worship of the six limbs, one should worship [the deities] upon the petals.
Bhairavī is in the east, and Bhairavī immediately after that.

Then, one should worship the goddess Indrākṣī, who is dark-hued, and subsequently the goddess Saṃhāriṇī; these Śaktis are to be worshipped in sequence upon the petals starting from the east according to their proper order.

With that, one should worship in the sequence beginning with "Oṃ ekānaṅgābhidhāyainena" and so forth. Having worshipped according to one's means with the root mantra (*mūla*), having recited the *Gāyatrī*, and having recited the root mantra as much as possible, one should offer the recitation (*japa*), praise, and bow down.
Then, using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should cast the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) into the north-flowing stream with the *astra-mantra*. Thereafter, in the presence of Caṇḍaraśmi...
One should establish [it].
In that regard, the mantra is as follows:
O Goddess who dwells upon the mountain on the earth, since the northern crest has arisen and you have been permitted by Brahmā, go as you desire.
Just as the Gāyatrī [is recited].
"Oṃ, let us know Vairocanī; let us meditate upon Chinnamastā; may that Goddess inspire us. This is the summary, and likewise [the rest].
Now, what is the use of saying more? Whatever [sin] there may be, such as the killing of a Brahmin, this mantra burns it away through one hundred thousand recitations; of this there is no doubt.
Even the approach of one who should not be approached and likewise the eating of what is forbidden—
once uttered, the mantra consumes them just as fire consumes fuel.
She should always be worshipped at night with black gram, meat, liquor, and other offerings;
this mantra must always be kept secret and never disclosed.

Lack of resolve, obstacles, extreme lack of faith in the practice of recitation (*japa*), laziness, cowardice, and incapacity— of these there is no doubt they cause the failure of the mantra. Thus, there is no fault of the enemy, nor hatred, nor impurity, nor even [the violation of] the observance (*niyama*).
Because the mantra is already perfected, there is no need for prior exertion in this matter.
Whether waking, sleeping, rising, eating, or engaged in sexual intercourse,
one should constantly recite the mantra that bestows the attainment of all desired goals.
O King, in battle, in the royal court, in combat, or in the peril of enemies,
for one who constantly recites this mantra, Māra does not exist.
Having written the mantra on the hand, it is prescribed that one should form a fist;
it will quickly paralyze everything until the fist is released.
Having written the mantra on his own hand, a man should touch it to his mother;
thus the sick person is released from severe illness and attains long life.
By means of the white meditation alone, one can raise up a dead man;
one will certainly raise up even a dead man bitten by hundreds of great serpents.

By means of red [sindūra], subjugation is attained; the entire world is drawn under one's power. By means of yellow [sindūra], one may paralyze everything, including the people of the world, horses, elephants, and so forth.
By the mere meditation upon Kṛṣṇa, a man may cause his enemy to vanish;
he may even kill him without effort through meditation on Kṛṣṇa—of this there is no doubt.
And the practitioner of mantras performs the libation with milk, or with milk-rice (pāyasa), or with water,
honey, or even wine.
By means of the prescribed rite of libation (tarpaṇa), performed by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras respectively, accomplishment proceeds spontaneously.
Now, the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). Likewise:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the procedure for the installation of the fire,
by which the desired accomplishments arise for the practitioner.
The fire-offering rite (homakarma) should be performed according to one's desire, and one should contemplate the mantra;
thereafter, one should perform recitation (japa), by which the spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) arise.
Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, one shall obtain the desired accomplishment;
O Goddess, everything is achieved through recitation and fire-offerings, without a doubt.
The practitioner should always offer oblations with water,
meat, betel-leaf, fish, meat, and various liquors.
O Goddess, an offering of meat bestows the accomplishment of mantras;
therefore, one should always offer an oblation with meat with every effort.
In that case, without material offerings, satisfaction does not come to the Goddess.
For six months, if one consumes curd mixed [with it], his prosperity shall become stable.
Likewise, goat meat together with blood, saturated with ghee;
The practitioner who performs ten million oblations with white oleanders (karavīra) shall bring even a king under his control,
provided he performs the homa correctly.
By performing one hundred thousand oblations, he shall restore to life even one bitten by Kāla;
he who offers sesame seeds and flowers together with clarified butter performs this rite.
O beautiful goddess, having offered ten thousand *bandhūka* flowers with clarified butter as an oblation, he attains his desired supreme accomplishment.
The Goddess, who bestows the fruit of all accomplishments,
becomes pleased with him who performs the oblation of sesame seeds and rice with clarified butter.
O beautiful goddess, the worlds come under his control;
O lovely one, he should perform the fire-oblation with milk-rice and ghee.
"By performing this for three periods of twilight for just one month, one shall attain mastery over speech.
Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you this first procedure for the sequential fire-offering."
Furthermore, I shall explain specifically regarding the fulfillment of desires:
one should mix beef with honey and perform the fire-oblation (homa) using the left hand.
Even the gods fall under the power of fate, how much more so insignificant humans?
Spittle, tooth-sticks, sweat, and likewise the application of unguents—these too are subject to it.
By performing a fire sacrifice with the name [of the target] joined to the word "name" (*nāma*), one shall bring the three worlds under control.
[One should offer] food mixed with the blood of a menstruating woman that has been vomited up.
O fair-faced one, having performed a fire-oblation with the meat of a ruru deer mixed with clarified butter, one will certainly and immediately draw [the target] along with his human hair.
Whoever performs a fire sacrifice with human flesh mixed with honey attains all accomplishments, even those difficult for the gods to obtain. (97b)
O Goddess, the best of practitioners should recite it one hundred and eight times at the three junctions of the day.
Within six months, there is no doubt that you shall enjoy the entire earth;
with their minds filled with affection, the ḍākinīs will bestow sovereignty upon him.
Such is the detailed explanation.
As for that [point], this [matter] should be investigated in another tantra.
Then, for one year, he remained committed to his vow, subsisting on fruit alone,
being supremely devoted to Viṣṇu and dedicated to the power of Śiva.
One should daily recite the mantra according to one's ability while meditating on the Goddess as described;
furthermore, one should diligently avoid the fruits of the bottle gourd and the pumpkin.
Then, when a year has passed, he becomes equal to the Sun and Antaka in power;
by his capacity he is Viṣṇu, and by his knowledge he is Bṛhaspati.
He is omniscient like the Teacher, radiant as the sun;
he is praiseworthy, virtuous, fortunate, well-born, and wise.
He becomes a hero, always courageous, happy, handsome, and accomplished;
and after one year, his body appears in a divine form.
If there should be any transgression therein, then the Goddess—
who bestows the fruits of all desires— becomes enraged and swiftly slays that man.
Furthermore, I shall proclaim the knowledge that reveals the substances:
now, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, in the darkness at midnight.
Having entered within the house while the ten musical instruments are played,
the best of practitioners should with devotion either recollect or meditate upon the form of the Goddess.
Having brought this one young woman— who goes with five men, who has beautiful teeth, is lovely, well-behaved, and possesses a charming smile— [he said:]
Having given her garments, ornaments, and gold as prescribed,
and having caused her to put on the garment, he, being well-composed, should cast the cloth far away.
Having first drawn the mandala, one should draw a hexagon therein; around it,
one should depict a woman who is shameless and adorned with ornaments.
There, one should seat her naked with her hair disheveled;
O Dear One, one should worship the deities of the limbs as described in the mandala.
There, the best of practitioners, having visualized the Goddess in her form, should worship her with various flowers— white, yellow, and red.
One should recite the mantra a thousand or even ten thousand times with a spirit of devotion,
and there, from the time of dawn until the bath, one should offer the bali-oblation with the mantra.
The practitioner should satisfy that woman with garments, ornaments, and decorations;
he should feed the Brahmins and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru with devotion.
By this method, Lakṣmī shall obtain every science;
and by her glance, a man shall teach even those sciences never seen before.
Even the goddess Lakṣmī would belong to those who are base; what need is there to mention anything else?
Within a single night, one obtains both knowledge and wealth—of this there is no doubt.
Having meditated upon and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Chinnamastā for two nights, the Guru himself should recite her mantra one hundred and eight times;
or he should recite it three hundred times daily, or one thousand and eight times.
O Great Goddess, within six months one's speech shall become composed in prose;
within half a year, one will certainly attain mastery over the scriptures.
After three years have passed, he becomes like another Vāgīśvara;
by the mere sight of him, those who debate are considered to be deprived of their luster.
They flee away to the ground like elephants out of fear of a lion;
[this is done] with a tenth part of the limb-mantras, in accordance with the root-mantra.
"Or one should recite [the mantra] once daily; some say [it should be done] at every session, O Śivā," and so forth, in detail. Om.
The fourth chapter, titled "Worship."
Now,
having first given that [seed-syllable] adorned with the fourth vowel,
one should contemplate Viṣṇu as the moon, mounted upon the letter *ra*, radiant and blazing with light.
Then one should add the letter *takāra*, and the fourth [vowel]...;
thereafter, one should join the letter *hakāra* conjoined with the long *ākāra*.
And then one should utter the syllable *phaṭ*, which completes the perfected mantra.
The letter *ha* is followed by *para*. The fourth vowel is *ī*. The half-moon (*indvarddha*) is the fourth [dot], which is the anusvāra.
The letter *tra* is *tra*. The fourth vowel has been mentioned. Thus, the mantra is *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. That which begins with the seed-syllable of Śrī—its seed is Śrī, who is all...

The seed-syllable beginning with Vāgbhava (Aiṃ) bestows the state of the Lord of Speech; although it is stated here that the mantra is complete only when ending with Phaṭ, nevertheless, because of hearing the praise [beginning with] "Kriyānana... [and so forth], the first three syllables belong to Nīlasarasvatī through the modesty of action.
Thus, from hearing the curse of Vasiṣṭha, the curse culminates when the letter *sa* is removed. For this very reason it has been said:
Sarasvatī, who is ever blue and whose grace toward the worlds is swift,
will especially manifest through my favor in the Kali Yuga.
In this context, although the letter *sa* is not explicitly heard in the tantras, it is obtained through the extraction of the seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhū*),
because the female seed-syllable itself is established as being the bride.
Therefore, it is said in the Muṇḍamālā:
Then the Vidyā is established as having the nature of Tārā and Candra;
Candra is the syllable *sa*, and she who has that as her nature is established as being conjoined with it.
The meaning is that it is beneficial for others. That same [mantra] consists of three syllables; if it ends with *phaṭ*, it is the Ekajaṭā mantra.
That same [mantra], beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with *phaṭ*, is the Tārā mantra. As it has been said:
This great mantra of three syllables, ending with the word *phaṭ*, resides in the heart;
though endowed with five rays of light, it is the burner of the fuel of ignorance.
The syllable Oṃ consists of five rays. As it has been said:
This great vidyā, Jaṭāpuṅgavadhāriṇī, is the end of the weapons;
when her face is joined with the beginning of the Vedas, she is Tārā, the savior from the three worlds.
The syllable Oṃ is the beginning of the Vedas; likewise, it is stated in another Tantra:
The pair of *lajjā* (the seed-syllable of the bride), followed by the long *tanucchada* (the letter *va*),
and then *sārasvata* (the letter *sa*)— this is declared to be the four-syllabled mantra.
The pair of modesties is *hrīṃ hrīṃ*; the seed-syllable of the bride is *strīṃ*; the long tree-foliage is *hūṃ*. Thus, *hrīṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ*.
If the word *phaṭ* follows at the end, it becomes a five-syllabled mantra.
At the end of that, at the end of the four syllables; likewise, the Tāra (Oṃ), Śakti (Hrīṃ), and the Vadhū-bīja (Aiṃ) at the end, followed by the long Tanucchada (Vaṃ), the Astra (Phaṭ),
and Agni (Raṃ) with Vadhū (Aiṃ) at the end— this becomes the seven-syllabled mantra.
Tāra is Oṃ; Śakti is Hrīṃ; Vadhū is Strīṃ; the long Tanucchada is Hūṃ; the Astra-mantra is Phaṭ;
Admi Vadhū is Svāhā. Thus: Oṃ Hrīṃ Strīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā.
Likewise,
the mantra is proclaimed in the scriptures as being enveloped by the long *varman* [syllable];
and the seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhū-bīja*) is likewise encased by the subsequent syllable of qualities (*guṇākṣara*).
Dīrghacarmā is *huṃ*, *madhūbīja* is *strīṃ*; therefore, *hūṃ strīṃ hūṃ*.
Likewise.

If it is independent, the seed-syllable of the consort (*vadhū*) is said here to consist of a single syllable; the consort’s seed-syllable is *strīṃ*. Therefore, [it is] *strīṃ*. Likewise: "The single *tāra* in the lotus, followed by the pair; one should utter [them] in the great lotus."
Padmāvati, ending with two *ṭha*s, having one *jaṭā*, and possessing the color of seven suns;
three *tanta*s, *hūṃ*, the *tāra* (*oṃ*), by that: *vrīṃ vrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ oṃ*. *Padme padme mahāpadme padmāvati svāhā*, two *ṭha*s, *svāhā*.
Likewise, in the Phetkāriṇītantra:
Seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, resplendent like a cluster of moons,
the Daughter of the Mountain questioned him as she sat upon his chest.
"O Īśāna, O Omniscient One, how do those whose wealth is asceticism obtain [this]?
Having acquired what knowledge... did they perform [these deeds] that transcend the Bhārata?
Having heard these words, the Supreme Lord laughed and spoke to the Daughter of the Mountain.
Having abandoned his beloved, he spoke, and she, the virtuous one, cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (sādhu sādhu).
