Listen, O Śakti, to this Great Vidyā which burns away the fuel of worldly attachment;
having obtained it, great-souled beings [attain success] in virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
Nothing whatsoever remains unachievable for poets of pure intellect;
[their power] is such that it can even paralyze the opponent.
Furthermore, by offering oblations (*bali*) to the learned, one causes the loss of knowledge;
and that which is impure, if spoken, leads to the laughter of the assembly members.
Or one should bring even a king who is a disputant under the control of a minister.
By the mere knowledge of the mantra and through its recitation, one shall attain omniscience;
by the simple act of placing it upon the tongue, even a mute shall become a skilled poet.

One’s intellect becomes unimpeded in the scriptures, and one gains victory even over the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), within three days from [consuming] honey. O Garbhaka, the mantra-practitioner should properly place this on the tongue. If he is not already a scholar, he will not fall into foolishness.
Having bowed to Tārā, the savior from the three worlds, according to the Mahācīna-krama...
I shall proclaim the sixfold means; listen, O Omniscient One, to the cause [of liberation].
That is the sequence.
Mental worship is divine; mental visualization and so forth are all auspicious. There is never a time that is inauspicious.

There is no distinction between day and night, nor between twilight and the dead of night; for those entitled to the practice of touch, it matters not whether they are clothed or seated, nor their location, body, or house.
One should not contemplate purification here; rather, the mind should move in a state free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).
One should always worship the Goddess, even without having bathed or eaten.
At midnight, in a very pure location, one should cause the offering to be given with the bali-mantra;
one should not harbor hatred even toward women, and the worship of women is especially important.
Having placed a large conch shell at the place of recitation, one should perform the recitation while moving upward;
even while approaching a woman, touching her, or looking at her, wherever one may be, as long as one has not yet reached the crown of the head.
Edibles such as betel-leaf and other foodstuffs according to one's taste,
as well as meat, fish, curd, honey, milk, vegetables, sugarcane products, and the like.
Having offered all substances, beginning with food, as oblations, one should perform the recitation while consuming them;
for him, there is no restriction regarding the directions and so forth, nor any restriction regarding remaining standing.

In the practice of this great mantra, there is no restriction of time regarding the recitation, nor concerning offerings such as arghya or other oblations; rather, it is said here that one may follow whatever rules accord with one's own inclination.
By that, no unrighteousness arises, and thus dharma becomes great; here,
one should act according to one's own will, moving about with a joyful mind.
Having accomplished his purpose, Viṣṇu was well-pleased with the worship performed using auspicious bilva leaves, meruvaka flowers, and so forth, though devoid of tulasī.
[He bestowed] the threefold knowledge, the Akṣiṇī [mantra], and a single liṅga extending for five krośas.
Or even if a crest-lock (cūḍaka) has fallen or been killed in battle—
having performed the ritual [of cremation] and so forth near it—
one should go to an empty house, a temple devoid of a deity, or an uninhabited interior of a dwelling.
In a temple of the gods, in a place devoid of deities, or in a solitary, secluded dwelling.
Either on Mount Urjara, or in a desolate place, or at a crossroads.

On my soft crown of the head and on other tender spots,
one should achieve supreme accomplishment by resorting to a seat or a cushion.
Likewise:
"A yogi who is perfected through the power of cultivation becomes a great poet;
even if one is dull-witted or a fool, by being intent upon the power of cultivation, [he attains this]."
By reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, one obtains the desired consort.
One should perform this with a steady mind, thinking: "I am not a scholar nor a great poet."
Through the constant practice of cultivation, this will surely come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
With hands, feet, nails, and teeth exceedingly pure, with a mind well-restrained even toward the faults of others, and silent,
he who is devoted to the lotus feet of Hari and Hara becomes for a long time an abode of Sarasvatī.
Manu, having reflected, declared that even for the most excellent son, one's own prowess should be withheld; how much more so for another who is not of one's lineage?
Likewise.
One should always conceal both this mantra and the guru;
for through that, the vidyā becomes potent, whereas it would become powerless through disclosure.
The progenitor, the giver of the Veda, and the teacher of the sacred formulas are venerable;
however, one should always regard the teacher as even more important than one's father.
O dear one, the instruction, the mantra, and likewise the ritual offering must be understood by the wise; for the accomplishment of this mantra comes through greed [for its power].
Whispered recitation is a hundredfold more effective, and mental recitation is a thousandfold;
through the *mālā* of Mahāśaṅkha, perfection was attained without delay.
In the Kubjikā Tantra.
In whatever mantra this conduct is found, that is the Dharma seen as beneficial;

One with a pure mind should worship here; thus there will be accomplishment born of liberation.
By means of specific ritual services, one may bring the king’s wife under control;

101b) Whether it be a blue [mantra] or another [mantra], even if it is placed third, there is nothing whatsoever that causes an obstacle.
When a practitioner who has mastered the mantra applies it to the head and other parts of even a fool, he becomes eloquent;
behold the marvelous power that surpasses even Vācaspati!
And they were neither afraid nor distressed.
Knowledge [elevates] the Brahmin who is self-restrained and a speaker of Brahman;
to him I shall [bestow myself] through proper application.
A wise person should not lead this human prowess of one's own body to another lineage.
[One should practice] the science...
there, the ritual beginning with the morning duties and ending with the Mātṛkā, [should be performed]. Sacrifice...

Having meditated on Māyā, who is of a red color, one should visualize that the semen and the ashes of evil are blown away by the fire born from her; then, one should contemplate [the syllable] upon the forehead.
One should meditate on a tuft of hair with the luster of snow, and that which arises from it as nectar;
having visualized one's own bone covered by that, one should contemplate the Self therein.
"Free from all sins, stainless, and of the nature of the deity," and so forth.
Now, the manual (paddhati). This has been stated in the Tantracūḍāmaṇi:
Having brought water with the mantra *oṃ vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ*, one should worship it;
with the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, one should likewise perform the washing of the feet.
Oṃ hrīṃ sarvaśuddhānte dharmagātri, thereafter [say] sarvapāpāni śamaya, and then utter the remaining words.

*Vikalpā nayā svāhā*. O Dear One, that indeed is the sipping of water (*ācamana*). With that [mantra]: *Oṃ hrīḥ suviśuddhadharmagātri sarvapāpāni śamaya aśeṣavikalpān apanaya svāhā*. *Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—this is the consecration of the ground. *Oṃ dāraya dāraya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

The shatterer of obstacles: *Oṃ pavitraṃ vajrabhūme* (Oṃ, pure vajra ground). *Oṃ phaṭ* at the end is the purification of the ground. Then, one should perform the consecration of the flowers with the mantra: *Oṃ śatābhiṣekeśamaya triyamāśraye tataḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Then: *Oṃ maṇidhari padaṃ tataḥ vaśaṅkarī hūṃ phaṭ*.

*svāhā* is proclaimed as protection. *Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi sarvaśaṅkari hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—this is the binding of the topknot (*śikhā-bandhana*). *Oṃ*, followed by the words *puṣpaketu rājaśabdādarhateti*; after that, at the end of the word *samyak*, the word *saṃyuktāya*; then: *oṃ puṣpe supuṣpe puṣpānte puṣpasambhave*.
From the word "flower" (*puṣpa*): *ca yāvakīrṇe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* at the end is for the offering of flowers.
(102b) *oṃ puṣpaketurājārhate samyaksaṃyuktāya oṃ puṣpa supuṣpa puṣpasambhave*.
*Puṣpatrayāvakīrṇa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus is the consecration of the ground.
Oṃ dāraya dāraya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā—this is for the shattering of obstacles (*vighnadāraṇa*). Oṃ kāmarūpa-pīṭhāya—anena (? ityāṃ (?)—this is the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) with the seat.
Following the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed. As it has been said: at the end of the root [mantra], Oṃ e jaṭā... [etc.]

Thus it has been said: "The seed-mantra *Hūṃ* is the power (*śakti*) belonging to the sage [Atri]; it bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*). [It is joined] with the first letter of the vowels, etc."
Having performed the placement [of mantras] in sequence from the big toe to the tips of the feet, one should likewise perform the placement upon the directions.
Having said, "She whose form is the unbroken Vāg-bīja," she is the beloved of the Fire-god.
Having said "Brahmavāgrūpiṇī," one should [offer] to the three eyes with "Vauṣaṭ. Having said "Rudravāgrūpiṇī," and then "Sarvavāgrūpiṇī," one should perform the six limbs in sequence.

103a) One should perform the placement [of mantras] in sequence as follows: "Hrāṃ, obeisance to the heart of you whose form is the entirety of speech," and so forth. Likewise, having uttered "Ekajaṭā," one should say "Hrāṃ, obeisance to the heart. Hrīṃ.

One should place [the mantra] on the head with "Tāriṇi śirasā svāhā. Having said "Hrūṃ vajrodake," one should also say "śikhāyai vaṣaṭ. Having said "Hraiṃ ugrajaṭe," one should utter "kavacāya hūṃ. Having said "Hrauṃ mahāparisare," one says "netratrayāya vauṣaṭ. And for "Hraḥ piṅgograikajaṭe," [one says] "astrāya phaṭ."
Also "phaṭ. Here, the ritual placement (nyāsa) follows immediately after the root mantra.
Thus it has been said:
"At the end of the root mantra, the heart [mantra] for Ekajaṭā is proclaimed," and so forth.
Likewise, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, one should meditate upon the Goddess.
Then, one should meditate upon a red lotus (*raktabhānam*) arising from the syllable *oṃ* in the intermediate space.
Furthermore, one should meditate upon a vessel of lotuses above that, arising from the syllable *ṭāṃ*. Above that, one should again meditate upon the syllable *hūṃ*, which has the appearance of blue.
Then, one should meditate upon oneself as Tārīṇī, who arises from the syllable HŪṂ, is adorned with the seed-syllable,
and is the transformation of the flaying knife.

She bears a blue lotus that destroys the darkness of ignorance and protects the worlds;

Her armlets were fashioned from a multitude of smoke-colored serpents,

Mounted upon the two feet of a corpse, with her left foot raised upward,

One should employ this yantra, which is joined with the eight vajras, consisting of the vowels in their sequential order and the consonants beginning with 'ka' according to their proper sequence.
Wrapped in yellow cloth and placed upon a square base,

Having thus written [the mantra] three times in sequence within the form of a nine-cornered [figure], one should perform the root-ritual ablution (mūlācamana) and then bind the topknot (śikhābandhana).

Having worshipped the root mantra— which brings about subjugation (*vaśyakarī*), which is the essential nature, and which effects universal purification— with equal offerings of perfumes and flowers, the practitioner [should worship] within the center of the *yantra*.

| Then one should apply it. For him there is a destination, but not for any other here. Oṃ ma oṃ ma, that is the truth.
Having omitted the three seed-syllables from that entire twenty-second syllable [mantra], the name should be employed; thereafter, that very same seed-syllable [should be used].
"Trayam" (the triad) is one mantra; "nāma" (the name) encased by the first seed-syllable is another; likewise, "nāma" encased by two first seed-syllables [is yet another].

Thus says another. Likewise, there is also the method wherein the name is enclosed by two *kūrca* seeds (*hūṃ*). Similarly, there is also the method wherein the name is enclosed by two *māyā* seeds (*hrīṃ*).
Thus, by that fivefold method, there are five mantras. Their worship and so forth are accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, having satisfied the Guru, one should receive the King of Mantras.

The Guru, for his part, should grant it to a disciple of noble birth who is devoted to knowledge and diligent in service; having touched a woman and taken her for himself, he should do so alone at night in a secluded place, in a temple of Śiva, reciting it one hundred thousand times or half that number.

Having recited [the mantra] beginning with *oṃ ma oṃ ma satyam*, there is no other way for success (*siddhi*) to occur than through that which is real (*tatsat*). Here, indeed, whether it be the mantra of Kālikā, Vātārāmanā, Tripurā, or Durgā, the summary is: *āma oṃ tat sat*.
Now I shall describe the internal sacrifice (antaryajana), which bestows both seen and unseen fruits;
the wise practitioner should perform meditation on the Guru as previously instructed.
One should bathe in the pure sacred ford of Puṣkara, which flows from the heart;
or one should bathe in the Bindu-tīrthas, and for such a person, rebirth no longer exists.

"O Iḍā and Suṣumnā, you who carry the auspicious waters of Śiva, full of the water of knowledge, within this body—what need has he who always bathes in those two with the waters of Brahman for the waters of the Gaṅgā or even Puṣkara? Thus ends the section on bathing.
That meditation in which the eternal union of Śiva and Śakti arises is the Sandhyā for those established in the Kula; it is recognized as Samādhi.
Thus concludes the twilight ritual (sandhyā).
Having become the moon, sun, and fire, one who belongs to the family [of the lineage] does not [consume] the supreme nectar;
with that divine nectar, I satisfy the deity of the family.

With the mantra *Hūṃ*, Kuṇḍalinī, who has the form of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, having arisen and pierced the supreme Bindu, should satisfy [the deity] within the *Kula*... this is the supreme vessel. With a mere fraction (*kalā*), one should satisfy the one who moves in the mouth. Thus it is said.
[The mantra] consisting of the nature of the seed-syllable (bindu) and the [deity’s] form, with each syllable beginning from the fixed [syllable] and ending with the seed-syllable;
"Namo... is proclaimed as the internal [mantra].
Drawing in the *iḍā*, this [practitioner]— by means of the heart-mantra and the mantra of his own body,
by means of the mantra of Śiva, and through the teachers— [attains] the form of the heart and the head, [free from] sleep.
113a) Now, as for meditative absorption (dhyāna):
One should meditate on the light, equal to the reality (tattva), situated within the two petals of Śānti and resting upon a pair of lotuses, through the application of Kula and Akula.
Likewise,
the Kulayogins should always meditate upon that which resides between the two Śṛṅgāṭas, enclosed by the two Śaktis, as being in a state of eternal equilibrium (samarasa).
Likewise.
Having brought about the dissolution of the sun and moon situated between the rays and the fire located at its place,
the king of yogis remains full.
Likewise.
Whatever radiance is employed in the supportless, empty state, one should always deposit that within the womb; this is the meditation for those who are detached.
Thus concludes the meditation. Now, the worship.

Whatever object serves as the flower for the *arghya*, one becomes identical with that at that very moment. Since the intellect’s state of identity with that [object] does not endure, one should worship with the thought "I am He" (*so'ham*).
Just as flowers are [the objects] of the senses.
Furthermore, those two eaters are without effort, without egoism, without passion, without pride, and likewise without delusion or intoxication. They are without desire and are again devourers.
The wise know that freedom from envy and greed constitutes a compassionate nature;
non-violence is its supreme flower, as is the restraint of the senses.
Compassion is a flower, forgiveness is a flower, and wisdom is the fifth flower;
thus, one should worship the Supreme Deity with these seven flowers.
Thus ends the worship.
The fifty-fold garland has been proclaimed; the thread consists of Śakti and the essence of Śiva.
Kuṇḍalinī Śakti is the knot, and at the end of the Kalās, there is the abiding on Meru.
Having made the syllable *kṣaṃ* the Mount Meru, one should recite the sequence from *a* to *la* and from *la* to *a*, and then offer it into the supreme splendor.
Now, the fire sacrifice (*homa*): having visualized oneself as undivided, one's own essential nature is the self of the knowledge of the Supreme Self, which is beyond all other selves.
Having meditated upon the navel as being joined with a square, a dot (*cit*), a crescent moon, and a girdle, and adorned with the *yoni* in the form of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*),
one should offer oblations into the fire of knowledge situated in its center. At the end of the root mantra, within the fire in the form of consciousness at the navel,
one should mentally offer the clarified butter of the poison of worldly objects, which is perpetually ignited by the lamp of ignorance, while the mantra serves as the wick.
Hā! With this, one should offer the first oblation.
Then, ending with the root [syllable].
With the mind as the ladle, one should constantly offer the oblations of dharma and adharma into the blazing fire of the self,
by way of the path of Suṣumṇā.
Thus one should offer the second oblation at the end of the root mantra.
Holding the ladle of Unmanī with the hands of Light and Space,
[one offers into] the vessel filled with the oil of the digits of merit and demerit.
One should offer the third oblation.
At the end of the root [mantra].
In this inner fire, which blazes without external fuel, I offer as oblations the entire universe— from the earth up to Śiva— in order to consume the darkness of delusion.
Having thus performed the internal sacrifice, one becomes directly composed of Brahman;
indeed, one certainly becomes free from both sin and merit.
Now, regarding Gāyatrī in the Kumārītantra:
The word "kālikāyai" is declared, followed by "vidmahe";
thereafter, one should say "śmaśānavāsinī mahī."
Having uttered "Tanno Ghorapadam," one should recite "Pracodayāt. Therefore: "We know Kālikā, we meditate upon her; may she impel us toward the Terrible (Ghora)."
By the mere remembrance of her, millions of great sins truly come to an end for the practitioner;
it is not otherwise.
114a) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
which directly bestows all accomplishments and destroys even the greatest sins.
By the gods for the sake of divinity, by the *siddhas* for the sake of attaining power,
by the *pannagas*, *rākṣasas*, mortals, and by the *munis* desiring liberation.
I shall always explain the goddess known as Dakṣiṇā according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise.
His speech, consisting of both prose and verse, arises in the assembly;
by the mere sight of him, the disputants are considered shorn of their luster.
Even kings fall into servitude; what then of other people?
[Who could achieve] the freezing of fire, the solidification of water, or the stopping of the sun’s motion?
By means of this, one becomes a master who can instantly reverse day and night;
indeed, he shall become beloved by all people here and increase his fame.
And at the end, he attains the state of being a Gaṇa of the Goddess, which is difficult for men to obtain;
having become as radiant as the moon and sun, he shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas.
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and likewise sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached—
all these become auspicious indeed for one who contemplates only the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

In speech he shall be equal to Vāgīśa (the Lord of Speech), in wealth he shall become a lord of riches like Kubera, among women he shall be equal to Kāma, and toward his enemies he shall be like Yama.
"All this comes about quickly through the binding of the *yoni-mudrā*; such things have been stated. What else, moreover, shall be told?"
Nothing is difficult to obtain for him who should remember Ghoradakṣiṇā.
Then, having completed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with the *mātṛkā* [nyāsa], one should perform the *ṛṣi*-vidyā-deity placement (*nyāsa*).
This has been stated in the Kālikopaniṣads:
Bhairava is its seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh its metre (chandas), Kālikā its deity (devatā), *klīṃ* its seed-syllable (*bīja*),
*hūṃ* its power (*śakti*), and *hrīṃ* its pin (*kīlaka*); its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of poetic composition.

"Having known the seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), and deity (daivata) of this mantra, [one attains] the fruit of the mantra," and so forth. For this mantra: Bhairava is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, Dakṣiṇakālikā is the deity, *krīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *kūṃ* is the power (*śakti*), *krīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the recitation (*japa*) regarding the stated purpose, with Aniruddha-Sarasvatī as the witness. Having thus recollected—
Having performed the placement [of mantras] on the head, face, and heart, one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa). As it has been said:

The practitioner of mantra should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the first letters of the six groups of consonants, joined with the long vowels and the fire-seed (*ra*) and the dot (*bindu*), either three times or once, as is appropriate.

The first letter of the first class is *ka*; joined with the six long vowels and the fire (*ra*), it becomes *kṛ*. With the nasal dot (*bindu*) following, one should perform the placement either three times or once, in sequence starting with "to the Heart, *namaḥ*," and so forth, extending from the thumb to the little finger for the heart and the other [limbs].

Likewise: even though [the purification] is threefold, the knower of mantras, being most excellent, should perform it seven times at the root with the mantra; thus the entire [rite] becomes purified. Then, one should meditate upon the Goddess Dakṣiṇā, who possesses the form as previously described, when she is [manifested] as Karālā... [and so forth].
One should meditate upon the divine Cāmuṇḍā of the south, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
her lotus-like hands holding a freshly decapitated head and a sword in the upper left and lower right respectively.
She has the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*) and holds a water-pot (*darvī*) in her right hand;
she possesses the luster of a great cloud, is dark-complexioned, and likewise naked.
Her neck was powerless, her garland of severed heads was smeared with dripping blood,
and she was terrifying with two arrows resting upon her shoulders as ear-ornaments.
She has terrible fangs and a gaping mouth, with full and elevated breasts;
she wears a girdle made from a multitude of corpses and has a smiling face.
Her face is made radiant by streams of blood flowing from her two corners of the mouth;
she is of terrible form, exceedingly fierce, and dwells in the cremation ground.
Thus, whoever should meditate upon the Goddess, the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires.
In his hand there is always every accomplishment, without a doubt;
[he holds] her who resides upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse.
She was surrounded on all four sides by auspicious jackals of terrifying howls,
and together with Mahākāla, she was intent upon the ecstasy of inverted union.
Having thus meditated upon her with a serene face and a smiling lotus-like countenance, and having worshipped her with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the *argha* vessel.
Then, having placed the yantra before him, he should cause it to move. As for the yantra:
One should first draw a triangle, and then another triangle;
one should place a nine-cornered figure there and install Śivā in its center.
The meaning is that the leaf consists of fifteen [syllables] in this manner.

According to the view of some, it is a nine-cornered [figure] situated within a hexagon; according to the view of others, it is so because of the location of its beautiful form through the differentiation of the mantra-sentences consisting of five types.
It should be understood that both [the mantra and the yantra] possess authoritative validity. Thus, having placed the yantra before oneself,

meditated upon it in the form described, invoked it with the root mantra, displayed the gestures (mudrās) such as invocation, and offered water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings with the root mantra, one should worship within the fifteen-cornered [mandala] in a counter-clockwise direction.
The wise practitioner should likewise place Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, Virodhinī,
and Vipracittā outside upon the hexagon.
One should place Ugrā, who is fierce, of fierce luster, and blazing, in another triangle;
likewise, one should place Nīlānghana and Valākā in yet another triangle.
One should place Mātrā, Mudrā, and Mitra within another triangle;
all of them are dark-complexioned, sword-bearing, and adorned with garlands of skulls.
115b) Holding a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) in their left hands and smiling,
one should worship them in sequence with "Oṃ, homage to Kālī," and so forth, having first gone outside and then [proceeding] to the inner periphery.
Likewise:
Outside the mandala, one should likewise [worship] Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Māheśvarī,
Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, and Aparājitā.
And having likewise worshipped Vārāhī immediately thereafter,
an offering (bali) as well as worship must indeed be given to all of them.
And even unguents should be prepared according to one's means;
a woman should always be honored with every kind of worship.

Then, having placed flowers, sandalwood paste, and so forth upon the head of the Goddess, having offered the food oblation (*naivedya*) and other offerings, and having gratified her three times, one should likewise [gratify] Mahākāla; then, having recited the mantra as much as possible and offered the recitation (*japa*), one should maintain [the state]. As it has been said:
Having worshipped with great effort,
one should offer [the oblation] and, having duly entrusted it once more into the heart and the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), it should be held by the wise in the southwest,
in a pure place.
Because of such [scriptural] observations as these.
Now, the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
The practitioner of mantras, pure and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
likewise, even while impure both by day and night, he should recite it one hundred thousand times.

The practitioner of mantra should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part [of the recitation], as well as the libation (tarpaṇa) and the consecration (abhiṣecana); the procedure for both the homa and the tarpaṇa is said to be the same as that for the worship (pūjā).
Having thus worshipped the Goddess, who burns away impurities, according to the rules, and having likewise offered the *bali* oblation,
some say that there is no fixed measure for the construction of the *yantra*, such as the eight-petalled lotus and so forth. Regarding this, another text states:
Because it is seen.
Thus it is stated in the Kālikopaniṣads: "A triangle, another triangle, a nine-cornered figure, and a lotus; having worshipped the Goddess therein with all her limbs," and so forth.

Thus, some maintain that the *puraścaraṇa* consists of exactly two hundred thousand [recitations]. In reality, however, the *puraścaraṇa* consists of only one hundred thousand. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kālikopaniṣads*:

In this way, one should repeat the King of Mantras one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*). This is because it is seen [in scripture] that "one crosses over all evil," and so forth. As for what was stated regarding two hundred thousand repetitions, the intention is that this is for the sake of a superior fruit due to a difference in context. For this very reason, it is said in the Upaniṣads after describing [the fruit of] one hundred thousand: "Then, indeed, he who recites this Kālikā-mantra..."

Like a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) who is naked at night, he is always incapable of sexual intercourse; being disciplined, he performs recitation, worship, and so forth, and offers libations with the water from the female organ (*bhagodaka*), and so on.
Now follow the rites for the fulfillment of specific desires.
Having meditated upon her who has a serpent as her sacred thread, whose remaining hair is fashioned into a crescent moon, who wears a mass of matted locks, and who stands near Mahākāla.
The *kūrca* mantra is *hrīṃ*, and likewise the pair of seeds at the end;
having thus meditated upon the Goddess, one should worship her with red flowers.
Driven by desire and overwhelmed, women emerge in a state of agitation;
abandoning each their own husbands, they embrace him as if he were a deity.

The meaning of "ante tathaiva" (likewise at the end) is that one should write the seed-syllables at the end of the phrase "dakṣiṇakālike. Having meditated upon the first [goddess] as red, holding a trident in her hand, and the other as bearing a single trident and stationed within Mahākāla, [one should worship] with yellow flowers.
Having worshipped each one individually at the beginning, one should likewise join them at the end within that very tantra;
[and also] the Lord of the Netherworld and the Winged One.
He shall become the most excellent among all possessors of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
A man should mutter ten thousand recitations while beholding the vulva of a woman in her menses;
even if it is meaningless, his speech shall become composed of both prose and verse.
From his mouth there issues speech that further enhances poetic meter;
and it should be recited during sexual union for the sake of liberation from great sins.
Likewise, for the sake of acquiring wealth or for union with another's wife—
if there is no sexual intercourse with a woman, then one should carefully discharge the semen.
Then, having cast it aside for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims,
one should go to a cremation ground with disheveled hair and naked.
One should recite it ten thousand times for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals;
there, having mounted a corpse, the best of mantra-knowers should perform the recitation.
Having practiced sexual union ten thousand times, one who is devoted to the Supreme Being attains the supreme perfection, which is very difficult even for the goddesses to obtain.
Attraction, subjugation, binding, eradication, and so forth;
likewise, paralyzing, deluding, terrifying, and causing diminution.
Having attained eloquence, wealth, many sons, great popularity,
and being beloved by all;
He indeed attains the power of moving through the sky and even divinity;
for him there is neither old age, nor disease, nor death, nor even dissolution.
There is no joy through mere humanity, nor is there the downfall of speech and body;
rather, he shall eternally be endowed with the twenty-four accomplishments.
Having worshipped the Goddess in a cremation ground a thousand times with *vilva* leaves smeared with the blood of one's own body, one shall attain equality with the Lord of Speech (*Vāgīśa*).
Having worshipped the Goddess here thousands of times with a vessel joined with mercury,
and having worshipped the Goddess in the cremation ground, he attains all supernatural accomplishments (siddhis).
One shall become wealthy, powerful, eloquent, and beloved by all women;
one shall be happy, of this there is no doubt, just as [is taught] in the Mahākālavaca.
Cemetery (śmaśāna) [text unreadable] (118a)
By that, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) would be as honored as ten thousand ages.
All success shall be his; he becomes eloquent and a hero.
There is nothing on earth that is difficult for him to obtain, if it even exists.
Having fashioned the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the shape of a womb (yoni), measuring one span (vitasti) in depth,
and likewise extending one cubit (hasta) in width, one should also prepare it similarly below.
In that regard, the ritual action of establishing the fire within the mantra must indeed be performed;
one should first offer an oblation to the deity Mahākāla.
Surely [one succeeds] with meat, with food, with blood,
and especially with an *argha* offering of black flowers and one's own blood.
One who delights in material offerings should likewise offer oblations in a cremation ground,
having bathed, wearing white garments, pure, and with a restrained mind.
This should indeed be performed during the day for the sake of accomplishing all desires;
at night, one remains naked with disheveled hair, engaged in sexual intercourse.
For all the twice-born, two kinds [of observances] are prescribed here;
for all the Śūdras as well, there is the great vow (mahāvrata) both by day and by night.
Such is the summary.
Now, the mantra of Bhadrakālī, according to the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
Having extracted the seed-syllable *prāsādanī*, one should utter the word *kālī*. Then, having spoken the word *mahākālī*, [one should utter] the pair *kili* thereafter.
This great mantra of Bhadrakālī consists of *phaṭ* at the end and *agnipriyā* (svāhā) at the end;
its seed-syllable of grace is *hauṃ*, followed by *agnipriyā* (*svāhā*). Thus: *hauṃ kālimahākāli kili kili phaṭ svāhā*. Likewise:
Having propitiated [the deity], one should daily recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
likewise, the garland of beads should be arranged with one hundred and eight strings.
One should meditate upon that Great Goddess Bhadrakālī, the remover of fear,
whose hollows are filled with hunger and desire.
Keśī is indeed Dantī; I am not [she]. Sudantī makes this entire world her single morsel while sleeping.
Bhakālī... Prayāga is here...
the Goddess, the Great Goddess, who causes the destruction of enemies. As desired...

The Goddess, through meditation, bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and liberation; this is the summary, as no further distinction is stated here. [Regarding] the garland of the moon, the garland of human bones, the consumption [of substances], and so forth, it is likewise... [as before].
Now follows the mantra of Mahākālī from the Phetkāriṇītantra.

Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the great mantra of Mahākālī. It consists of the syllable *pra* joined with the fire-syllable (*ra*), conjoined with the *nāda* and *bindu*, and likewise the two *kroḍha*s again.
Take the animal (paśu) from the feet; the armor (varma) and weapon (astra) are the beloved of fire (anala-vallabhā), which consists of fourteen syllables.

* * Rudhira is the letter *ra*; Ūrdhvakeśī is the letter *e*. Thus: *phreṃ phreṃ*, two *krodhas* (*hūṃ hūṃ*), armor (*hūṃ*), weapon (*phaṭ*), and the beloved of fire (*svāhā*). The fixed syllable is *oṃ*. Thus: *oṃ phreṃ phreṃ*.
HŪM HŪM! Seize the sacrificial victim! HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ!

Likewise, there is no need for further deliberation here regarding the ritual placements (*nyāsa*), purifications, the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*), and so forth. Then, one should [worship] Kālikā in a black pitcher completely filled with black water.
Having worshipped with devotion in the various directions, endowed with the splendors of Brahmā and the other [deities], and so forth.

In this context, although the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth have not been written down, they should be performed as extracted from the general chapter, according to what was stated for the mantra of Dakṣiṇakālī; or else, because of that specific context, it refers to the supreme praise. Alternatively, there is a prohibition against specific *nyāsa* and the like.
Now, meditation.
She has five faces, is exceedingly fierce, and possesses three eyes in each face;
she holds a spear, a trident, a bow, an arrow, a sword, a shield, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, adorned with sixty-four arms and causing her enemies to flee,
the practitioner shall accomplish whatever he desires in his mind.
From the east up to the northeast, the second [set] is situated within the parts of the jars;
by this it is meant that one should worship the powers (śaktis), beginning with Brāhmī, from the east up to the northeast.
Likewise, one should then place Kālī, the great destroyer, upon the pericarp;
when the city of fire has been kindled and restrained by the syllables of her name.
Being pure, one should likewise offer oblations while reciting the mantra of the Goddess;
the fuel-sticks should be of *picumarda*, and the wood for the fire-drill should be of *vibhītaka*.
Through the homa of yellow virājikā, a bodice, lac, a long necklace, house-soot,
charnel-ground bone, and vibhītaka charcoal, [the desired result is attained].
Through the yoga of the Kālikā mantra, one slays an enemy within seven days;
likewise, expulsion is accomplished at midday, and killing at twilight.
Facing south from the edge of the village situated in the southern direction, and so forth.

Vicumarda, nimba, vibhītakatvaca, amṛtā, and gṛhadhūma—this is known as *soma*. Here too, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is as before; the summary is that there are eight thousand [recitations], since no specific number has been mentioned.
In this *Nigamasāranirṇaya* composed by Śrī Ramāramaṇadevaśarman,
this chapter concerning the ritual procedure, worship, and meditation on the mantra of Kālikā is concluded.
